# “Automate everything that can be”: counting showed 66 repair jobs had never run on a schedule, and I added only six

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/automate-sorted/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / August 2026

  On my app Toreca Dash the instruction was: “automate everything that can be automated”.

  On 28 August 2026, the first thing I did was count. 66 repair processes had never once been called from a schedule. This article records how I counted, and why I did not put all 66 on a schedule.

  Numbers come from my work log of 28 August 2026.

## Counted: 66 only worked if you hit the URL by hand

  I matched 319 HTTP endpoints against 184 scheduled jobs by function calls, not by name, because something with a different name can still be called from a scheduled job.

  The result: 66 only ran if someone hit the URL by hand. Articles that could be fixed stay broken until a person remembers “time to run that”.

## I did not schedule all 66 at once

  The 66 fell into three groups:

- Needed continuously (needed whenever new data arrives) → put on a schedule.

- One-off migrations (backfill*, reclassify* and so on) → do not schedule. Running them daily is wasted work and only adds room for accidents.

- Destructive or needing human judgement (deleting orphaned products, manual re-linking) → do not schedule.

  A new scheduled job runs once the moment it is deployed. Before adding any, I rehearsed all of them with a dry run (no writes) to see what they would hit.

## The six I added

    Job | Dry-run result

      Fix empty deadlines on X articles | 32 targets, 0 updated

      Fix aggregator-derived store names | 5 (an account’s promotional text had become the seller)

      Fix shipping fees counted in the price | 0

      Fix links to generic products | 0

      Fix titles of split articles | newly built

      Fix aggregator-derived deadlines | newly built

  I spread their start times. Running them together fights for concurrency slots and lengthens the queue. Scheduled jobs went from 184 to 190.

  The remaining candidates (deadline repair, broken product-image repair, Rakuten affiliate-link repair) take over 2 minutes and their dry runs did not finish in time, so I held back. I do not add one without checking it.

## The product catalogue was already fully automatic

  To “can the product catalogue be automated too?” the answer was “it already is”. All 15 genres had an import from the official catalogue, updated an hour earlier. Linking articles to products is automatic: 1,406 of 1,415 measured were linked. The rest were “new sets not yet on the official site”, which come in automatically once the official site lists them.

## The queue kept growing

  Counting also turned up another thing. The queue length was growing 81, 86, 91 within 45 seconds.

  The cause: the function that adds jobs (enqueue) only checked “is it running”, and did not check jobs already waiting in the queue. While the concurrency limit was reached, the time for a “every minute” job kept coming, and the same job piled up many times.

  I made it remember the names of waiting jobs and not add them twice. The queue stayed at 0.

## What I learned

> Automation is not putting everything on a schedule. Count, sort, check, then add.

- Count first. 66 had never been called. Match by calls, not names.

- Sort. Add only what is needed continuously; not one-off migrations or destructive jobs.

- Check with a dry run before adding. A new scheduled job runs the moment it is added.

- Spread the times. Running together lengthens the queue.

- Before queueing, check “is it waiting” too. Checking only “running” lets it pile up.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/automate-sorted/).

# “The server went down and I cannot recover it” was wrong: only inbound SSH had been blocked

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/misdiagnosis-down/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / August 2026

  My app Toreca Dash’s server became unreachable from 3:10 a.m. on 28 August 2026. I wrote in my notes: “the server went down; I cannot recover it from here”.

  That judgement was wrong. I only learned that when it came back at 10:15. This article is the record of why I was wrong and what the work I did in between produced.

  Written from my work log of 28 August 2026.

## What I saw, and what I concluded

- Ports 22 (SSH), 80 and 443 of the server were all closed.

- A traceroute reached a carrier backbone in Singapore and stopped just past it.

- The hosting provider’s (Hetzner) status page showed no incident for that region.

  From that I concluded: “the server has stopped, and I cannot recover it from here (it needs a restart in the provider’s console)”.

## What was true: the server had been running all along

  When it became reachable at 10:15 and I checked:

    What I checked | Result

      Server processes | had been running all along (uptime 7 days 10 hours)

      Jobs completed | 4,100

      192 scheduled jobs | kept running normally

      What was blocked | only inbound SSH

  The server had not stopped. Only connections from outside (SSH) were blocked. Nothing behind the app had stopped.

## A second mistake: the “pile of repairs” was made by me

  Meanwhile I also noticed “41 hourly repairs have piled up” and blamed that on the server too.

  In fact I had created it: I called an endpoint that does not accept a dry run (a no-write rehearsal), thinking it was a check. What I took as a check ran production work 41 times.

## The alternative route: deploy only what I needed elsewhere

  Because I could not get into the server, I deployed just the checks and repairs I needed to Cloud Functions, individually (firebase deploy --only functions:name). I did not touch any scheduled jobs. Those HTTP endpoints stay after the server comes back and can be used for checks as they are.

  I also noted what to do after recovery: first, send the day’s changes to the server. That day I had added 8 scheduled jobs, so they would run as catch-ups right after deploy. All had been run by hand from dry run through real run, so running them does no harm.

## What I learned

> “Cannot connect” is not “stopped”.

- Do not conclude from one angle. Ports can be closed while the process keeps running.

- Look at other signals. Are notifications arriving, is data being updated, what is the app’s state? Some things are visible from outside.

- Before writing “cannot recover”, write how much you actually know. All I knew was “SSH does not connect”.

- Do not run production while “checking”. An entrance with no dry run cannot be rehearsed.

- Keep an alternative route for when you cannot get in. A place where I could deploy individual functions helped.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/misdiagnosis-down/).

# “ヤマダ電機” versus “ヤマダデンキ”: spelling variants and duplicates had three overlapping causes

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/store-name-variants/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / August 2026

  In my app Toreca Dash, the same store’s name was written differently, such as “ヤマダ電機” and “ヤマダデンキ” (both Yamada Denki). Two reports came: “spellings vary” and “articles are duplicated for the same reason”. The instruction was: “make sure it does not happen for other stores either, thoroughly”.

  This article records that three causes overlapped, and the process of fixing with a general rule instead of a synonym table.

  Written from my work log of 25 August 2026.

## Three causes overlapped

- Store names were compared only by “contains”. The two Yamada spellings contain neither one another, so they were different stores.

- Deadlines were compared to the millisecond. The same “until 26 Aug” was 23:59:00 from the aggregator and 23:59:59 from X, a 59-second difference that stopped them being seen as duplicates. Four real products were like this.

- The dedupe job was manual-only and had never run automatically. Even if I make it as a “one-off repair”, articles arrive daily, so duplicates are born daily.

## The fix: no synonym table

  I made a comparison key (storeNameComparisonKey). It drops corporate forms, symbols, spaces and full/half-width, turns katakana into hiragana, and unifies “電機 / 電器 / でんき”.

  I do not make a table of store-name synonyms. It would recur whenever a new store appears. I made a general rule that unifies different writings that sound the same.

- Deadlines are compared as dates (Japan-time dates) and I require the same sale type instead. Even on the same day, first-come and lottery are different cases.

- Articles that have no store name (sellerName) and only a store name in the category are included. Aggregator and official-site articles are mostly like that, and I had overlooked them wholesale.

- When hiding as a duplicate, always set the hidden mark (hiddenByDuplicate).

- I added an hourly scheduled run.

- The spelling itself is also pulled to the majority of real data. I keep no list of correct spellings. On a tie, katakana wins, then string order, so the answer does not change at each run and cause a rewrite war.

## Two dangers found in testing

  Both found by tests after the fix.

- If you key only on the part before “＠”, a store whose name itself contains ＠ gets an extremely short key. “Card Shop ＠ Home. Kagoshima” would become a key like “card shop” and be equated with other stores. The comparison key does not cut at ＠. (Names with an advertising tail are caught by the contains test.)

- If “one is the beginning of the other means the same name”, branch names disappear. “Yellow Submarine” and “Yellow Submarine Akihabara” would merge and lose the branch. I treat them as the same only when the addition begins with a note marker such as “＠”, “【” or “（”.

  I checked 17 real patterns and found 0 mismatches.

## Result

     | Before | After

      Store-name spelling variants | 2 | 0

      Duplicates with same product, deadline and store | 7 groups | 0 groups

  As a bonus, 23 store names with an advertising tail like “○○ ＠ staff wanted” were unified too. When there are duplicates, the one kept is the one with a price and a result-announcement date.

## What I learned

> Fix with a general rule, not a list; and run the fixing job automatically.

- Do not compare only by “contains”. Different writings do not contain each other.

- Do not compare to the millisecond. Compare by date and sale type.

- A “one-off repair” is not enough for what is born daily. Run it automatically, regularly.

- A synonym table recurs with new stores. Use a general rule for same-sounding writings.

- Merge only notes. Never erase a branch name.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/store-name-variants/).

  More in English

- Toreca Dash (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/torecadash/)

# “One page = one case” was false: articles of a shop taking 6 products on one form were hidden just for sharing a link

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/one-page-many-cases/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / August 2026

  My app Toreca Dash twice received the report “several products are accepted, yet there is only one article”. I thought I fixed it the first time, but the second report came.

  This article records the real cause, and a story from the same period: a field I created that the app never read.

  Written from my work log of 25 August 2026.

## The real cause: duplicates decided by link alone

  After the first report I had fixed it as far as “they are treated as duplicates because the link is the same”. But existing articles stayed hidden, so I got the same complaint again.

  The culprit was runHideDuplicateLinkArticles, a job that judges duplicates by link alone.

  The real data: one mail-order shop takes lotteries for 6 products on a single Google Form. All 6 articles have the same URL. The job hid 5 of them as “duplicates”, so users saw only one product.

  The fix: change the grouping unit from link to link + product. The same link with a different product is a different case. For articles whose product is unknown, there is nothing to tell them apart, so they are treated as duplicates by link alone as before.

  “One page = one case” does not hold for card lotteries. Stores that accept several products on one form or one announcement page are common.

  I restored the articles that had been hidden as link-only duplicates, only those whose product or title differs from a displayed article with the same link (7 articles): 5 from the mail-order shop (all 6 products now show), 1 from a large game store and 1 from another chain.

## The server created “entry tiers”, and the app never read them

  Since 23 August the server had been reading entry conditions with an AI and extracting entry tiers (entryTiers): “Players Club: identity-verified tier versus unverified tier”, “Group A and Group B”, “Bic Camera Suica card members only”. They were in the real data.

  But the iOS app never read this field. I was paying for the AI and users could not see it. I added the field to the app and show it in the detail screen as “Entry tiers”.

  You can find such server/app mismatches mechanically: extract the fields the app reads from the source (grep) and compare them with Firestore’s real data.

## Announcement text had got into the product list

  Event notices such as “ONE PIECE Card Game corner [advance entry / lottery] Monday 31 August, JUMP SHOP Tokyo Station” had been registered as products.

  A list of phrases cannot keep up, so I rejected them with a general rule: a concrete date. A trading-card product name does not contain a calendar date like “31 August”. “Vol.3”, “Set 2” and “2025 issue 19” are not dates and are unaffected. I tested 10 patterns with 0 mismatches and deleted the 6 existing ones.

## What I learned

> Doubt the premise. Check that what you built is used.

- Do not assume “one page = one case”. Stores accepting several products on one form are common.

- After fixing, look at existing articles. Fixing the entrance does not bring hidden articles back.

- Cross-check the fields the server makes and the app reads. You can pay the cost and users still see nothing.

- A general rule beats a list of phrases. “A concrete date means it is not a product name.”

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/one-page-many-cases/).

- Toreca Dash (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/torecadash/)

# English and katakana names share no characters: a fingerprint gate rejected 42 correct matches

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/transliteration-gate/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / August 2026

  My app Toreca Dash fetches each product’s market price from a site with real trading records and shows it next to the official price. But the health check said:

  Market-price link rate dropped: 177 / 449 (39%)
  I could have written it off as “new sets are not on that site yet”. But when I searched that site, the products were there. This is the real reason and the fix.

  Written from my work log of 24 August 2026.

## The products were on the market-price site

  Mine     Expansion Pack "30th CELEBRATION"
Market   Pokémon Card Game MEGA Expansion Pack "30th Anniversary Celebration" Box (exists)

Mine     QUARTER CENTURY TRINITY BOX
Market   Yu-Gi-Oh! OCG Duel Monsters Quarter Century Trinity Box (in katakana; exists)

Mine     Start Deck Blue Kuzan [ST-33]
Market   One Piece Card Game Start Deck "Blue Kuzan" (exists)

## The cause: a fingerprint check that structurally cannot match

  This match re-checks the AI’s chosen candidate in code too, with whether the products’ proper-name tokens really overlap (a fingerprint check, productNamesShareFingerprint). I had added it on 8 August as a defence against the data corruption of merging unrelated products, and it is itself correct.

  But for this market-price match alone, the comparison structurally cannot succeed. My product names are the maker’s official English names, and the market site’s are often in katakana, so no character is shared.

  In the real log (26 hours), 42 candidates were rejected as “fingerprint mismatch”. Looking inside, most were correct matches.

    Mine | Market site

      PHOTON HYPERNOVA | Photon Hypernova Box (katakana)

      CHAOS IMPACT | Chaos Impact Box (katakana)

      ROMANCE DAWN [OP-01] | Booster Pack Romance Dawn Box (katakana)

      RAGE OF THE ABYSS | Rage of the Abyss Box (katakana)

      Expansion Pack “30th CELEBRATION” | Expansion Pack “30th Anniversary Celebration” Box

  And one of those 42 was the very product from report [111] “the market price is too cheap, suspicious” (30th CELEBRATION). I had earlier fixed “lottery prices mixed into the market price”, but a deeper cause remained: it had never been linked to the real market price at all.

## The fix: do not weaken the fingerprint; add a second, narrow judgement for this match only

  Loosening the fingerprint check would loosen its other uses too (registering aliases, merging duplicates) and the original corruption would return. I never weaken it.

  Instead, only for candidates the market match rejected on fingerprint, I added a second judgement on one point: “is this the English and katakana forms of the same proper name?” (snkrdunkNamesAreTransliterationMatch).

- Candidates with conflicting product codes are rejected without asking the AI. (OP-01 vs OP-17, however similar they sound.)

- The AI answers only “do they correspond in sound?”, and if unsure, always false. A language difference such as “English version” counts as a different product.

- Everything passed is logged (“confirmed as an English/katakana spelling variant”) so it can be checked later on real data.

## Check on real data: dry run first

  A “not found” verdict has a 7-day cooldown. Only for the 148 products with displayed articles, I lifted the wait and had them judged again. It is a bulk rewrite, so I checked the count with a dry run before running it.

## What I learned

> A correct gate can structurally reject correct matches. Do not weaken the gate; add a narrow second judgement.

- Do not write it off as “can’t be helped”; actually look. The products were there.

- Count a gate’s rejections and read them. Most of 42 were correct matches.

- Do not weaken the gate. Its other defences would fall too.

- Add a narrow second judgement. Reject code conflicts without the AI; allow the AI to say false when unsure.

- Log what passes. You can verify it later on real data.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/transliteration-gate/).

  More in English

- Toreca Dash (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/torecadash/)

# Looking up an ambiguous store name returns Shizuoka, the middle of Japan: I judged by Google’s own answer, not a list of chains

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/geocode-shizuoka/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / August 2026

  My app Toreca Dash shows store locations on a map and sorts by distance. A report said “the location shows Shizuoka”. Store locations come from passing the store name to Google’s place search (Places API).

  The cause: when you query with an ambiguous store name, Google returns the middle of Japan (Shizuoka and Aichi). This article records the measurement and the fix of not listing chain names.

  Written from my work log of 25 August 2026.

## Measured: the answer to an ambiguous name is Shizuoka or Aichi

  I pass a rectangle covering all of Japan as a location hint (locationbias). With an ambiguous name and nothing to decide by, Google returns the middle of that rectangle, which is Shizuoka and Aichi. I measured it with the API.

    Query | Google’s answer

      Yamada Denki | Yamada Denki Tecc Land Hamamatsu (Shizuoka)

      San-A | San-A Kaken, Kakegawa Factory (Shizuoka)

      Hobby Station | Toreca Station Toyohashi (Aichi)

      Book Off | BOOKOFF Kakegawa (Shizuoka)

      Hareruya | Hareruya Shizuoka (Shizuoka)

      Omusubi | a rice-ball shop in Hamamatsu (Shizuoka)

  “San-A” meant a retail chain, but the answer was a different company’s factory with a similar name.

## The fix: judge by Google’s own answer, not a list of chain names

  I did not make a “list of ambiguous chain names”. It would recur whenever a new chain appears. Instead I wrote a function (geocodeMatchIsTrustworthy) that judges from Google’s own answer.

- If the queried name is only the head of the returned name and the rest is a branch name, reject. (Yamada Denki → …Tecc Land Hamamatsu.) If only “store” was added, it is the same shop.

- If the name has a branch hint (“… store”, hall, mall…), accept as before.

- If the returned name equals the queried name or is a part of it, accept. Do not accept the reverse. (San-A ⊂ San-A Kaken is a different company.)

- Otherwise, judge by whether the name and address share 2 or more characters. (Stores with Ikebukuro, Totsuka, Sapporo or Takadanobaba in the name pass here.)

  On 25 real patterns, all 9 wrong ones were rejected and all 16 correct ones accepted. The only miss was one written in Roman letters.

  I cleared the 30 articles with a wrong location baked in and 22 store cache entries, and resolved them again. Clearing the cache costs one API call per store.

## A similar story the same day: the notification’s store name was “LivePocket”

  A report said “the notification’s store name is LivePocket”. When no store name could be found, the category (“LivePocket”) was used as the last fallback. LivePocket is a place that takes applications, not a store. So when unknown, return null. The caller uses the article title if there is no store name. LivePocket titles begin with the store name, like “Kiddy Land LaLaport Fujimi store …”, which says it more correctly.

## What I learned

> Check an external answer for trustworthiness using the answer itself.

- With nothing to decide by, an external service returns a plausible answer. The middle of Japan: Shizuoka and Aichi.

- Do not make a list of chain names. It recurs when a new chain appears.

- Do not accept the reverse containment. San-A is not part of San-A Kaken.

- Clear baked-in values and resolve again. The cache too.

- When unknown, null. No name is better than a wrong one.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/geocode-shizuoka/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

- Toreca Dash (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/torecadash/)

URL: https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/swallowed-failure/

# If you throw failure away, the screen lies: a calendar that said “registered” with none added, a frozen OCR, a notification without a store name

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/swallowed-failure/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / August 2026

  In developing my app Toreca Dash, bugs of one kind appeared in a row: failures I had swallowed made the app show a false success. This article records three.

  Written from my work log of 25 August 2026.

## 1. “Registered N events” while none reached the calendar

  The app can export lottery deadlines to the iPhone calendar. A build warning (result of 'try?' is unused) led me to review it. try? is a Swift way of discarding a failure. The feature called save with try? store.save(...) and try? store.commit(), throwing failures away.

  As a result:

- Nothing reached the calendar, yet it said “Registered N events”.

- Only the “exported” record remained.

- Pressing again said “no new items to register”, so they could never be registered.

  The fix: return failures to the caller and count only successes. Devices with no default calendar are detected first and told. The messages are split by cause; before, every failure said “access is not allowed”.

## 2. When text recognition fails, the screen freezes

  The feature that reads text from an application image (OCR) also discarded failure with try? handler.perform([request]). If recognition failed, the callback was never called. The “reading…” spinner never stopped, and the only way out was to close the screen.

  The fix: on failure too, return to a “finished recognising (found nothing)” state.

  The build warning result of 'try?' is unused is a sign of swallowing. Run the build and read the warnings regularly.

## 3. A notification without the store name: forgotten in the buffer

  A different story with the same shape. A report said “the notification has no store name”. The article had the store name (sellerName) correctly. The notification did not show it.

  Lottery and reservation notifications are put in a buffer and sent in batches (to hold them in quiet hours and to limit the rate). But the store name was not carried into the buffer. When sending, looking for the store name found no information, and only the category (“LivePocket”) remained.

  This was partly surfaced by the earlier fix. When I fixed “the notification arrives under the name LivePocket”, I made it return null when the store name is unknown. That forgotten carry-over changed its symptom from “wrong store name” to “no store name”.

  The same gap existed in both buffers (by genre and by product), so I fixed both. For the 5 already buffered I filled in the store name from the article and confirmed it appears when sent.

  The same gap had happened on 17 August with another field (product names). The lesson: when putting something in a buffer, carry every field that will be used at send time. The other two buffers, which store the finished wording as is, do not have this problem.

## What I learned

> If you throw failure away, the screen lies.

- Return failures to the caller. Discarding them makes the display differ from reality.

- On failure too, return to a “finished” state. If a callback is never called, the screen freezes.

- Record success only on success. If it stays after a failure, you cannot retry.

- Read the build warnings. A try? warning is a sign of swallowing.

- Put every field used at send time into the buffer. The same gap shows up later in another field.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/swallowed-failure/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

- Toreca Dash (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/torecadash/)

URL: https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/truncated-answer/

# Candidates were found, yet reading the answer failed every time: a URL cut at 200 tokens, and a search that returned 400 on hyphens

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/truncated-answer/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / August 2026

  In my app Toreca Dash, aggregator-derived articles get their links replaced with the store’s official announcement page. But developer-mode reports kept coming, seven in a row: “the correct announcement URL is this one; do it properly”.

  Looking into it, candidates were being found, and the step that reads the answer failed every time. This article records the real cause and a very similar case from the same period.

  Numbers come from my work logs of 23 and 24 August 2026.

## The real cause: the AI’s reply was cut off at 200 tokens

  The step that chooses the official announcement page asks an AI at the end: “which candidate is that store’s announcement?” I had set the reply’s length limit (max_output_tokens) to 200.

  But the reply contains a long URL with Japanese percent-encoded, which exceeds 200 characters on its own. The reply was cut off, could not be read as JSON, and raised Unterminated string in JSON.

  WARN [application link] official page judgement failed [shop / …]: Unterminated st…
→ all 10 targets: "not found"
  Candidates had been found. It fell over every time at reading the answer. I raised the limit to 800, and added a rescue that, if it is still cut, does not discard everything but re-extracts just the "url": "… part.

## Still 0 adopted after the fix: the AI was obeying my instruction

  Even after fixing the JSON, 0 were adopted. The log showed candidates but “none adopted”. The cause: the AI was following the instruction faithfully. Store announcements read like this:

  "[App members only] Reprint / Pokémon Card Game, 4 types, about the lottery sale"
  They name no individual product. My instruction said “do not choose it if the product differs”, so the AI refused.

  I fixed two things:

- In addition to the search by product name, always also search site:store-domain lottery and merge the candidates. (“Only when the search came up empty” never triggered, because one unrelated page was always returned.)

- Add to the instruction: “if the store’s own announcement page covers several products and gives no individual names, you may choose it”. Other stores and aggregator sites are never chosen, even if they cover several products.

  The result: 3 of 10 were replaced with the store’s official announcement page.

  I also made a list of app-only stores (stores that give lottery information only in their app), so the app can say “please check in the app”. Only stores known to have an app; I do not add by guess.

## A similar case: Rakuten’s keyword search failed on hyphens (24 August)

  The log kept showing “Rakuten Ichiba per-set search failed”, for Yu-Gi-Oh! alone for 8+ sets. Rakuten’s API failed the whole request with 400 wrong_parameter depending on how hyphens are used in the keyword.

    Keyword shape | Result

      "A - B" (spaces around the hyphen) | 400

      "A B " (trailing space only) | 400

      "A B-" (ends with a hyphen) | 400

      "AB-" (a word with no space, trailing hyphen) | 200 (OK)

  Yu-Gi-Oh! product names often put a subtitle between hyphens, as in “LIMIT OVER COLLECTION - THE RIVALS -”. Sets of that form had never once been found by the per-set search.

  The fix has two steps: (1) remove spaces right after a hyphen, (2) drop trailing hyphens and spaces. “LIMIT OVER COLLECTION - THE RIVALS -” became “LIMIT OVER COLLECTION -THE RIVALS” and returned 200. I confirmed the same problem happens with the Rakuten Books API, and applied the same sanitising to the four functions that pass keywords.

## What I learned

> When candidates were found but the result is 0, suspect the place that reads the answer.

- Set a reply length limit from what is returned. A percent-encoded URL is long.

- Do not throw away a failure; salvage it. You can pull the needed part out of cut-off JSON.

- An AI is faithful to instructions. If the instruction does not fit how things are really written, it correctly refuses.

- Separate an external API’s quirks by measuring. 400 and 200 split on the hyphen position.

- The same quirk exists wherever the same API is used. It happened on Rakuten Books too.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/truncated-answer/).

# A function named “load from iCloud if newer” compared nothing: a 20-record history could become 1

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/icloud-overwrite/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / August 2026

  My iPhone app Toreca Dash has a record of applications that users build up themselves: which lotteries they entered and how they turned out. It is a personal record built by hand, and once lost it cannot be recovered.

  On 23 August 2026 I read a file I had not yet reviewed (1,076 lines) and found a path where this record could vanish entirely. It began with trusting a function’s name.

  Written from my work log of 23 August 2026.

## The name says “if newer”; the body compares nothing

  The function that syncs with iCloud was named loadFromICloudIfNewer: “load from iCloud if it is newer”. But the body never checked whether anything was newer; whenever iCloud changed, it replaced everything with that content.

  What can happen:

- Device A has 20 records (and so does iCloud).

- Device B is installed fresh. iCloud’s first sync is asynchronous, so just after launch the records may be empty.

- On device B, one record is added, and saving overwrites iCloud with [1 record].

- Device A receives the change notice and goes from 20 records to 1 (19 lost).

  The code had an export/import feature, described as being “to prevent all data vanishing when you change phones”. The author knew this area was fragile.

## The fix: compare update times, and never overwrite with empty

- Store an update time (entriesUpdatedAt) on both device and iCloud, and import only when the other side is newer, so the function does what its name says.

- Even for old data with no time yet, always prevent overwriting with empty content.

- On the first restore on a new device, inherit iCloud’s time.

## What I learned

> A function’s name may state the spec, but the body may not match.

- Do not trust names; read the body. “IfNewer” compared nothing.

- Be extra suspicious of writes to data that cannot be recovered. A record built by hand does not come back.

- “Empty” is a dangerous value. Make “never overwrite with empty” the last line of defence.

- First sync is asynchronous. Empty right after launch does not mean no data.

- Read the unreviewed files. Large, old files hide the most.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/icloud-overwrite/).

# With no ads, 25 real-device checks were blocked: test ads in developer mode only, and no hard-coded prize names

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/test-ads/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / September 2026

  My app Toreca Dash has a daily lottery (omikuji) feature. “Watch a video to try” starts the draw animation after a video ad.

  On 11 September 2026, reviewing the real-device checklist revealed a problem: because ads were not being served yet, 25 of the 163 checklist items could not be verified.

  Numbers come from my work log of 11 September 2026.

## Without an ad, you cannot check what follows

  Before review and before serving starts, my own ad slot has no inventory. The omikuji’s “Watch a video to try” stays at “Preparing an ad…” and cannot be pressed. Everything after it (the draw, the animation, the prize applying, entering a delivery address) cannot be verified. 25 of the 163 items (15%) of the real-device checklist were blocked.

## Use test ads only in developer mode

  I use the test ad units Google publishes. Test ads always have inventory. Switching to them only in developer mode lets me verify through to the end on the same path as production.

     | Production | Developer mode

      Banner | My ad unit | Google’s test unit

      Rewarded (video) | My ad unit | Google’s test unit

      Native | My ad unit | Google’s test unit

      App open | My ad unit | Google’s test unit

  Developer mode is enabled only by “tap the version 7 times” and “only on the same device ID”. Users never see it. Ad rules say test ads are for your own device only; this satisfies that.

## Never hard-code prize names anywhere

  Another, similar story. After I changed the omikuji prizes, I was told “some text is still the old one”. I will keep changing prizes, each time.

  Looking into it, the display side was correct:

- The prize list, the terms and the result card all read one and the same setting (lotteryConfig/publicStatus).

- The process that changes prizes writes both “current” and “public” in the same transaction, so they cannot drift.

- Temporarily unlocking Pro features is decided by a separate field (perk), not the prize name.

  What was stale was two places with prize names hard-coded:

- Three items of the real-device checklist (shown in the app), written like “Medium luck says ‘ads hidden for 24 hours’”.

- The fallback text used when the setting has not arrived.

  I rewrote the checklist to not name prizes (“the prize names currently set in the admin page appear as they are”), and the fallback to “Prizes are being prepared”. I added an item “right after changing prizes, the prize list, terms and result card all show the new prizes” (164 items). Since I change prizes every time, I put “where to look each time” into one item.

  I did keep an old wording in the server’s “defaults when no setting exists”, because wording and effect are paired (hidden-ads text and the ad-free unlock). Neutralising only one side would make “unlocked but no explanation”.

## What I learned

> Make a way to verify what you cannot verify; do not hard-code what changes.

- For things that come from outside, such as ads, provide a test path. Relying on production inventory leaves what follows unchecked.

- Keep the test path for developers only. Guard it with 7 taps and the device ID.

- Do not hard-code wording that changes every time. Read from one setting; write in one transaction.

- Do not fix only one half of a pair. Fix wording and effect together.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/test-ads/).

# “That’s just a Beyblade” came back after I added a gate: the blocked value leaked in another form

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/leaked-value/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / September 2026

  My app Toreca Dash received three reports: “this is just a Beyblade”. An app that gathers trading-card information had a toy, Beyblade, registered as a product.

  On 6 September I had added a gate: “do not create a product if the product name contains a toy’s name”. Yet it came back. This article is about a value I had blocked coming back in a different form.

  Numbers come from my work logs of 6 to 11 September 2026.

## I added the gate, but the toy’s name had vanished from the product name

  The store announcement was:

  New toy: Beyblade X
(1) CX-19 Random Booster Kuro Tread set
(2) CX-00 Tigerage FT3-60T
  An AI builds product names from it, and the products created were:

  "CX-19 Random Booster Kuro Tread Select"
"CX-00 'Tigerage' FT3-60T"
  Neither contains the word “Beyblade”. My gate rejected a product name that contained a toy’s name. Because the AI’s product name no longer had it, the gate let it through. The value I had blocked (the toy’s name) returned in another form (a product name without it).

## The fix: judge on the announcement text, not the product name

  I moved the judgement to the announcement body, not the product name. The body states the toy’s name.

  But “contains a toy’s name, so reject” would not do. Store announcements sometimes list both toys and card games, such as “[Beyblade] [Dragon Ball Card Game]”. Rejecting would remove real lotteries. So the rule is: reject only when no card-game word appears at all.

  Counting on real data:

    What I checked | Count

      Articles that touch a toy line | 44

      Of those, matching the rule (no card-game word) | 31

      Of those, displayed | only the reported one

      Articles with a card-game word (all kept) | 13

## What I learned

> A blocked value comes back in another form. Follow where the value goes.

- When you add a gate, follow where the blocked value leaks. Stop it creating products and it survives in a title or another field.

- Judge close to the source of the material. The original announcement is more reliable than a product name processed by an AI.

- Do not reject on “present” alone. Listings are mixed, so limit it to “no other word at all”.

- Count what remains for a rejecting rule. I confirmed the 13 stay.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/leaked-value/).

# Checks that logged “deferred to next run” had never run: three time budgets counted from the same start

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/budget-starved/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / September 2026

  Behind my app Toreca Dash is a process that checks and fixes articles’ “sale type”. Inside it was a part that ran “25 checks in rotation”.

  On 11 September 2026, after adding a meter that times each stage, I learned that those 25 checks had never run once. The log kept saying “deferred 18 items to the next run for the time budget”. That “18” meant not some of them but all.

  Numbers come from my work log of 11 September 2026.

## Three budgets were counted from the same start time

  The process had three stages, each with a time budget.

    Stage | Budget | Measured

      ① Main loop | 420 s | uses all 425 s

      ② Always-run slot | 780 s (total) | only 360 s really usable; ends at 861 s

      ③ Rotating 25 checks | 700 s (total) | ② overruns 700 s, so 0 checks every time

  The three budgets were counted from the same start time: ① 420 seconds, ② 780 in total, ③ 700 in total. It looks as if each stage has room. But ② can only use 360 seconds of its 780 after ① used 425, and when ② ended (861 seconds), ③’s “700 in total” was long gone. ③ was judged “out of budget” before it started, every time: 0 checks.

  The log’s “deferred 18 items to the next run” meant sending everything to the next run, every time. “Next run” never came.

## The fix: do not widen by feel; allocate from the job’s time limit

  I stopped widening the numbers by feel. Instead I allocate from the job’s own time limit. The limit is written in one place (REPAIR_SALE_TYPES_TIMEOUT_SEC) and each stage’s deadline is that times a ratio.

    Stage | Deadline (share of the limit)

      ① Main | 23%

      ② Always-run slot | 67%

      ③ Rotation | 93%

  The limit became 1,800 seconds. Since each deadline is a share of the whole rather than a continuation of the previous stage, later stages keep their budget even if an earlier stage uses everything.

## Add a meter: which stage was heavy was invisible

  Another cause: I had widened the limit without knowing which of the 12 was heavy. So I log the seconds each step takes. Heaviest first as measured:

    Step | Time

      Attach replacement articles to hidden, already-notified ones | 119 s

      Find the application link from the QR in the announcement image | 102 s

      Fix the unit of the reference price | 48 s

      Copy the reference price | 46 s

      Fix articles with neither a link nor an application method | 41 s

## What I learned

> “Next run” only means something if a next run is certain.

- Counting budgets from the same start starves the later stages. If an earlier one uses it all, the later one has 0.

- Count the “deferred” log lines. If everything is deferred every time, it has never run.

- Allocate from the job’s total limit, not by feel.

- Measure each stage first. Widening limits without knowing what is heavy does not help.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/budget-starved/).

# I fixed a timeout three times and it did not stop: the culprit was a second process under the same lock

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/timeout-third-fix/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / August 2026

  The job in my app Toreca Dash that rechecks Rakuten Books stock timed out 17 times a day. A timeout means a run does not finish within its limit (480 seconds).

  I fixed it three times, and it did not stop. The real culprit was in a place I had not looked, each time. This is the record of how I tracked it down.

  Written from my work log of 25 August 2026.

## First fix: fetches had no timeout

  The first thing I found was that fetches had no time limit. If an external site never replies, the process waits forever. I added a limit. But the 17 timeouts a day did not stop.

## Second fix: the screening of items that became buyable

  Next I suspected the resale-price screening of items that had become purchasable. It includes calls to an external API, so a path that could hang remained. When screening skips an item, the notification count stays 0, so the symptom does not reveal it.

  I extracted the whole handling of one item into a single function (processOne()) and wrapped it in a Promise.race (take whichever finishes first) with the remaining time as the limit. After deploying, 0 timeouts in 7 minutes, and the log said “checked: 12 (rest next time because time ran out)”, a normal finish.

  The lesson: putting a limit only on “the spot that looks stuck” is not enough. The time budget is only checked at the head of the loop. If any unbounded wait remains inside one item’s processing, the job runs to the hard limit. Put the limit on the whole processing of one item.

  But the timeouts had not stopped.

## Third fix: the culprit was a second process under the same lock

  The reason three fixes did not work: none of the places I limited was the real one.

  The culprit was a second process (runRevalidateRakutenBooksAvailability) running under the same “prevent double runs” lock.

- It re-fetches every Rakuten Books reservation and first-come article and calls the API one by one.

- Rakuten’s API has a 1.5-second interval limit.

- It had no time limit at all.

  However many limits I put on the first process (the stock check), the second ran to 480 seconds. The log shows the first one’s completion message, so it looked like “it finishes normally yet times out”.

  I gave the second process a “remaining time” limit too. It runs every minute anyway, so cutting it short loses nothing. 15 minutes after deploying, 0 timeouts.

## A bonus: a site that erred every time

  Another bug found along the way: a game company’s shop site returned an infinite redirect loop (maximum redirect reached) with a plain fetch, logging an error at every recheck (a dozen or so a day). The scraping service’s “escalation memory” already knew it needed a stronger setting.

  The fix: hosts remembered in the escalation memory go straight through the scraping service without trying a plain fetch. I did not list host names by hand. The memory builds up automatically from real failures, so new sites need no extra work.

## What I learned

> When chasing a timeout, first count everything the function calls.

- One scheduled function can contain two or more processes. Three times I looked only at the first.

- Put the limit on the whole processing of one item. One suspect spot is not enough.

- “Finishes normally yet times out” means suspect another process. The completion message may be the first one’s.

- Log the time of each segment. Next time it will be obvious at once.

- Prefer memory built from real failures to hand-written lists. It works on new sites automatically.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/timeout-third-fix/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

- Toreca Dash (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/torecadash/)

# “It gets cleaned up later” hid an entrance bug: 400 near-identical products were re-created every day

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/cleanup-hides-entrance/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / August 2026

  My app Toreca Dash has a nightly clean-up job that merges duplicate products. “It will be cleaned up later, so it is fine.” That was the belief, and in that place an entrance bug was re-creating near-identical products every day.

  A full check on 27 August 2026 showed that 437 products had been created that day alone, and 410 of them had no articles attached.

  Numbers come from my work log of 27 August 2026.

## The cause: it only looked for an exact name match

  The step that registers products from the official catalogue decided “does this product already exist?” by exact name match only.

  Existing "Expansion Pack「Ancient Roar」"  ↔  Catalogue "Expansion Pack Ancient Roar"
Existing "V Starter Deck Grass (full-width space) Bulbasaur"  ↔  Catalogue "V Starter Deck Grass Bulbasaur"
  Differences in brackets, spaces or full-width versus half-width made it say “not there yet”, and near-identical products were re-created every day.

  The duplicates were later cleaned up by the weekly and daily merge jobs. That is why I did not notice. In between, users see the same product twice and article links split.

  The fix was to compare with the same normalisation the merge job uses (it absorbs brackets, spaces and full/half-width). The catalogue itself also has spelling-variant duplicates, so within one run I keep one per key.

  The lesson: a mechanism with a clean-up job “for later” hides entrance bugs. If the clean-up count is about the same every time, it is not that things are cleaned; they are being created every day.

## Another: six products absorbed into one

  Six Magic: The Gathering “FINAL FANTASY” Commander decks (Psionic Spell, Limit Break, Counter-Blitz, Trans-Reanimate and others) were all absorbed into one product.

- Another set’s name gets into a product’s aliases.

- It shows up as an AI candidate.

- It leads to the next wrong match.

  That is a self-multiplying loop. Cleaning the aliases alone did not fix it, because the AI kept choosing the same product. I added a filter that removes products whose quoted proper name differs (namesDifferentQuotedVariant) to the candidate list too. With it gone from the candidates, the AI can answer “new product” and the correct one is created.

  To remove false positives, when the quoted text is a generic word, place name, store name, quantity or state, it is not treated as a proper name. On real data, before this condition 6 of 12 were false positives.

  There was also an idea I did not adopt: a strong rule “delete if the product’s proper name is not in the aliases”. 6 of 43 were false positives (different sets with the same code, names containing “+”), so I dropped it.

## My own repair put a deadline on first-come sales

  I ran a repair job that inherits dates from articles of the same announcement page (inheritDatesFromSameAnnouncement). It gave a first-come sale (sold until stock runs out) the deadline of a lottery article on the same page. A first-come sale has no deadline, and users would see a false “you can buy until that day”.

  In both places that inherit (the save-time step and the repair job), first-come articles no longer get a deadline. I deleted the one that had been affected.

  The lesson: after running a repair job, compare the audit before and after. Looking only at “how many were fixed” hides anomalies you added yourself.

## What I learned

> A later clean-up hides entrance bugs.

- If the clean-up count is the same each time, they are made daily. It is not being cleaned up.

- Use the same normalisation at the entrance and in the clean-up. If the entrance is stricter, the clean-up covers for it.

- Cleaning aliases alone does not stop self-multiplication. Remove it from the AI’s candidates.

- Count false positives before a strong rule. 6 of 43 means dropping it.

- Compare audits before and after a repair. To find the anomalies you added.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/cleanup-hides-entrance/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

- Toreca Dash (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/torecadash/)

URL: https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/secret-in-logs/

# A secret token was in the logs in plain text: scrub at the one exit that cannot be forgotten

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/secret-in-logs/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / August 2026

  While checking the logs behind my app Toreca Dash, I found that an external service’s secret (an API token) was written in plain text. It was 24 August 2026.

  It had been a to-do I had marked “no deadline, optional”. Looking at the server’s real logs, it really had leaked. This article records the cause and the fix: scrub at a place that cannot be forgotten.

  Written from my work log of 24 August 2026. No real value is included.

## A real token was in the log

  The server log had lines like this (the token part was real):

  WARN [recheck] fetch via the scraping service failed [https://…]:
request to https://api.scrape.do/?token=<the real token>&url=… failed, reason: read ETIMEDOUT
  The cause: the error message of the HTTP library (node-fetch) includes the request URL as is. The token= in the URL carries the secret.

## I had “fixed” the same thing before

  On 19 August the same thing had happened with Rakuten API credentials. I wrote a function to scrub secrets from log strings (redactSecretsForLog). But it only works where it is called explicitly. There are over 50 places that call the scraping service, and I had forgotten some.

## The fix: scrub at the single exit every log goes through

  So that I would not repeat the same fix, I did two things:

- Scrub at the log exit (fmt()). Every server log goes through it, so it cannot be forgotten. It scrubs URL query values such as token, api_key, secret, applicationId, accessKey, affiliateId and setCookies, and also the raw form of the X-monitoring login cookies.

- Rebuild the error in the function that calls the scraping service. Before returning it to callers, re-create the error with the scrubbed text. That function is also used on the event-driven side (Cloud Functions triggers), so this covers that log too.

  I checked four real log strings. I also checked that ordinary log lines do not change (an unrelated = like deadline=2026-08-30 must not be scrubbed).

## What about logs already written?

  Even after the fix, logs already written still hold the real token. They can be read only with administrator rights on the server, so urgency was low, but if it worries you, reissue the token in the service’s dashboard and replace the value in the server’s settings. At the time of this record I had left that as an item awaiting a decision.

## What I learned

> If there are 50 places where you can forget, do it once at a place you cannot forget.

- A countermeasure you must call explicitly leaks when forgotten. Forget one of 50 and it leaks.

- Scrub at the single exit. Put one at the place every log goes through.

- Check you are not scrubbing too much. Test that ordinary logs do not change.

- Things already written do not vanish. Decide whether to reissue.

- Do not trust a third-party library’s error messages. They can include the URL as is.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/secret-in-logs/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

- Toreca Dash (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/torecadash/)

# Moving from Cloud Functions to a ¥4,300 server: ¥3,700 a day, Yahoo! failing in the EEA, and five traps

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/vps-migration/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / August 2026

  The back end of my iPhone app Toreca Dash originally ran on Google Cloud Functions (billed per function for the time it runs). When the free trial ended on 16 August 2026, from 17 August it cost about ¥3,700 a day (about ¥106,000 a month).

  This article records how I moved that code almost unchanged to a server (VPS) at about ¥4,300 a month: what I decided, what I corrected later, and the traps.

  Numbers come from my work log of 20 August 2026. I do not include server addresses or connection details.

## Why move: waiting time was billed too

  About 97% of the Cloud Functions bill was CPU time (vCPU seconds). But nearly all of my functions just wait for scraping targets and AI replies, and that waiting was billed in full.

  On a flat-rate server that structural waste disappears.

  I also considered Cloudflare Workers. The Firestore admin SDK does not run there and hundreds of places would need rewriting to another API, so I dropped it. On a VPS the current code runs as is.

## What I chose, and where I first got it wrong

    Item | Details

      Provider | Hetzner Cloud

      Spec | 2 vCPU, 4 GB memory, 80 GB SSD

      Location | Singapore

      Price | €26.99 a month (about ¥4,300)

  I first built it in Helsinki (€5.99 a month). Then I rebuilt it.

  The reason: Yahoo! Shopping’s API blocks access from the EEA and the UK. Calling it from Helsinki returned not the API response but a notice page, “For customers in the European Economic Area and the UK”, with HTTP 403. All 15 genres failed. It is a legal geo-block, not bot detection, so retrying never helps. From Singapore it returns HTTP 200 normally.

  I deleted the Helsinki server; it had cost €0.02 (about ¥3).

  Hetzner’s pricing gives a €7 a month discount only in three European locations. The cheapest line (CX) is sold only in Europe. So “cheap location = EEA = Yahoo! dies”. Do not go back to Europe for the price.

  Singapore also helped by being closer to Japanese sites: the Pokémon card new-arrival check went from 52.7 seconds to 15.8 seconds (3.3× faster).

## Run the code unchanged: intercept require

  I wrote a runner (runner.js). The original code (index.js) is not changed at all.

  Instead of copying 132 schedules by hand, I intercept require and replace firebase-functions with my own, making the calls that register schedules just add to a list. Then I load the original code, and all definitions are collected automatically. The counts collected:

  132 scheduled jobs / 256 HTTP endpoints / 9 Firestore triggers
  Not copying by hand was right. One schedule is written as the template string `every ${X_CHECK_INTERVAL_MINUTES} minutes`. Copying by eye would have got it wrong. I matched all 132 mechanically and confirmed they agree.

  The 9 Firestore triggers (functions that fire when data changes) do not fire on the VPS. I left them on Cloud Functions (they are event-driven and cost almost nothing). The 256 HTTP endpoints stay there too, because the app and admin page call them.

## Five traps I hit in the move

### 1. There were 15 secrets, not 5

  My earlier notes said “5 secrets”. Counting every environment variable in the code gave 15. The missing 10 included Rakuten, Google Maps, Yahoo!, X authentication, the billing integration, a membership-site session and a debug secret.

  A missed secret does not raise an error; it quietly returns 0 results. Extract the variable names from the code mechanically and count them.

### 2. A secret value contained newlines

  The membership-site session secret is in a “one line per site” format, so the value itself contains newlines. Written naively into an env file, line two onwards becomes separate variables and 3 of 4 sites quietly die. I made the env-file reader understand escaped newlines (\n).

### 3. A write-blocked rehearsal looped forever

  Rakuten’s and Yahoo!’s APIs need a spacing between calls (rate limiting). The code writes “last call time” to Firestore and waits until it advances. In a rehearsal where all writes were swallowed, the time never advanced and the loop never ended. (Cloud Functions was also updating it every 1.5 seconds, so “someone else updated it, wait again” repeated forever. A Rakuten Ichiba job not returning for over 15 minutes revealed it.) In rehearsal I let just that rate-limit record through.

### 4. “Writes on, notifications off” silently deletes notifications

  The job that sends notifications in batches deletes the pending list once it counts them as sent. Stubbing only the sending while allowing writes would delete without sending, losing notifications. So during the rehearsal stage I did not register seven notification-related schedules on the VPS. They are removed from the skip list only when notifications are turned on.

### 5. A new exit IP quietly stops one scraper

  A supermarket site was fetched with a plain request and had no fallback. From Japan it was 200, from Singapore 403. I compared all 75 hosts from both Japan and Singapore: 6 are “visible from Japan, not from Singapore”; 5 of those already went through the scraping service or had a fallback and were fine. Only one broke. “403 from Singapore” alone is not proof of breakage. Check whether it goes through the scraping service.

## The order of the move: not to send notifications twice

- Stage 1: read only (no writes, no notifications) and compare fetch counts with Cloud Functions.

- Stage 2: write, but leave notifications to Cloud Functions.

- Stage 3: delete only the 132 scheduled functions from Cloud Functions.

- Stage 4: turn notifications on in the VPS.

  Always keep exactly one side sending notifications. If both send at once, users get the same notification twice.

## What I learned

> A service billed by time does not suit code that mostly waits.

- Look at the billing unit. If waiting is billed, scraping and AI calls are expensive.

- Hosting has legal limits. The cheap place may be a place you cannot use.

- Look for a way to move without rewriting. Interception and mechanical matching avoided hand-copy errors.

- Count settings by machine. 15, not 5.

- Move in stages to avoid duplicate notifications.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/vps-migration/).

- Toreca Dash (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/torecadash/)

# I opened the links of displayed articles and compared them: about 60 mistakes, and three mistakes in my own first check

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/destination-check/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / September 2026

  The articles in my app Toreca Dash link to store and shopping-site pages. Even if an article’s title and price are right, if the linked page is closed or about a different product, it is no use to the user.

  On the night of 15 September 2026, asked to “check the destination content too”, I actually opened the links of displayed articles and compared the content with the article: product, store, whether open, sale type, deadline and price. About 60 mistakes turned up.

  Numbers come from my work log of 15 September 2026. The check itself made no writes; I fixed the findings separately.

## How I checked

- X posts (361): 0 deleted. The text had been compared in earlier checks.

- Non-X (703, excluding Yahoo!): I read the destination directly or via the scraping service (with a Japanese IP) and judged with an AI. Amazon always goes through the scraping service.

  My first version of the check got three things wrong:

- I opened Amazon from Singapore. Prices showed in Singapore dollars and I saw another seller, and judged that “wrong”.

- I read Rakuten as garbled text. I had not detected the character encoding (EUC-JP).

- I opened 501 Yahoo! pages six at a time. The production IP was refused with HTTP 489 (see another article (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/self-inflicted/)). I stopped partway through Yahoo!.

  If the checking tool is wrong, the count of “mistakes” inflates. I fixed encoding detection, opening Amazon from Japan, and judging only by stock of “this exact item”, then reran.

## Mistakes found (about 60)

    What | Count | Fix

      Amazon “invitation request” shown as pre-order or first-come | 10 | Make it a lottery

      Amazon “pre-order” shown as first-come | 7 | Make it a reservation

      Rakuten Books “pre-orders open” shown as first-come | 3 | Make it a reservation

      Shops closed temporarily (Yahoo!) | 6 | Hide

      Sold out or closed but still displayed | many | Hide

      Link goes to a different store or an ended lottery | 3 | Go back to the store’s X post

      Link goes to a different product | 2 | Hide

      Price mismatch | about 10 | Correct

      Empty store name | 1 | Fill in

  The most frequent was the wrong sale type. On Amazon there are “invitation requests”, neither first-come nor pre-order. Treating one as first-come means users cannot buy however fast they are. The earlier code only marked the invitation and did not correct the sale type.

  Some sold-out pages did not match my sold-out wording. A Yahoo! sold-out page says “out of stock” on screen, but matched none of the keywords. So I now judge by the stock data embedded in the page for that item ("stock":{"isAvailable":false). The data is more reliable than the wording on screen.

## “Opening the application link goes to the site’s top page”

  Found in another check the same day. The QR code on a store’s lottery image pointed to a URL that, actually opened, redirects to the site’s top page, not an application page.

  I added a check to the single gate that adopts application links. It opens the URL, and if the original URL has a path other than the top but the destination path is empty (or a file name that looks like a top page), it does not adopt it. If it cannot be read (403, timeout), it still adopts, since many stores use bot protection and unreadable is not a sign of badness. The same URL is held for 6 hours.

## What I did not fix, and could not fix

  It matters that I did not count everything found as a “mistake”. There are cases I checked and did not fix.

- Rakuten Ichiba “sold out”: the page data said in stock (a setting hides stock counts). The AI misread it.

- Amazon “See all buying options”: other sellers exist, so it is not necessarily sold out.

- Amazon English titles: auto-translated names; the product was right.

- 85 pages I could not read: Rakuten Ichiba (via ad links), membership sites, LINE, Google Forms and so on.

  I keep results in three groups with reasons: fixed, not fixed, could not read. “Not fixed” needs a reason too.

## What I learned

> Even if title and price match, you cannot know until you open the link.

- Actually open the link. Looking only at the article cannot show that the destination is closed.

- Check the checking tool first. Country, encoding, parallelism: a wrong tool inflates “mistakes”.

- Embedded data beats screen wording. Judge sold-out by stock data, not text.

- Do not make everything found a “mistake”. Keep reasons for what you do not fix.

- Do not treat “could not read” as bad. Bot protection makes unreadable normal.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/destination-check/).

  More in English

- Toreca Dash (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/torecadash/)

# Four things from a full sweep of 61 audits: 51 jobs clumped at 4 a.m., a lock that expired in 55 seconds, and a price-filling idea I decided not to add

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/audit-sweep-61/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / September 2026

  My app Toreca Dash has 61 audits that find anomalies. In the early hours of 8 September 2026 I ran them all and checked every item that was not 0 against real data, one by one.

  This article is four stories from that work. Three are things I fixed; one is a story where I measured, and deliberately did not add it.

  Numbers come from my work log of the evening of 7 to the morning of 8 September 2026.

## 1. 51 once-a-day jobs were clumped at 4 and 5 a.m.

  At 04:53 the measurements were:

- The 14 concurrency slots were full, 8 waiting.

- 6 jobs timed out at the 540-second limit.

- The “instant sell-out monitor” and the “Amazon fastest lane” I wanted to protect were skipped 9 times each per hour.

  The cause was clumping in time. Counting once-a-day jobs: 27 at 4 o’clock and 24 at 5; at 1 o’clock and from 10 to 21, 0.

  The fix was not to edit times one by one, which would not apply to jobs added later. I fixed the mechanism that spreads start times. The spread was a flat 270 seconds; for jobs with an interval of 6 hours or more it now spreads up to 1,800 seconds (30 minutes). 27 jobs over 30 minutes is about one per 67 seconds, so 3 to 5 run at once.

  I kept it to 30 minutes so it does not spill into the next hour’s slot and break time-based order like “check at 2, fill at 3”.

## 2. A patrol meant to be “every minute” took 181 to 480 seconds per run

  The Rakuten Ichiba patrol was meant to run every minute. Measured, one run took 181 to 480 seconds. The harm was threefold:

- It occupied a concurrency slot almost all the time.

- It timed out at the 480-second limit (4 times in 2 hours) and the results were thrown away.

- It held the Rakuten API allowance (one call per 1.5 seconds, shared by all jobs) the whole time, cutting the share of the instant sell-out monitor.

  The effective interval was 3.5 to 6 minutes. And after a timeout it restarts from the same first genre every time, so later genres never get a turn.

  I switched it to the five-genres-at-a-time rotation proven on Rakuten Books.

     | Before | After

      One run | 181–480 s | 50–83 s

      Timeouts | 4 per 2 hours | 0

      Interval per genre | 3.5–6 min | 3 min

  I found one more thing. The lock that means “if the previous run is still going, do not start” (preventing double runs) expired after only 55 seconds. For jobs with a 480-second limit and 181–480 s real runs, a run that slipped past the runner’s skip (a manual run, a catch-up right after restart) could run twice at once, doubling Rakuten API use and hitting first-come monitoring. I set both to 480,000 ms. A lock’s expiry should be at least the job’s timeout.

## 3. Stop counting anomalies you cannot fix

  If you keep counting things that cannot be fixed, real anomalies get buried. I revisited three.

- “Lottery with no deadline: 77” became 0. Scanning the text of all 89 real cases, only 5 contained a date-like value, and those were not application deadlines (“lottery results 9/5”, “pick up by 9/13”). The store simply did not write one, and nothing can be done. Now only items that have both deadline wording and a date in the text count as anomalies.

- “3 stopped scrapers” became 0. What was counted were state records with no run time, not jobs. The main code excludes them, only the audit did not.

- One store’s “0 items for 173 hours” was normal. Fetching its three categories worked (16 and 6 items), and all were “point-exchange only” (0 yen). There was just no lottery or pre-order at the time.

  But “0 items” has two meanings: (a) no product matches (normal), (b) the page layout changed and nothing can be read (broken). If you cannot tell them apart, real breakage is buried (the previous day’s Pokémon Center (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/blocked-page/) was exactly this). So I now put the number scanned into the completion message.

## 4. A case I measured and deliberately did not add

  397 products had unknown official prices, which stops first-come notifications. The filling job had, measured, zero results.

  Official price unset: 397
Has a price at a regular store: 51
Two or more stores agree: 0
  The “two or more stores agree” condition had effectively never been satisfied. Accepting one store would fill 51. All were kinds with no catalogue price (imported Magic cards and so on).

  I still did not add it. Regular stores discount. If I record a discounted price as the official price, the price check’s ceiling (official price × 1.08 plus margin) becomes lower than the real price and legitimate listings are removed as resale. At 10% off, the real price is 1.11× and exceeds the ceiling. And over-deletion draws no complaints, so I would not notice.

  I wrote down what to do first if I add it:

- Compare the 51 prices by eye with official sites and the manufacturer’s suggested price (confirm whether they are discounted; do not guess a factor).

- Mark single-store-based prices and add margin to the ceiling only for that mark.

- After adding, count hidden articles before and after.

## What I learned

> Clumping is invisible until counted. Record the decision not to add, too.

- Count clumping in time. 27 at 4 o’clock, 0 from 10 to 21.

- Jobs hold something you cannot see. A lock’s expiry should be at least the timeout.

- Do not count anomalies you cannot fix. If the number does not fit, doubt how you count.

- Distinguish what “0 items” means. Show the number scanned.

- If you decide not to add something, keep the reason and the conditions. Even when measurement shows a gain, if it risks over-deleting, I do not add it.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/audit-sweep-61/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

- Toreca Dash (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/torecadash/)
