# Four real lotteries silently thrown away: a regex, dates without a year, batched answers and null

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/silent-discard/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / August–September 2026

  My iPhone app Toreca Dash has many places that decide “this is out of scope” and throw an item away. Throwing away looks like the safe side: if it is wrong, only some junk is missing from the screen.

  But mistakes of this kind give you no reason to notice them. A real lottery can be thrown away and nothing shows. This article describes four cases where I silently dropped, or nearly dropped, real lotteries.

  Numbers and dates come from my work logs between 28 August and 20 September 2026.

## 1. “x.com” matched “e-starbox.com” (31 August)

  If a link is a social-media link it is not a store page, so I do not use it. I listed the sites to exclude and joined them into one regular expression.

  new RegExp(["x\\.com", "note\\.com", ...].join("|"))
  That also matches inside other host names. x\.com matches the end of e-starbox.com, and note\.com matches mynote.com.

  The real damage was on the lottery service “Lottery Rotobox” (shoplottery.e-starbox.com). Its application links were judged “social media, not a store link” and never adopted once.

  The fix: host-only entries match only right after // or a dot ((?:^|//|\.) in front). I tested 13 examples, both URLs that should pass and URLs that should be blocked. An exclusion list looks like the safe side, so nobody doubts it.

## 2. A date with no year was read as six years ago (28 August)

  Store and aggregator posts write dates like “30 August (Sun)” without a year. I had an AI read the text to extract deadlines.

  For one aggregator, Pokémon card items came back as 30 August 2020, six years ago. A past deadline is rejected at the entrance gate, so all Pokémon card items from that source were never imported. One Piece and Dragon Ball happened to be read as 2026, which hid the problem.

  The fix was to put today’s date in the prompt and “do not fill in a year before today”. Readable items went from 0 to 46. “A year consistent with the post date” is not enough, because when the post date is unknown the year is undetermined.

## 3. The number of batched answers did not match (19 September)

  Sending one AI request per post costs one request each. So I batched several posts into one call to classify their sale type. I joined multi-line post bodies as “1. text”, “2. text”, separated by newlines.

  The AI cannot tell a newline inside a post from the boundary between posts. On the day X monitoring resumed, the number of answers did not match 8 times. On a mismatch the code marked the whole group “out of scope”, so real lotteries in those groups were dropped together.

  Worse, even when the count matched, some answers belonged to different posts. A Yu-Gi-Oh! lottery was thrown out as out of scope.

  The fix: pass a JSON array ([{no, text}]) or headings that cannot appear in the text (“[Article N]”), make the reply include numbers, and on a mismatch ask one by one instead of falling back to “out of scope”.

## 4. “Cannot decide” read as “none” (20 September)

  One function guesses the card genre from a post. When two or more genres appear, it returns null (“cannot decide”).

  Another job used it to detect “no card words (a toy-only announcement)” as !fn(text). There, null was read as “none”.

  A roundup post that lists Pokémon, One Piece, Yu-Gi-Oh!, Dragon Ball and Gundam model kits has several genres, so it returns null. That was read as “zero card words”, and because “Gundam” was found, as a toy announcement.

  Left alone, the daily bulk job at 05:15 would have hidden 129 real, displayed lotteries (for 9 products such as 30th CELEBRATION). I stopped it because I ran a count-only dry run before the real run. The dry run said 129, and that is how I noticed.

  The fix: to detect “none”, use the function that returns all matched genres and check that its length is 0.

## What I learned

> Mistakes in what you throw away raise no complaints, so count them yourself.

- Exclusion lists are wrong too. The safer something looks, the less it is doubted.

- Test what should pass, too. Testing only what should be blocked can hide a block on what should pass (case 1 used 13 examples of both).

- Give the AI every premise. Today’s date, separators. If you do not, it silently uses another premise.

- Do not default to “out of scope” on a count mismatch. If the fallback is “discard”, real items vanish together.

- “None” and “cannot decide” are different answers. Do not blindly negate null.

- Count before a daily bulk job. The 129 was known in advance.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/silent-discard/).

- Toreca Dash (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/torecadash/)

# “Checked” marks on articles that had never been read: the t.co relay page

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/tco-relay/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / October 2026

  My iPhone app Toreca Dash collects trading-card lottery information from store posts on X (Twitter). Each post links to an application form. The app also opens that link to check the deadline and whether entries have already closed.

  A report came in: “the deadline is wrong”. It turned out to be worse than a wrong deadline: the app had never read the linked page at all, and yet the article carried a “checked” mark.

  This is written from my work log of 16 October 2026 (the investigation and its numbers).

## The symptom: a closed form still shown as open

  The reported lottery was a game shop’s “30th CELEBRATION card set, 9 types” announcement on X. The Google Form it linked to said “Responses are no longer accepted”. In the app, the lottery was still shown, with an empty deadline.

  The odd part: the article had a “checked whether it has closed” timestamp. It had been “checked” and nobody noticed it had closed, so the check was not looking at the page.

## The cause: t.co returns a different page if you pretend to be a browser

  Links in X posts go through the short URL t.co. Normally it redirects to the real page (HTTP 301).

  But if you open it with a browser User-Agent, it does not redirect. It returns a roughly 500-byte page that redirects with JavaScript. Both of my reading functions opened t.co with a browser User-Agent and “follow redirects”. So:

- No redirect happened, so the final URL was still t.co.

- The text I read was the relay page’s HTML, not the form.

- I had never read the form at all.

  I had added the browser User-Agent on 6 August. This bug was a side effect of that change.

## How widespread was it?

  To check whether this was one case, I looked at every displayed X lottery or reservation article with a t.co link.

    What I checked | Result

      Displayed articles with a t.co link | 220

      Of those, relay page returned | 220 (all)

      Of those, actually a closed form but still displayed | 9

  The 9 were spread over several stores, so it was a systemic problem.

  One more clue I could not ignore: a daily job that fixes empty deadlines had been reporting “126 targets, 0 updated” every day. Not “nothing to fix” but “could not read, so could not fix”.

## The fix

  I put the redirect lookup into one function, fetchTcoTarget:

- Open t.co without a User-Agent, and do not follow redirects (redirect: "manual"). Take only the first target.

- If a target comes back, use it.

- If a relay page comes back, read the meta refresh tag inside it to get the real target.

- Then open that target with the browser User-Agent.

  Whether you send a User-Agent changes what comes back, so I split the uses: resolving a short URL uses none; reading the real page uses the browser one. I added a regression test.

## What to do with the wrong “checked” marks

  Fixing the code is not enough. The wrong marks stay on the articles. An article with the mark counts as “already checked” and is skipped.

  I removed the mark from 195 articles (X lottery/reservation posts that link to a post and have a t.co link), then ran the closed-entry check and the deadline re-extraction by hand.

    Job | Before | After

      Deadline re-extraction (targets / updated) | 126 targets, 0 updated (every day) | 123 targets, 14 updated

  The same day I also changed the closed-entry check: articles with no deadline every 6 hours (with a deadline, every 24), 80 articles per run instead of 40, 7 minutes at most. Now that t.co can be read, a closed form should not stay up for a whole day.

## What I learned

> Write “checked” only when you could actually read it.

- Write the mark only on success. If you mark an unreadable page as checked, it is never looked at again, even after the fix.

- After fetching an external page, check it is the page you meant. Is the final URL still the short URL? Is the text the right kind of page?

- “0 updated” every day can be a symptom. Tell “nothing to do” from “could not do”.

- When you change a network setting, review everything that uses it. A User-Agent added in August broke t.co reading two months later.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/tco-relay/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

- Toreca Dash (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/torecadash/)

# Before cutting Gemini cost, I doubted the meter: price, breakdown and cache were all wrong, and the cache threshold changed when I re-measured

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/gemini-meter/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / September–October 2026

  My iPhone app Toreca Dash uses Google’s Gemini (AI) to classify posts and match products. You pay for what you use, so I have worked on the cost several times. This is the record of two of those rounds.

- 4 September: before cutting anything I checked the measurement, and all three parts were broken.

- 16 October: I re-measured when the cache works, and it disagreed with my September conclusion.

  Numbers come from my work logs of 4 September and 16 October 2026. The model is gemini-3.1-flash-lite.

## Three parts of the meter were broken

  I was asked to cut cost. The first thing I did was not cutting, but checking whether the numbers were right. Cutting with a broken meter means cutting the wrong things. I found three faults.

    Fault | What happened

      Wrong prices | The code used $0.10 input and $0.40 output per million tokens. The real prices are $0.25 and $1.50, so cost was under-reported by about 2.6×.

      Labels collapsed | The per-purpose tally read a key that does not exist (params.system; the real one is system_instruction). 31 purposes were merged into one lump, so I could never see which prompt was expensive.

      Cache not counted | 31% of input was cache hits at 1/10 the price, but everything was counted at full price, about 40% too high.

  One more thing: the “second most expensive” item, “(outside jobs)” at ¥195 a day, was not a production problem. It was me running things by hand. When judging production, exclude manual runs.

  With the meter fixed, the cost was about ¥606 a day (¥18,168 a month); minus the cache, about ¥13,200 a month. Nearly all of it was input tokens: the instructions and candidate lists I resend every time.

## September: the cache starts above about 8,000 tokens

  Gemini discounts repeated long prompts (implicit caching) from the second call, at 1/10 the price for the cached part. I sent the same instruction three times at different lengths.

    Prompt length (input tokens) | Cached tokens

      5,209 | 0

      8,490 | 4,079

      17,070 | 12,263

  The conclusion then was “it works above about 8,000 tokens”. Effective tokens are input − 0.9 × cached. Padding a prompt to reach the threshold costs more: stretching 4,200 tokens to 8,500 gives 4,814 effective tokens, more than before. The cache only pays off for prompts that are already large.

## October: the threshold was about 4,000 tokens

  I measured again with the production key, this time through the interactions API. The result differed from September.

    Prompt length (input tokens) | Cached tokens

      1,770 | 0

      4,093 | 2,031 (from the 2nd call)

      7,017 | 4,076

  It worked from about 4,000 tokens, in chunks of about 2,038 tokens. September said 8,000, October said 4,000. I have not found out why. A difference in how I measured or a change on the service side are possibilities, but I do not know which. What I do know is that the cache threshold is not a fixed fact; re-measure it.

  My production prompts were 1,000 to 2,500 tokens, so the fixed part never reached the threshold and hits were 0 all day. Input is almost all of the cost (output about 1%), so a working cache looked like a big saving.

## Padding the prompt shifted 9% of the answers

  I tried stretching the prompt to about 2,300 tokens with “notes that do not affect the judgement”. I compared old and new answers on 90 real cases.

- 8 answers (9%) differed, between “other”, “lottery” and “first-come sale”.

- At about 2,600 tokens it still did not hit the cache.

  It lowers accuracy and does not even get cache hits, so I withdrew it and never shipped it. Text that “does not matter” still changes an AI’s answers. Do not add it without checking.

## What is left

  On real data the biggest single item is product matching: on average 7,151 input tokens, 297 times a day, about ¥83. Narrowing candidates, batching and skipping the AI when the title equals the product name are already in. Going further means fewer candidates, that is, less accuracy, so I left it.

  If I cut more, it will be by shortening prompts, checking agreement on real data one at a time, and not chasing the cache with padding.

## What I learned

> Before cutting cost, doubt the tool you cut it with.

- Do not write prices from memory. Check the official price page. The 2.6× under-report was a copied price.

- Print one real breakdown and look at it. 31 purposes collapsed into one still add up to the right total.

- Check that your own work is not in production numbers.

- Re-measure conditions. September’s 8,000 was October’s 4,000.

- Test “harmless” changes on real data. 90 cases showed a 9% shift.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/gemini-meter/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

- Toreca Dash (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/torecadash/)

- Firestore cost in yen (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/firestore-91/)

# Firestore cost in yen: 91% of reads came from one place, and my first cache did not work

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/firestore-91/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of the Toreca Dash app / September 2026

  The back end of my iPhone app Toreca Dash (a Japanese trading-card lottery and restock alert app) runs on Firebase’s Firestore database and a set of scheduled jobs. I had been reporting the cost of Gemini (AI) and of a scraping service in yen every day. I had not been reporting Firestore at all.

  On the night of 4 September 2026 I converted it to yen for the first time. It was almost the same as Gemini. This is the record of how I found that 91% of the reads came from one place, why my first cache did not work, and how I fixed it again.

  Numbers come from my work log of 4 September 2026. Prices are the real Tokyo-region prices.

## Once it was in yen, there was a cost nobody was watching

    Day | Reads | Writes | Cost per day

      28 Aug | 2.18 million | 120k | ¥226 (about ¥6,777 a month)

      1 Sep | 3.66 million | 134k | ¥368 (about ¥11,028 a month)

      3 Sep | 4.21 million | 162k | ¥427 (about ¥12,810 a month)

  The free tier is 50,000 reads a day. I was reading 84 times that, and it had grown 89% in a week, growing with every new article. A cost that is not shown in yen might as well not exist: about ¥13,000 a month, and nobody noticed because it was not in the report.

## A meter found it in three minutes

  I added a meter that counts which job reads which collection, and how much. The answer came as soon as it was in.

  8,725 reads  X monitor | products   ← 91% of the 9,593 measured
  197 reads  X monitor | news_items
  For each post, the X monitor asks an AI “which product is this about?”. To build the candidate list it re-read every product of the genre each time. The Pokémon genre has 693 products, so matching one post cost 693 reads. If I had searched the code, it would have taken much longer. Count before you search.

## The first cache barely helped

  The fix sounds simple: remember the list after reading it. I first cached for 60 seconds. It barely helped.

  The X monitor handles up to 32 accounts at the same time (Promise.all). What happened was:

- The first call sees “not in the cache” and starts reading.

- Before it finishes, the other 31 calls also see “not in the cache”.

- All of them read the same 693 products at once.

  I measured one re-read every 23 seconds. A cache remembers a finished result; callers that arrive during the read have nothing to find.

  The fix is to remember the pending promise, not the result. The first call stores its promise; the other 31 wait for the same one. However many calls arrive together, there is one read.

  // An illustration of the idea: cache the pending promise, not the result
cache.set(genre, { at: Date.now(), promise: loadProducts(genre) });
// callers always await cache.get(genre).promise
  I added three rules with it:

- Drop the cache the moment a product is created or deleted. Otherwise the list shows products that no longer exist, or creates the same product twice.

- Another function read the same products under the same conditions. I moved both to one cache so one side does not miss it.

- The cache lasts 10 minutes per genre.

  Measured in a quiet period and converted to a day, 5.07 million reads became 277,000.

## Another one: reading 3,085 documents every 5 minutes and using 146

  After the product cache, the next item at the top of the meter was a job that rechecks Rakuten Books stock every 5 minutes with this query:

  news_items where saleType in ["reservation", "guerrilla"]
  It returned 3,085 documents and then filtered to Rakuten Books in code. Only 146 were relevant: 95% was wasted. At 288 runs a day that is about 888,000 reads, roughly ¥2,400 a month.

- Cache the target list (only references and ISBNs) for 2 hours.

- But re-read the fields used for decisions every time, so I never write based on stale values. It is only 146 documents, so it is cheap.

  Reads fell from 888,000 to about 79,000 a day (−91%).

## What I learned

> A cost you do not show in yen does not exist.

- Fix the meter first. A cost you do not look at can grow unnoticed.

- Count before searching. One “job × collection” tally showed where 91% went in three minutes.

- For concurrent code, cache the pending promise. A cache of finished results lets everyone who arrives together walk past it.

- Filter before you read. Reading everything and keeping 5% is paying to throw away 95%.

- Confirm final numbers the next day. “5.07 million to 277,000” was a quiet-period measurement.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/firestore-91/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

- Toreca Dash (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/torecadash/)

# Setting the rules of Negaeri Shogi by playing AI against AI: one change that worked, six that broke

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/negaeri-balance/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-17
Development log of Negaeri Shogi / September 2026

  Negaeri Shogi (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/negaeri-shogi/) is a shogi-style game on a 6×6 board played a bit like Othello. Pieces you sandwich defect to your side and are promoted at the same time. If the new moves of a promoted piece create another sandwich, the flips continue. That is a chain.

  The rules come down to about ten numbers. I did not set them by feel. I ran dozens of AI-vs-AI games per candidate and measured. Only one change really worked; most of the others broke the game. I keep the ways they broke here.

  The numbers come from the measurement log in the game’s README (as of 13 September 2026). They are AI-vs-AI results. Balance between human players has not been verified enough yet.

## What I measured, and how

  The AI is a home-made alpha-beta search. I made depth-3 AIs play each other and counted:

- Share of drops that cause a flip. If low, most moves do nothing.

- Average game length. Too short means a one-sided game.

- First player’s win rate. Closer to 50% is fairer.

- Share of games with a chain of 3 or more. Chains are the point of the game.

- Lead changes. Too few: whoever is ahead early wins. Too many: it flips every move and feels random.

  Candidates were compared at 40 games each; final numbers use 100 games. Anyone can re-run it with the README commands (npm run report, npm run sweep).

## The first rules barely did anything

  At first a sandwich only worked along the directions a piece can move in shogi. In AI-vs-AI games, only 2% of drops caused a flip. Games lasted 16 moves and the first player won 71%. A flipping game where almost nothing flipped.

    Stage | Drops that flip | Avg. moves | First player wins

      Start (move directions only, empty board) | 2% | 16 | 71%

      All 8 directions | 8% | — | —

      Formation start position | — | 29 | —

      Pieces next to the king are safe | 42% | 51 | 33%

      One extra pawn in hand for the first player | 42% | 61 | 47%

      Board edge counts as the end of a sandwich | 81% | 53 | 59%

  The first player’s win rate jumps 71%, 33%, 47%, 59% because each rule change moved the advantage somewhere else. Every change needed a fresh measurement.

## The change that mattered: the edge is an anchor

  If a run of enemy pieces ends at the edge of the board, it counts as sandwiched. Pieces pushed against the edge defect together. This took flipping drops from 42% to 81%. Compared with other ideas at 40 games each:

    Idea | Flips per move | Games with a 3+ chain | Lead changes

      Before | 0.76 | 15% | 7.0

      Edge as anchor | 2.51 | 85% | 7.4

      + dropped piece is promoted too | 3.06 | 80% | 9.9

      Dropped piece promoted, alone | 0.72 | 13% | 5.0

      Chain limit of 3 | 0.71 | 8% | 5.8

      Piece-count result at 60 moves | 0.69 | 3% | 4.8

  Promoting the dropped piece too adds flips, but lead changes rise to 9.9 and the lead flips nearly every move, which thins out the shogi side of the game. I left it out (one setting turns it on).

## What I tried and dropped

    Idea | What happened

      Off-direction sandwiches reach only 1 square | Games with a 3+ chain fell from 95% to 13%. The reach of a sandwich was the engine of chains.

      5×5 board | Flips per move rose from 2.88 to 5.99, but the first player won 70%. Games were short (35 moves).

      Remove the king guard | Games ended in 17 moves on average and the first player won 95%. Guards defect at once and the king is left bare.

      Chain limit of 8 | Almost identical (2.86 vs 2.88 flips per move). The limit of 5 hardly mattered.

      Dropped piece promoted by a big flip | More flips, but 9.9 lead changes: it flips every move.

      Piece-count result at 60 moves | Games with a 3+ chain fell to 3%.

  The most useful row was “a limit of 8 changes nothing.” Raising the limit sounds like it should add chains. Measured, the result barely moved, so the limit of 5 was not doing much. I was about to tune a number that did not matter.

## Pieces next to your king never defect

  In this game a piece next to your own king does not defect. Removing that rule is the third row above: 17 moves on average and a 95% first-player win. Guards defected in a single move and the king was taken early. It is one plain sentence in the rules, and the game does not work without it.

## Current numbers (100 AI-vs-AI games, depth 3)

    Measure | Value

      Average length | 52.7 moves

      Board fill | 61%

      Drops that flip | 81%

      Flips per move | 3.08

      Games with a 3+ chain | 87%

      Games with a 4+ chain | 38%

      Average lead changes | 10.4

      Games with no lead change | 0%

      Games where the loser led at some point | 98%

      Point at which the result is decided | 81% of the way through

      First player’s win rate | 61%

  The board changes hands again and again and stays close to the end, yet it is not luck: a depth-3 AI beat a depth-2 AI in 20 of 24 games (as first or second player). 98% of games end by taking the king, so sandwiching stays a means and the shogi goal stays the goal.

## Still unsolved: the first player’s edge

  In the final measurement the first player won 61% (59% in an earlier, separate measurement). That is 11 points from 50%. I tried five handicap setups and found none clearly better.

    Handicap | First player wins

      None | 33%

      One extra pawn in the first player’s hand (current) | 61%

      One extra pawn on the first player’s side of the board | 38%

      Move one of the first player’s board pawns into hand | 64%

      Extra pawn in hand for the first player and extra pawn on the board for the second | 27%

  Pieces come in whole units, and the same “one pawn” is worth very different amounts depending on where it is placed: a point-symmetric addition moved the result by +5 points in one case and −34 in the other. Adding up small pieces cannot tune it to 50%.

  In online play, matchmaking gives the first move to the lower-rated player, which partly cancels the gap. That is not a fix. Games between humans are still to be checked.

## What I learned

> Half the changes that felt like good ideas broke the game when I measured them.

- Build the measuring tool first. Being able to run AI-vs-AI games automatically is what let me compare six ideas under the same conditions.

- Some numbers do nothing. The chain limit gave the same result at 5 and at 8.

- Ideas that break the point of the game only show up in measurement. “Reach one square” looked like it would restore each piece’s character; it cut chains from 95% to 13%.

- Say what is not fixed. The first-player gap is still 61%.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/negaeri-balance/). Numbers come from the README measurement log (13 September 2026). Negaeri Shogi (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/negaeri-shogi/) is free to play in the browser.

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

- Negaeri Shogi (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/negaeri-shogi/)

# Pokémon card sleeves and loaders: sizes and what “pt” means

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/card-supplies-guide/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-16
A buying guide / October 2026

  There are many ways to protect Pokémon cards: sleeves, loaders, deck boxes, binders. This guide lists what to check before you buy, so that what you order actually fits.

  One thing first: this is not a hands-on comparison. I could not find an official size table from the manufacturers, so the numbers are the “commonly stated” ones from shop pages and explainer articles. I separate what I could confirm from what I could not, and I do not recommend a specific product.

## The short version: three things to check

    Check | How

    Card size | Pokémon cards are “standard size”, commonly stated as about 63 × 88mm. Sleeves made for “small size” cards (about 59 × 86mm, for example Yu-Gi-Oh!) may not fit.

    Sleeve size | Choose sleeves labeled for standard-size cards. Outer size is often listed as around 66 × 91mm. Read the product page’s “compatible size.”

    Loader “pt” | A thickness grade. A bigger number takes a thicker card. 35pt is the usual rule of thumb for an ordinary card.

## Sizes: standard and small

- Standard: Pokémon, Magic: The Gathering and others. Commonly about 63 × 88mm.

- Small: Yu-Gi-Oh!, Duel Masters, Weiß Schwarz and others. Commonly about 59 × 86mm.

  A standard card does not fit in a sleeve made for small cards. A small card in a standard sleeve is loose. Look for “for Pokémon cards” or “standard size” in the product name first.

  Several explainer articles agreed on these numbers, but I could not confirm them on an official Pokémon Card Game page.

## Sleeves: choose by use

- For play: use the same sleeve for every card in the deck. Differences in back pattern or color can show which cards are which (tournament rules differ, so check the rules of the event you enter).

- For storage: sleeves protect the surface. Some people double-sleeve valuable cards (inner sleeve plus outer sleeve).

- Count: bags of about 100 are common. A deck is 60 cards, so one bag is enough.

## Loaders: what “35pt” means

  “pt” is a unit of card thickness. 1pt is one thousandth of an inch (about 0.0254mm), so 35pt is about 0.89mm: roughly the thickness of one ordinary card.

- 35pt magnetic loaders: some shop pages list an outer size of 73 × 110 × 8mm, an inner size of 64 × 90mm and a compatible thickness of about 1mm.

- With the sleeve on: some loaders take a sleeved card, some do not. If you want to load a sleeved card, check that the product says so.

- Thicker cards: loaders of 55pt, 75pt, 100pt and more also exist, used for thick cards or sleeved cards.

  The sizes above come from shop pages, not from a manufacturer’s official figures. They differ by product.

## Other items: deck boxes, binders, box protectors

- Deck boxes: check how many sleeved cards it holds.

- Binders: check pockets per page (9-pocket and so on) and whether sleeved cards fit.

- Booster box protectors: check the box dimensions so it matches the sealed box you own.

## Buying checklist

- Decide what it is for (a deck you play, cards you store, a sealed box).

- Confirm standard size or small size.

- Read the product page’s compatible size and count.

- For loaders, check the pt and whether sleeved cards fit.

- Scan the reviews for “did not fit.”

## What I could not confirm

- The card size on an official Pokémon Card Game page

- Official inner-size tables for sleeves and loaders from manufacturers (I only saw shop-page figures)

- Whether a given product takes a sleeved card (I did not test)

- Quality or durability of any product (this is not a hands-on comparison)

  Checked on October 16, 2026. Products change; check the product page before you buy.

## Sources

- Torecamap: Pokémon card sleeve sizes (https://torecamap.co.jp/column/pokemoncard-sleeve-size/) (explainer, in Japanese)

- Torecamap: trading card sizes (https://torecamap.co.jp/column/tradingcard-size/) (explainer, in Japanese)

- 35pt loader sizes: several shop pages (not the manufacturer’s official figures)

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/card-supplies-guide/).

# ITMS-91064 “Invalid Binary”: NSPrivacyTracking was true but NSPrivacyTrackingDomains was empty

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/itms-91064/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-08
Development log of Torecadash / October 2026

  I uploaded my iOS app, Torecadash, and Apple's automated review rejected build 877 as an “Invalid Binary”. The error code was ITMS-91064. The cause was a combination of two entries in the privacy manifest (PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy). This is what happened and how I fixed it, written from my commit history.

## What happened

  Build 877 was rejected as an “Invalid Binary” by Apple's automated review (October 6, 2026). In other words, it was stopped by a machine check, before any human reviewer saw it.

## The cause: tracking declared, but the domain list was empty

  The privacy manifest had these two entries:

    Key | Value

    NSPrivacyTracking (whether the app tracks) | true

    NSPrivacyTrackingDomains (domains used for tracking) | an empty array

  Apple's check rejects this combination as a contradiction: the app declares that it tracks, but lists no domain at all.

  Should I have just set NSPrivacyTracking to false? No. The app shows AdMob ads (banner, native and app-open) and personalizes them for users who agreed to ATT (App Tracking Transparency). The app really does track, so true is the correct declaration. The thing to fix was the empty domain list.

## The fix: list the domains

  However, Google does not publish an official list of tracking domains for AdMob. So I added widely used ad-serving domains:

- googlesyndication.com

- googleadservices.com

- doubleclick.net

- google.com

  I confirmed that the Release configuration builds (xcodebuild reported BUILD SUCCEEDED).

## What I have not verified

  The commit only records that the build succeeds. At the time of writing, I have no record of whether Apple accepted the fixed build. I also could not check whether the domains above cover every domain AdMob uses for tracking, because there is no official list.

## What I learned

> A declaration and its contents can be cross-checked by a machine.

- If you declare that you do it, write the contents (the domains) too. One without the other is rejected as a contradiction.

- When rejected, don't escape by deleting the declaration. If the app really does it, keep the declaration true and fill in the contents.

- When there is no official list, write down how far you verified.

  This article was written from the commit record (October 6, 2026). It is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/itms-91064/).

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# App Store review sent “Guideline 2.1 Information Needed”: the six things Apple asked for

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/review-info-needed/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of Torecadash / October 2026

  I submitted my iOS app, Torecadash, to App Review for the first time on October 6 (4:24 a.m. Pacific time). What came back was not a rejection but an email saying “additional information is needed.” This is a summary of what Apple asked for.

  I do not write the review result in this article. I will add it once there is one.

## What arrived

  It was Guideline 2.1 “Information Needed — New App Submissions.” The reason given was that this developer account has little review history. Apple wanted more information so it could understand the app well enough to finish the review. It was not a finding that the app is defective.

## The six things requested

  I was asked to reply in App Store Connect and also to put the same content in the “App Review Information” notes field. The six items (summarized):

- A screen recording on a physical device. On a device with the latest OS, starting from launching the app, show the normal flow of use. If there are account registration, login and deletion, user-generated content (including the report and block mechanisms), or paid features, include those too.

- The purpose of the app and its intended users. What problem it solves and what value it provides.

- How to start using the main features. If login is required, the credentials or sample files.

- A list of the external services used. Data providers, authentication, payments, AI, and so on.

- Differences in features or content by region. If there are none, say that it works the same in every region.

- Proof of rights if the app deals with a highly regulated field or third-party protected material.

  The email also included a list of common problems: bugs and crashes on a real device, a demo account if login is required, screenshots that show actual use, submitting in-app purchase products together with the app, and so on.

## How it connects to what I fixed before

  The first item mentions account deletion and reporting user-generated content. These overlap with what I had fixed before submitting (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/torecadash-review/) (Japanese). Account deletion removed map posts too and revoked the Sign in with Apple token. Posts had a banned-word check and a report-review queue. I had also already drafted the review notes: the main features work without login, where deletion is, reporting of posts, and what Pro includes.

  So the mechanisms existed, but I lacked something to show them. The screen recording in item 1 is exactly that.

## What I learned

> In a first review, you have to show the reviewer that it works.

- The recording on a physical device is explicitly required to start from launching the app.

- Put the same content in the notes field as in the reply. You can reuse it for the next submission.

- Before submitting, check that you can answer the six questions yourself. If the answers come quickly, you save one round trip with review.

  This article summarizes the email I received. It does not include the submission ID or other identifiers.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/review-info-needed/).

# Firebase 12 does not work with Xcode 15.2 (Swift 6.0 required): why I pinned Firebase 11.4.0 and AdMob 11.5.0

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/xcode152-sdk/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of Torecadash / October 2026

  I build my iOS app, Torecadash, on a 2017 Mac with Xcode 15.2. In this environment, newer versions of the Firebase iOS SDK and the AdMob (Google Mobile Ads) SDK do not build. This is which version breaks and which version I pinned, written from my hand-over notes (July 2026).

  The version numbers are as of July 2026. The situation may be different with the latest versions today.

## The environment

- Mac: MacBook Pro 13-inch (2017). macOS tops out at Ventura (13.7.8) and cannot go higher.

- Xcode: 15.2, the latest that runs on Ventura. It officially supports up to iOS 17.2.

- My iPhone runs iOS 26, so I cannot install onto the device from the local Xcode with a cable. The only way to test on the device is to build with Xcode Cloud and distribute through TestFlight.

- Locally I only check that xcodebuild compiles. SwiftUI previews almost never render on this Mac.

## Firebase: pinned to 11.4.0

  The newer the Firebase iOS SDK, the newer the Xcode it requires. My notes recorded this:

    Firebase version | What happens

    12.0.0 and later | Requires a Swift 6.0 toolchain (Xcode 16.2 or later)

    11.12.0 and later | Also requires Xcode 16.2

    11.5.0 onward | A bug in FirebaseDataEncoder.swift (Firebase issue #15029)

    11.4.0 | Confirmed to work reliably

  So I set the Swift Package Manager rule to Exact Version 11.4.0. Xcode keeps suggesting the latest version, and I do not follow it.

  One point is easy to get confused about. Xcode Cloud (the cloud build) runs the latest Xcode, but the pinned setting is kept as it is, so cloud builds succeed without trouble. If you pin to suit the old local Xcode, the same version also builds on the newer Xcode in the cloud.

## AdMob: pinned to 11.5.0

  For the same reason, I pinned the AdMob SDK (swift-package-manager-google-mobile-ads) to 11.5.0 (July 22, 2026).

- 11.6.0 and later: The SDK depends on Apple's MarketplaceKit, which requires Xcode 15.3 or later. On Xcode 15.2 the build fails at link time with Undefined symbols errors related to MarketplaceKit.

- A caveat for 11.5.0: This version does not yet have the new Swift-style class names (BannerView, RewardedAd, and so on). You have to use the old names with the GAD prefix (GADBannerView, GADRewardedAd, GADRequest, GADMobileAds, GADFullScreenContentDelegate, and so on).

  When I upgrade Xcode and raise the version later, I will need to rewrite the class names, not only change the version number. I left that in my notes.

## What I would tell someone in the same situation

- Pin with “Exact Version.” With an “up to next” rule, Xcode picks a newer version you cannot use.

- Write down “from which version it breaks,” with version numbers. A few months later, when you have forgotten why you pinned, the reason is still there.

- The limits of your local environment can be relaxed in the cloud. You can keep testing on a real device through Xcode Cloud and TestFlight even with an old Mac. (The free tier has a monthly limit, though. See builds not arriving in TestFlight (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/torecadash-ci/), in Japanese.)

## What I have not verified

  The version numbers in this article come from my July 2026 notes. I have not checked what the Xcode 15.2 constraints look like with versions released since. The “breaks from this version” boundaries are the build results at that time.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/xcode152-sdk/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# iOS app freezes and is killed (0x8BADF00D): a SwiftUI computed property ran on every redraw

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/torecadash-watchdog/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of Torecadash / October 2026

  For my iOS app, Torecadash, I received a report: “the app crashes a lot.” Reading the device log, I found that the app froze and was force-quit by the OS. The cause was that it recounted 951 articles every time the screen was redrawn. This is written from my commit history.

## What the log showed

  The hang log from the device had the exit code 0x8BADF00D and the line Failed to terminate gracefully after 5.0s. It means the OS (the watchdog) killed an app that did not respond within 5 seconds. The main thread was stuck in processing that went through NSKeyedArchiver. The device was also hot (Thermal State: serious), so work that normally finishes instantly took more than 5 seconds.

## The real cause

  What froze was the list of product articles in the “Following” tab, in a case with 951 articles.

  The article list (articles) was just a computed property. SwiftUI evaluates the view (body) many times, even when the article data has not changed. Each time, it redid four filters, a transformation and a sort over 951 articles on the main thread.

  Normally this finishes instantly, so you do not notice. Only when the device slows down from heat does it exceed 5 seconds and get killed.

## The fix

  I changed it to recompute on a background thread only when something actually changes: the article data, the receive mode, or the sort option. The result goes into a state for display (displayArticles, @State), so the main thread is no longer blocked.

  // (Illustration only. Not the actual code.)
// Before: every time body is evaluated
var articles: [Article] { fetched.filter…filter…map…sorted }

// After: compute in the background only on change, and keep the result
@State var displayArticles: [Article] = []
// recompute when fetchedArticles / receiveMode / sortOption change

## What I have not verified

  The only verification recorded in the commit is that xcodebuild succeeded (BUILD SUCCEEDED). There is no record that the freeze is gone on a real device. A hot device is hard to reproduce, so it is not easy to check. In this article I write “I identified the cause and changed the approach,” not “I fixed it.”

## What I learned

> Work that is instant on a normal day stops the app on a slow day.
  Computed properties are easy to write. But if you put one where it runs on every redraw, it gets slower in proportion to the amount of data. 951 items is not a small number. The obvious lesson, “decide where to put things by how often they are called,” came from a real device log.

  This article was written from the commit record (October 5, 2026).

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/torecadash-watchdog/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# No builds arriving in TestFlight: I had used up the 25 free Xcode Cloud hours (my first diagnosis was wrong)

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/torecadash-ci/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of Torecadash / October 2026

  While developing my iOS app, Torecadash, I hit a bug: “new builds are not arriving in TestFlight.” The first cause I came up with was wrong. This is where I went wrong, how I noticed, and what the real cause was, written from the numbers in my hand-over notes and commits.

## The first diagnosis: “[ci skip] is the cause”

  On September 2, I got a report: “there have been no builds since 9/1.” My first diagnosis was that [ci skip] in my commit messages was stopping the builds. I had been adding it to documentation-only changes so they would not use up Xcode Cloud’s free tier (25 hours a month). Along with the diagnosis, I even wrote a rule: “do not use [ci skip].”

## The timeline did not fit

  Looking at Xcode Cloud in App Store Connect, it said:

> You have reached your usage limit. The limit resets on September 8, your renewal date.
  Usage over the last 30 days was 493 builds, 28 hours 14 minutes. The free tier is 25 hours a month, so it was used up.

  What showed my first diagnosis was wrong was the timeline. Only three commits carried [ci skip], all on September 2. The builds had stopped on September 1. The cause came after the effect, so it could not be the cause. Worse, the rule I made was counterproductive when the quota was short.

## Why did it run 493 times?

  The workflow’s start condition was “any file changed.” Counting commits over the last 30 days:

    Last 30 days | Count

    All commits | 1,146

    of which touched the iOS app | 219 (19%)

    Builds run by Xcode Cloud | 493 (3.4 minutes each on average)

  So 80% of the time, I was building the whole iOS app although only server code or documents had changed. On top of that, “Clean build” was checked, so every build skipped the cache and took as long as possible.

## The fix is a setting, not a marker

- Change the start condition to custom file and folder rules, limited to the iOS app folder and the Xcode project.

- Uncheck “Clean build.”

  My hand-over notes estimate this takes builds from 493 to about 94, and time from 28 hours to about 5.4 hours a month. That is a calculated estimate, not a measurement after the change.

## What I learned

> Check whether a cause explains the facts, using the timeline, before settling on it.
  My first diagnosis stopped at the first plausible cause. Something that happened after the effect cannot be its cause. This check takes a minute if done before announcing the diagnosis. In my hand-over notes (§183) I left a warning that “this diagnosis was wrong,” as a record.

  The numbers in this article come from my hand-over notes and the commit record (September 2, 2026).

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/torecadash-ci/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# Firebase Auth: force-quitting the app created anonymous accounts in bulk (waiting for currentUser to restore)

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/apple-signin/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of Torecadash / October 2026

  In my iOS app, Torecadash, a user reported: “once I kill the app, it asks me to sign in with Apple again.” When I looked, 17 of the 19 users were anonymous accounts that had been created and thrown away. The cause was how I checked, with a single line, right after launch. This is from my hand-over notes and the commit record (August 14, 2026).

## The symptom

  It only happened when the app was fully quit by swiping it away and then launched again. Leaving to the home screen and coming back did not trigger it.

## Looking at the real data

  I opened the Authentication user list in the Firebase console:

    Users | Count

    Total | 19

    Signed in with Apple | 2

    Throwaway anonymous accounts (created and last signed in on the same day) | 17

  Ten of the 17 were from August 13 alone. A new anonymous account was being created every time the app started again.

## Cause: reading something that had not been restored yet, synchronously

  Right after launch, the app checked Auth.auth().currentUser on the spot. If nobody was signed in, it created a new anonymous account.

  But as Firebase’s own documentation says, currentUser is not guaranteed to be restored from the Keychain yet right after launch. If restoration is late, it looks as if nobody is signed in. Then, just before the existing Apple sign-in state is restored, the app creates a new anonymous account. It is a race condition.

  The race only happens on a cold start. When the app returns from the background, Firebase is not initialized again, so it does not happen. That matches the report exactly.

## The fix

- Stop checking synchronously. The moment restoration is known to be finished is the first call of the state listener (addStateDidChangeListener). I made the decision only at that point.

- Add one safety net. At launch, the account-management side (AccountStore) now compares against the real server-side state with reload(), corrects any mismatch with its local record, and leaves a diagnostic log.

## One more thing I found

  During the investigation I learned that Sign in with Apple had never succeeded on a real device since I implemented it on August 7.

- The first error was that the sign-in provider configuration could not be found. The Apple provider had never been enabled in the Firebase console.

- After I enabled it, a new error said the credential was already linked. An attempt made before enabling had actually gone halfway through, and the Apple ID was already linked to this device’s anonymous account. The app showed this as an error, but in effect the user was signed in. I changed it to treat it as success.

## What I have not verified

  This is an iOS-side change, so I cannot confirm the effect on a real device until it reaches TestFlight. My notes say the top priority is to check that the Apple link survives repeated force-quits and relaunches. There is no result in the record at the time of writing.

## What I learned

> The state right after launch is not settled yet.

- “Not restored yet” is different from “none.” If you decide “none” without waiting, you create a new one.

- Symptoms show up in real data. Opening the console showed 17 throwaway accounts. I would have had a hard time finding this by reproducing “the sign-in disappears” on my own device.

- “Never succeeded” shows up as a missing success record. The clue was that none of the registered accounts had any Apple information.

  This article summarizes my hand-over notes and the commit record (August 14, 2026).

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/apple-signin/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

URL: https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/logo-pop/

# A canvas becomes twice as large on Retina: inset:0 does not stretch it (a bug in a logo that bursts when you tap it)

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/logo-pop/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of Koshin Studio / October 2026

  The top of this site has a large logo. When you tap a letter, it pops and particles scatter. After I rebuilt the logo with my own typeface, I was told “the particles come out of a strange place, not from the letter” and “it is still shifted to the right.” It took three stages to fix. Here are the cause and how I found it, with measured numbers.

## Rebuilding the logo with my own typeface

  The old logo was set in Latin letters built on a Mincho skeleton. I replaced it with my own typeface, Koshin Pop (rounded Latin letterforms drawn from scratch). The font is under the SIL Open Font License 1.1, which allows use in a logo.

  I extract the outlines of the nine letters K O S H I N T U D from the font file and turn them into SVG paths (tools/logotype_pop.py). The logo is delivered as a picture, so the site does not ship the font file. The font has several shapes for the same letter (base, pop1, pop2), so I lined up three combinations and picked the one with the best rhythm.

## Stage 1: after a tap, the letter did not return to its place

  I recorded positions over time after a tap. The letters did not return to where they started.

    Letter | Center before | 2 s after

    K (top left) | (327, 306) | (320, 313)

    S (bottom left) | (331, 442) | (323, 435)

  That is about 7 px off. A matrix(1, 0, 0, 1, -46, -42) was left over: the scale was back to 1 but the position offset stayed.

  Cause: the animation library (GSAP) rewrote the position that was already set on the letter’s SVG <g> (transform="translate(x,0)") using its own calculation, and part of that correction remained afterward.

  Fix: I split the element into a layer that holds the position (outer <g transform>) and a layer that moves (inner <g class="ks-ch">), and switched the motion to the browser’s Web Animations (when it ends, the effect disappears and the original state returns). I checked all 12 letters: the centers did not move, and the transform after the animation went back to none.

## Stage 2: “it is still to the right”

  After that fix I was still told the animation sat to the right. My measurement said particles started within 2 to 13 px of the letter’s center. What I measured and what was seen disagreed.

  I had measured on a 1x display, counting particle positions in screen coordinates. When I measured on 2x (Retina) and 3x (phone) displays, the CSS size of the particle canvas (#burst) was wrong.

    Display | Viewport width | Canvas width (before) | (after)

    1280 px, 1x | 1280 | 1280 | 1280

    1440 px, 2x | 1440 | 2880 | 1440

    390 px, 3x (phone) | 390 | 780 | 390

  Cause: I positioned the canvas with inset:0 in CSS, but a replaced element such as a canvas does not stretch to fill with inset:0 alone. It keeps its intrinsic size (its pixel count). On a 2x display the pixel count is doubled, so the CSS size doubled too, and particles appeared at twice the coordinates (toward the lower right). On a 1x display the sizes are equal, so you cannot notice.

  Fix: set width and height to 100% explicitly. After the fix, the canvas matched the viewport on every pixel ratio.

## Stage 3: emit from the letter itself

  Finally I was asked whether particles could come from the letter itself. Until then they came from the center of the letter’s box, so for a letter with an empty middle like “O” they seemed to come from nowhere.

  I now pick points along the outline of the letter’s path (getPointAtLength), take their on-screen positions, and send particles outward from the letter’s center with some scatter. The bottom row is drawn as “letter = mask”, so I look up the path inside the mask that the rect refers to. In the captures, “O” emits from around its ring and “U” along its shape.

## What I learned

> When measured numbers and what people see disagree, suspect the conditions of the measurement.

- The viewer’s screen is not yours. I measured only on a 1x display and judged “the offset is small.” On a 2x display the particles came out at twice the position.

- Measure in the space people look at. I counted logical coordinates, so the on-screen offset was never visible to me.

- Measure the state after an animation ends, too. That letters did not return was invisible while I only watched the motion.

- Keep position and motion on different layers. If one element holds both, one overwrites the other.

  The numbers come from operating this site’s top page in a real browser (Chrome) on October 8, 2026. I have not confirmed the fix on an actual Retina device; I reproduced 2x and 3x pixel ratios with browser settings.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/logo-pop/).

# I counted “duplicates are practically zero,” but the audit reported 112 pairs

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/dup-zero/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of Torecadash / October 2026

  My iOS app Torecadash has a job that merges “duplicates,” where one product is registered as several products, every night. One day I counted by myself and recorded “duplicates are practically zero.” But the repository audit reported 112 pairs. My way of measuring was wrong. This is the story from my commit record.

  This is a development log of the app.

## I counted zero, and 112 pairs appeared

  Looking at the 112 pairs, for example one trading-card booster pack was registered split into 7 entries, even though the merge job was supposed to run every night.

## Cause: it timed out partway through, every night

  Running the merge over all genres takes about 15 minutes. But the time budget I had given the nightly scheduled run was 480 seconds (8 minutes). The order always starts from the same genre (Pokémon). So every night it timed out in the middle of Pokémon, and the later genres were never reached.

  My count was “zero” because only the range I was looking at (the first genre) was clean.

## The fix

- Rotate. Start from the genre after where the last run stopped, and stop when the time budget (6 minutes) is used up. The next night continues from where it stopped.

- First, run it to completion by hand. Running all genres to the end by hand took duplicates from 112 pairs to 0 and products from 2,753 to 2,570.

## What I already knew: one pass is not enough

  Two days earlier (September 5), I had learned something else about merging. When A is merged into B, B’s name can become the same as another C. Then one pass is not enough. In real data:

    Pass | Merged | Result

    1st | 138 | 53 new same-name pairs appeared

    2nd | 54 | 0 same-name duplicates

  Products went from 2,935 to 2,713. So the daily slot now repeats until nothing is merged (up to 3 times). This “timeout” problem sat even before that repetition.

## Three more things the same day

- Six open lotteries had disappeared because of another product’s list price. A 7,200 yen lottery (the official 360 yen × 20 packs) had been compared with another product’s list price of 27,500 yen left on the article and rejected by price. I added a condition: “fix only when it can be proven.” Across all real data, 10 matched the condition and all were sales at a normal price. I restored 11 to visible.

- False alarms in matching. Of 17 “article exists but hidden,” 9 had a replacement article visible under a different spelling of the same shop (like two different kanji spellings of the same store name). If the replacement is visible, it now counts as covered, which moved coverage from 87% to 90% and hidden items from 17 to 4.

- The audit itself had stopped. The reader part for audits misread a regular expression right after => as a division, and four audits were failing with ReferenceError. I changed it so that names it could not cut out are reported with a reason instead of being skipped silently.

## What I learned

> When you count “zero,” first doubt what you counted.

- The range you looked at is not necessarily everything. Only the first genre was processed every night, so counting only the first genre looks clean.

- For time-limited jobs, check whether it finished. Running and reaching the end are different.

- The tool that counts also breaks. When an audit has stopped, the result looks like “0 items.” You need a way to notice that it stopped.

  This article is written from my commit record (September 5 and 7, 2026).

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/dup-zero/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# Making a 10-second stopwatch ranking fair: 3 decimals, ties and write counts

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/stopwatch-rank/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of the 10-second stopwatch / October 2026

  Stop at exactly 10 seconds! (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/) is a game where you count ten seconds in your head and stop. It is three rounds and the smaller your error, the better. When I added a ranking to it, I had to decide “what is fair” in three places. This is written from the README and code comments in the repository.

## Display down to three decimals

  Error is measured with the browser’s performance.now(). According to the README, this clock is deliberately made less precise as a security measure (Spectre). Chrome is in 5-microsecond steps, Safari and Firefox in 1 millisecond.

  What would happen if error were shown to 6 decimal places? A device with a coarser clock more easily ends in 000 and gets an advantage. The README’s guess is that iPhones would take the top ranks. So I decided to cut to 3 decimals and align all devices. For the start of measurement, I use event.timeStamp of pointerdown rather than click, because click adds extra delay.

## Ties happen more than you think

  With 3 decimals, an exact 0.000 comes up with probability 1/1000 per attempt. The chance that any one of three attempts is 0.000 is about 1/333. If you build a “best of three” board, ties at 0.000 will pile up.

  So for a tie, the one with the smaller total error in the other two attempts ranks higher. If that is equal too, whoever submitted first. Someone who hit 0.000 and also did well on the other two ranks above, so they can be told apart from someone with one lucky attempt.

  The “total” and “average” rankings have exactly the same order (it is just division by 3), so they are one board. Separately I placed a “best single attempt” board. The idea is that the average is skill and the best single is luck.

## Counting writes

  The ranking is built on Cloudflare Workers and KV (a key-value store). According to the code comments, KV writes are 1,000 a day on the free tier. To stay within that, I decided the following.

- The board for each mode is stored under one key. One submission writes at most twice (today’s and all-time).

- Submissions that do not make the ranking, and submissions with the same name that are worse than before, are not written at all.

- Only one row is kept per name. One person cannot fill the board.

  Also, since scores are reported by the client, cheating cannot be prevented. The README says so. So I operate on the assumption that it is reset every day. Days are cut in Japan time, and today’s board disappears in 3 days.

## What I fixed around the launch

- The range of accepted error. I accept up to the slowest result the screen can show (99.999 seconds in 10-second mode). Even terrible results are accepted, since they will not stay on the board anyway.

- Do not cache the read before a write. If KV reads have a short cache, a new value is written over a stale one and submissions that came in between disappear. Only the read before a write has no cache. View-only reads stay cached.

- Retry when it could not connect. At first, if the game could not reach the ranking when it opened, it did not show the ranking box and never tried again. Even if the ranking backend came up while playing, there was no way back. When three attempts are done and the box is still hidden, it now reads once more.

- Stay quiet. Until it connects, the ranking box is not shown at all and there is no apology message. I decided that being silent is better than showing an empty box or red text.

## A stumble on launch day

  When I first deployed to Cloudflare Pages, I did not pass --branch. The name of the working branch I happened to be on was registered as the production branch of Pages. After that, deploying with --branch main only went to a preview, and the public URL did not change. I did not notice for an hour.

  I fixed the production branch to main in the dashboard. One more thing I had confused: the branch name shown on the “Production” row of the deployment list is the name at the time that deployment was made and is not rewritten when you change the setting. To see the setting, look at the “Production branch” column in the project list.

## What I learned

> Fairness is made of digits, ties and write counts.
  None of them looks like what makes a game fun. But cutting to three decimals and deciding tie-breaking in advance directly affect how convincing the ranking feels to players.

  This article is written from the repository’s README, code comments and the commit record (September 8 to 12, 2026). The clock precision per browser is as stated in the README.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/stopwatch-rank/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# From 16,177 titles to 6,091: how the anime quiz database was built by dropping over 60%

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/anime-db/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of the Anime Type Diagnosis / October 2026

  The Hardcore Anime Type Diagnosis (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/shindananime/) picks your “one anime of fate” from a database of more than 6,000 titles. Where did these 6,000 come from, and how were they narrowed down? This is how the quiz’s data was built, from the repository’s commits and the current real numbers.

## Three sources

- The title list of Annict (an anime tracking service): 15,971 entries.

- Anime on Filmarks (a movie and anime review service): 7,247 entries.

- My own list of classics: about 500 titles.

  The same title is merged into one. After merging there are 16,177 entries. From these I keep only what is usable for the quiz.

## The criterion for keeping: “clues to place it on the axes”

  The quiz describes each title on 6 axes (worldview, aftertaste, structure, subtaste, visuals, viewing style) and picks by closeness to your answers. So each title needs enough “clues to place it on the axes.”

  The clues are estimated from the number of words that appear in reviews (the review text itself is not kept; only the number of words is counted). Disparaging phrasing and negations such as “the animation collapsed” or “I did not cry” are not counted. A phrase like “god-tier animation” is not double counted. This “richness of clues” is given as a number from 0 to 1, and titles below 0.25 are dropped.

  Also, by default I exclude continuations of TV series and spin-off theatrical films (such as Doraemon or Conan movies). Standalone original films are kept.

     | Count | Share

    Titles after merging | 16,177 | 100%

    Dropped for too few clues | 10,086 | 62.3%

    Kept (the database) | 6,091 | 37.7%

  More than 60% of titles were dropped because they lacked clues. The quiz also does not use titles whose values on every axis are close to neutral (absolute value 0.15 or less). That removes 17 more, so the quiz actually uses 6,074 titles.

## What the remaining 6,091 look like

  The data was made on September 25, 2026, and I counted it again on October 8.

    Source | Titles

    Listed on both Annict and Filmarks | 4,354

    Filmarks only | 1,077

    Annict only | 619

    My classics list only | 41

    Richness of clues | Titles | Share

    0.8 or more (plenty) | 3,388 | 55.6%

    0.6 to 0.8 | 639 | 10.5%

    0.4 to 0.6 | 1,148 | 18.8%

    0.25 to 0.4 (barely) | 916 | 15.0%

  The median richness is 0.92. But 15% passed only barely. The axis values for these titles are less certain than for the others.

    Decade of broadcast | Titles

    2020s | 2,591

    2010s | 1,996

    2000s | 926

    1990s | 291

    1980s | 166

    1970s | 83

    1960s | 20

  Titles from 2000 onward make up 90.5%. I think older titles tend to have fewer words in reviews and find it harder to meet the criterion (this is a guess, not confirmed). Titles with an image number 5,632 (92.5%).

## Weak points of this method

- It is biased toward new and much-discussed titles. The more words in reviews, the more likely a title stays. Older titles and those rarely discussed are likely to drop. The quiz has a decade question that decides how much to downweight older titles, but the pool itself already leans toward newer ones.

- The number of clues is “how much was said,” not “taste.” Estimating 6 axes from word counts is a rough approximation.

- The data is as of when it was made. New titles have to be added every season.

## What I learned

> Most of the “6,000 titles” turned out to be “what was left of 16,000 after keeping those with clues.”
  It is tempting to say “covers all anime,” but in fact more than 60% were dropped for lack of clues. I think writing down how many I dropped and the criterion for keeping is what makes the quiz honest.

  The numbers in this article come from the quiz’s data (made on September 25, 2026 and recounted on October 8). Titles, review contents and rating scores are not included.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/anime-db/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# “80% was chosen over 82%”: the quiz’s match percentage disagreed with its ranking

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/match-percent/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of the Anime Type Diagnosis / October 2026

  At the end, the Hardcore Anime Type Diagnosis (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/shindananime/) shows “the one anime of fate” and two runners-up. Each has a number like “match 82%.” At one point this number disagreed with the ranking: “a title at 80% was chosen over a title at 82%.” I have re-measured how large the disagreement was, and I am writing it down.

## The number and the ranking used different yardsticks

  The quiz measures taste on 6 axes and computes a “closeness” (cosine similarity) for each title. But the final order is not decided by closeness alone. It is ordered by closeness × 0.82 plus the title’s rating (stars), popularity, era and taste elements (total).

  However, the match percentage on screen was built from closeness alone. The order was by the total and the display by closeness: two yardsticks. A title could rank first by total but have a lower closeness than second place. Then the screen showed “1st 80%, 2nd 82%.”

## The fix

  I changed it so the percentage comes from the same total as the order (September 25, 2026). The same day I fixed another contradiction in the display. Even when an axis bar’s value was exactly 0, it showed “leans X 50%.” It said it leaned when it did not. I made the minimum 51%.

## How big was the disagreement? Measure it

  The commit of the time does not keep the proportion. So I measured with the same 1,000 synthetic respondents (answering all 50 questions) as in the 12-question article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/shindan12/) (in Japanese). For the top 3 titles, I compare how the screen display would look in three ways.

- Old: integer % computed from closeness.

- Middle: integer % computed from total.

- Now: % to one decimal place computed from total.

  I counted two things. “Reversal” is when the 1st place % is lower than the 2nd or 3rd place %. “Tie” is when 1st and 2nd look like the same %. Answer noise is small (0.3), medium (0.5) and large (0.8).

    Display | Answer noise | Reversal | 1st and 2nd tied

    Old (closeness, integer) | Small | 40.3% | 14.1%

    Medium | 37.7% | 15.3%

    Large | 35.1% | 15.3%

    Middle (total, integer) | Small | 0.0% | 31.7%

    Medium | 0.0% | 30.1%

    Large | 0.0% | 27.7%

    Now (total, one decimal) | Small | 0.0% | 3.6%

    Medium | 0.0% | 3.9%

    Large | 0.0% | 3.8%

  With the old display, the top three were shown in reversed order for 35 to 40% of respondents. By this calculation about 2 in 5 people saw “the chosen first place is lower than the runner-up.”

## Fixing it produced another problem

  Computing from the total made reversals 0%. But with integer percentages, 1st and 2nd looking like the same % rose to around 30%. The top has titles with close totals. Rounding to integers erases the difference and they gather on the same number.

  So I changed the display to one decimal place (like 99.6%). Ties dropped to about 4%. It does not reach 0% because sometimes the totals really differ by less than 0.1%.

## Weak points of this measurement

- The respondents are synthetic. Real people answer differently.

- “Old” is a reconstruction: today’s ordering with the old display method applied. I did not run the code of that time. At the time, ratings and taste boosts had no cap, and the results may have differed.

- What I measured is only “does the display agree with the ranking,” not “is the ranking right for that person.”

## What I learned

> Make the number you show from the same yardstick you used to sort.
  It sounds obvious, but as calculations were added, only the order changed and the displayed number was left behind. Another point: rounding can erase a difference in rank. Where differences are small, just adding one digit brings back the visible order.

  The numbers in this article were measured on October 8, 2026 with 1,000 synthetic respondents (random numbers fixed). The commit record of that time is September 25, 2026.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/match-percent/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# The streaming buttons were shown even for titles you could not watch: making the quiz result screen true

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/result-screen/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of the Anime Type Diagnosis / October 2026

  The result screen of the Hardcore Anime Type Diagnosis (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/shindananime/) shows the cover of your title of fate and “where to watch” buttons. When I first built it, both the buttons and the images showed things that differed from reality. I recounted with my own data how large the difference was, and I am writing it down.

## The streaming buttons were the same two for every title

  In the first version, the streaming buttons on the result screen were only DMM TV and U-NEXT, the same two for any title. Pressing a button goes to that service’s search page. But the title is not necessarily available there.

  The quiz data includes, for each title, “which services stream it” (Filmarks streaming information). Of 6,091 titles, 4,489 (73.7%) have this. Counting whether the two buttons of that time really pointed to a place where you can watch, for these 4,489:

    The two buttons of that time | Titles | Share

    Both point to a place you can watch | 3,192 | 71.1%

    At least one points to a place you cannot watch | 1,297 | 28.9%

      of which both are places you cannot watch | 295 | 6.6%

  For one title in three or four, pressing the button did not find the title. It ended in “page not found.”

## The fix: narrow by real availability

- I increased the services from 2 to 12 (Netflix, Prime Video, Disney+, U-NEXT, Hulu, DMM TV, ABEMA, d Anime Store, FOD, TELASA, Lemino, Bandai Channel). I opened the search URLs in a browser to check them.

- Buttons are made only for services in that title’s availability.

- But showing all of them would stretch the result card too tall. I sort by major services first (priority Netflix, Prime Video, Disney+, U-NEXT, Hulu) and show only the top 3.

- For titles with unknown availability (the remaining 26.3%), there is no way to check, so I show the top 3 by popularity as before.

  Along the way I noticed that DMM TV’s search URL returned 404 (I changed /vod/search/ to /vod/list/).

  Availability is as of the time the data was collected. Streaming changes, so a title may not still be there when you press the button.

## The same thing was happening with images

  Some cover images were wrong or did not appear.

- http images do not appear. The quiz is served over https. If an image URL is http://, the browser blocks it as mixed content. (One official site had no certificate at all.) I treat http images as “none” and fill from an https image that comes later.

- Placeholder pictures were shown as real. “No image” placeholders and generic images shared by an official site are not the actual art. I now reject them.

- Logos got mixed in. Filmarks’ sharing image is a 240×240 square, and if the poster is not square, the company’s logo is put in the margin. I changed it to prefer another image embedded in the page (260×364, kept in the poster ratio). After re-fetching all 7,247 entries, the number using a poster-ratio image rose to 4,477 (89 are still in the old shape).

- No image at all. Most of the cause was that Annict and Filmarks split titles differently, so matching titles failed. By filling from images of the same series, the share with an image went from 77% to 86%.

  In the end, 92.5% of the 6,091 titles used by the quiz have an image.

## What I learned

> On a result screen, trust is decided less by looks than by “what happens when I press it.”

- Showing the same thing to everyone is easy, but wrong nearly 3 times in 10. Look at the real situation (availability) and narrow.

- Decide what to show when you “don’t know.” For the 26.3% with unknown availability, I fell back to the normal top 3.

- Reject what is not the real thing. Placeholders, generic images and images with a logo are worse than a blank, I decided.

  The shares in this article were counted on the quiz data (6,091 titles) as of October 8, 2026. The image counts come from the commit record (September 25, 2026).

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/result-screen/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)
