URL: https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/first-visit/

# Cutting six buttons to one: first-time players did not know what to press

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/first-visit/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of Sushi Stack / October 2026

  The title screen of Sushi Stack (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/) had six things you could press. Someone opening it for the first time did not know which to press. For the game portal launch, I narrowed “what a first-time player presses first” to one. I also wrote down, from my commits, two problems I fixed at the same time: saves vanishing, and what happens when you leave the screen.

## What a portal measures you by

  According to the commit, the portal I decided to submit to (CrazyGames) first has a trial stage (Basic Launch) shown to a limited audience for two weeks. Whether you move up to the next stage (Full Launch) is decided by these three things during that time.

- The share of people who start playing

- Average time played

- The share of people who come back

  Ads are disabled during this trial, so these are all that matters now. In other words, I had to improve two things by design: “people who open it start playing” and “they come back.”

## I narrowed it to one thing to press

  The title had six: Play, Menu, Ranking, Encyclopedia, Words and Info. To a first-timer, they all look equally heavy. So I rearranged it:

- One large “Play.”

- “Menu” as a thin second option.

- Ranking, Encyclopedia, Words and Info are folded into a thin row below.

  The ranking and the encyclopedia are “reasons to come back,” but they are not the first step the first time. That was my judgment.

## From the second visit, show that there is more

  The title shows the high score and how much of the encyclopedia is filled. But not to first-timers, because showing 0 points and 0 kinds means nothing.

## Inside the portal, saves vanish

  The portal runs the game in an iframe on a different domain. In some browsers, saving to the device (localStorage) is blocked inside it, and high scores and the encyclopedia vanish every time.

  If the portal provides a storage shelf (CrazyGames’ Data Module), I save there; if not, I keep it on the device as before. The portal’s part arrives later, so it keeps looking until it is found.

  The way I verified it was to plug in a fake storage shelf. When the shelf exists, it writes there and not to the device. Even in an environment where saving to the device throws an error, it starts and can be played.

## Leave the screen and it stops

  Until then, when you moved to another tab, only the deadline kept advancing, and it was already over when you came back. Now, when sent to the background, it pauses and the sound stops too. I actually fired the event for the screen being hidden (visibilitychange) and confirmed that it stops, that the score does not move after 1.5 seconds, and that it resumes.

## What I verified

- In all 14 languages, it fits on an iPhone SE screen.

- Across 7 screens × 3 languages, the 9:16 aspect ratio does not break.

- Two full playthroughs (163 moves in Japanese, 263 in English) at 60 fps with 0 errors.

## What I learned

> What a first-timer needs is not choices but a first step.

- “A reason to come back” and “the first step” are different things. The ranking and the encyclopedia have value, but they are not what a first-timer presses first.

- Saving may be unavailable depending on where it runs. That it worked on my machine does not guarantee it works inside a frame.

- Design what happens when someone leaves the screen. It is easy to build assuming people are watching all the time.

  This article is written from my commit record (September 7, 2026). The portal’s review conditions are as stated in the commit. After this, the game was rejected in review (Rejected by CrazyGames (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/crazygames/)).

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/first-visit/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)


---

URL: https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/typo-catalog/

# A typo born once multiplied across shops: the “30th SEREBRATION” incident

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/typo-catalog/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of Torecadash / October 2026

  In my iOS app Torecadash, a user reported: “this article duplicates another one, and the product name is odd.” When I looked, a misspelled product created just once was being reused every time an article from a shop arrived, and it kept multiplying. The cause, the fix, and the limits of the fix are written from my commit record.

  This is a development log of the app.

## What was reported

  Articles for the Pokémon Card product “30th CELEBRATION” were appearing at several shops under the product name “30th SEREBRATION” (a misspelling of CELEBRATION). They also duplicated the articles with the correct name for the same product.

## Root cause: a short heading did not match the official name

  Summaries posted by roundup sites have short headings like “‘30th CELEBRATION’.” The official name in the app’s catalog is “Expansion Pack ‘30th CELEBRATION’.” The short heading is shorter than the official name, so a one-direction check of “does the article title contain the official name” did not match.

  When there was no match, it went to AI matching. Along that path, just once, a misspelled product “30th SEREBRATION” was created. My commit guesses it came from a mistake when converting another spelling in the catalog (“30th セレブレーション” in katakana) to the Latin alphabet.

  The real trouble came next. Once a misspelled product is created, it is reused repeatedly as an “existing product.” Each time a new article arrived from a shop, the same typo and the same duplicate were mass-produced.

## First, fix the data

  I checked all shops. At three shops including Bic Camera, Sanyodo Shoten and Game Plaza, it duplicated an article with the correct name, so I hid one of each. The other 10 articles only needed their product reassigned. 13 articles in total. I deleted the misspelled product.

  I left one thing alone on purpose. The existing tool for merging products judged “SEREBRATION” and “CELEBRATION” as different products and refused. That gate is intentionally strict, so I did not loosen it. I fixed these by hand, one by one.

## The real prevention: pick up short headings by “exact match”

  Fixing the data alone would let it happen again. So I fixed the matching with the official catalog. I strip one generic form word (such as “Expansion Pack”) from the front of the official name, and treat it as the same product only when what remains exactly matches the article title.

  I chose “exact match” instead of “contains” so as not to pick up more specific, different products such as “30th CELEBRATION Card Set X.” Now it matches the official catalog correctly from the start, and never reaches the AI matching path where the typo was born. The results I confirmed:

- “30th CELEBRATION” matches the official product correctly.

- The misspelled “30th SEREBRATION” does not match (it is not wrongly treated as official).

- Existing exact matches, other genres and unrelated set names behave as before.

## Safety net: an edit-distance check, and its limits

  As a precaution, I also added a check at the point just before a product is created: “a candidate with a small edit distance from the official catalog is strongly suspected to be a typo, so reject it.” But this check alone cannot catch “30th SEREBRATION” against “Expansion Pack ‘30th CELEBRATION’.” The difference in length is too large, so the edit distance is far (I confirmed this).

  So the safety net does not work for this case. What works is the main fix above. I kept the safety net to catch other typos of the same length (for example, Weiss Schwarz names missing a “/”). I also built a read-only audit that finds catalog entries suspected of typos. At the time of the commit it found 21 suspects of the same shape.

## What I learned

> A mistake born once becomes “existing,” and multiplies.

- Wrong data multiplies by itself. What was created becomes the thing reused next time. Fixing the data is not enough; you have to fix the path by which it is born.

- “Exact match” over “contains.” Picking up widely drags in other products.

- Check the limits of a safety net and write them down. Instead of assuming “this check prevents it,” I checked first that it does not work for this typo.

- Do not loosen a strict gate. What the merge tool rejected was the correct behavior.

  This article is written from my commit record (September 28, 2026). How the typo was born is the commit’s guess.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/typo-catalog/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# The “9-pack set” was nine different products: the same product that never matched

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/torecadash-9set/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of Torecadash / October 2026

  My iOS app Torecadash collects lottery and first-come sale information for trading cards and notifies users. To check for gaps, I match and count listings on other roundup sites (Chusen Zukan, Pokechu) against the articles in my own app. When I measured on October 7, most gaps came from a small discrepancy: the same product that never matched. This is from my hand-over notes and commit record.

  This is a development log of the app.

## What I measured

  With read-only access, I checked “are all lotteries introduced by the roundup sites shown in the app?”

- Chusen Zukan: of 90 open lotteries, 49 (54%) were displayed in the app. 12 had an article but were hidden, and 29 were not in the feed.

- Pokechu: 18 of 21 (86%).

- X roundup posts: 606 posts in 72 hours. Only 9 linked to an article.

## Of the 12 hidden, 7 were because the row was wrong

  Looking at the 12 hidden, in 7 the roundup site’s row named a different product from the application page. Four shops of one chain said “energy card set,” and three others said “expansion pack.” The application page (the lottery form) and the shop’s X account showed it was actually a “card set, 9-pack set, 10,800 yen.”

  The app’s “price gate” (which rejects items whose listing price does not match the product’s list price) was correctly rejecting them. What was wrong was not the gate but the product mix-up. I reassigned the products and restored them to visible.

## What the “9-pack set” really was

  This “9-pack set” is a card set of Pokémon Card 30th CELEBRATION, which is 9 products, each a set of the starter trio from nine generations. The catalog had these 9 products registered correctly from the beginning. But each time a marketplace listing or X monitoring created a new article, a bug registered it as another product named after only one of the three, in several of the 9 products. For example, a product with only “Hinoarashi.”

## The same product, never matching

  The matching has a process that makes a “key” for comparing product names. It had a left-right asymmetry.

- On the other side, “card set 9-pack” has the trailing “9-pack” dropped before comparing.

- On the catalog side, “card set 9-kinds set” is not dropped.

  The same product never matched. As a result, the other side’s name was wrongly resolved to a different product such as “energy card set” or “expansion pack.” That was where the mix-up came from. I applied the same rule to both sides (drop “N packs,” “N kinds” and “set”), and also made names that carry a number specification not be settled to one by partial match. I confirmed that there are 0 key collisions across the whole catalog.

## Another hole: the previous article blocked the next round

  The main cause of “not in the feed” was elsewhere. The article ID was made from “roundup URL + shop + product,” and it did not include the lottery round. The expired article from the previous round stopped the new round’s article for the same shop and product from being created (“the same article ID already exists”). If the new round’s deadline is more than 1 day later than the previous one, it now creates an article with a different ID that adds the date.

## Result

    Coverage | Before | After

    Chusen Zukan (90 open) | 54% (49) | 91% (82)

    Pokechu | 86% | 90%

  The remainder are cases where the application page only says “various products” so the product cannot be identified, where the page has no clue to the shop name, and so on. They include ones I decided not to adopt for safety. The misses did not become zero.

## What I learned

> A gate that rejected correctly and wrong data are different problems.

- Before doubting what was rejected, look at why it was rejected. The price gate worked correctly; what was wrong was the product mix-up.

- The cause of “does not match” can be a left-right asymmetry in how you compare. The same product never matching was a mismatch of rules, not dirty data.

- You do not see gaps unless you count coverage. Only when the number 54% came out did I know where to fix.

  The numbers in this article come from my hand-over notes (§272, §281) and commit record (October 7, 2026).

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/torecadash-9set/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# Splitting a “9-pack set” by contents created 80 fake products

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/fake-products/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of Torecadash / October 2026

  While inspecting the product list of my iOS app Torecadash, I found 80 products that do not exist around the Pokémon Card “30th CELEBRATION Card Set.” There are only 9 official products. The other 80 were fake products created as a result of splitting a “9-pack set” by its contents. What happened and how I fixed it are written from my hand-over notes.

  This is a development log of the app.

## The 9-pack set was “one product”

  The lottery for a “card set (9-pack set)” that a shop offers is one product. In the catalog it is registered as a “9-kinds set” (10,800 yen). But the app’s product matching (the step that splits an article mentioning several products into one per product) split this title by contents. Names of the nine contents, such as “Mega Mewtwo X” and “Nyabby,” were each treated as a separate product.

  As a result, this is what it looked like:

    State | Count

    Original articles that had been split (parents) were hidden | 22

    Articles created by splitting (children) | 190 (63 visible)

    Fake products created for the children | 80

  On screen, one lottery appeared as if it were separate lotteries for each content item.

## The fix: stop the entry, then put things back

- Do not split at the entry. A title of the form “card set” + “N kinds” is not split.

- Restore the parents. I put the 22 hidden parents back onto the “9-kinds set” product. How I restored each differed (5 back to visible, 3 treated as duplicates because the same shop already had a visible 9-pack set, 13 whose deadline had passed, and 1 with no deadline).

- Detach the children. I marked the 190 children with a “wrong split” flag (hiddenByWrongSplit), hid them, and removed their link to a product.

- Delete the fake products. I deleted the 80. Before deleting, I confirmed that nothing referenced them and saved the original contents as a backup.

  There is an exception. A listing like “Starter Set ex Nyaoha / Hogator / Quaxly 3-kinds set,” where the title spells out all the product names, is still split as before. What I learned this time is that an “N-kinds set” is sold as one product.

## Other fake products found in the same inspection

- Things that are not cards. Products for apparel, figures, tournaments and music CDs had been created between September 3 and October 3. I added a gate at the entry for names that are not cards (looksLikeNonCardMerchOrEventName) and confirmed 0 false hits across the whole catalog. I deleted 25.

- Single cards. I deleted a total of 30 single-card products that came from Snkrdunk listings. Some of those single cards had a “list price.” Having a list price turned out not to be proof of an official cross-check. The proof is imageIsOfficial.

- A product combining three packs. I deleted one unofficial product that lined up several set names. Its 49 linked articles were all expired.

  To watch for these, I added an audit (audit_catalog_clean.js). Each time it counts five things: single-card products, products with several set names, mismatches between an application page’s title and the product, drift of list prices copied from products, and products with non-card names.

## What I learned

> A “split” process needs a “do not split” condition.

- Splitting one product into several multiplies fake products. Splitting should happen only after checking “is it really several products.”

- Count references before deleting. I deleted only after confirming zero references and a saved backup.

- Stop fake products at both the entry and the contents. An entry gate alone leaves what already exists. An audit counts what remains.

  This article is written from my hand-over notes (§272) (October 7, 2026). The counts are as written in the notes.

  Related

- The “9-pack set” was nine different products (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/torecadash-9set/) — the matching record for the same product

- I counted duplicates as zero, but the audit found 112 pairs (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/dup-zero/) — another record from the same day

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/fake-products/).

# Measuring Qiita’s “posting too frequently” limit: a new account could not create another article for about 30 minutes

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/qiita-post-interval/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
This site / October 2026

  I published summaries of this site’s articles on Qiita. But when I tried to create a second one right after the first, the new-article screen would not open and said “posting too frequently.” How long you have to wait did not seem to be written officially, so I measured it.

  I measured only this one new account (registered on October 8, 2026). This does not mean it is a general specification of Qiita.

## How I measured

- I record the time an article was published (for the first one, “14:19” from Qiita’s notification, which is only to the minute).

- Then about every 5 minutes, I open the “new article” screen in a logged-in browser. If it opens it is “allowed”; if I am redirected to the trend page it is “blocked.” I record this with the time.

- When it opens, I publish the next article right away and take the same record again.

- I did not do anything like slipping past the limit by posting. I only checked whether the screen opens.

## Results

    Interval | Previous article published at | Last blocked check | First allowed check | Publish until it opens

    1st → 2nd | 14:19 | 14:46:34 (blocked) | 14:51:50 (allowed) | about 27.6 to 32.8 min

    2nd → 3rd | 14:52:36 | 15:19:03 (blocked) | 15:24:18 (allowed) | about 26.5 to 31.7 min

    3rd → 4th | 15:24:59 | 15:30:29 (blocked) | 16:10:02 (allowed) | 5.5 to 45.1 min (unknown)

- The first and second were both around 30 minutes. The range exists because I only checked every 5 minutes. “It opened” somewhere between the last block and the first allow.

- The third is unusable data. The next check after 15:30:29 is not in the record until 16:10:02. The checks were not running for about 40 minutes (I have not confirmed why; the computer may have been asleep). The opening time is somewhere in there, and the interval is unknown.

- The wording “posting too frequently” could not be captured by the automatic check (I was only sent back to the trend page, and no message appeared). It is the wording I saw on my own screen.

## What I know and what I do not

> On this new account, I could not create the next article for about 30 minutes after publishing.

- Two measurements agreed at about 30 minutes. But it is only two. It is not a number that lets me say “exactly 30 minutes.”

- A personal blog from 2018 reported “you cannot post or edit for about 30 minutes after posting.” It is close to this measurement. But it is another person’s report from another time, and I do not know whether it is the same mechanism.

- I do not know whether it is a limit only for newly registered accounts or applies to ordinary ones too. I measured only one account.

- I also do not know whether the limit changes with the number of posts (from which post it gets longer), because the third was lost.

## Reflections on the measurement

- The check interval was 5 minutes. A 5-minute range was left each time. Checking every minute would shrink it.

- I did not notice that the checks had stopped. I needed a mechanism to warn me when there is no check record for a set time.

- The first publish time was only to the minute. I could take seconds only from the second onward, where I recorded the time myself.

## What I could not confirm

- Qiita’s official rule on posting interval (I looked, but found no public description).

- The interval for the third (the record is missing).

- The same measurement on other accounts.

- Whether the limit changes with the age of the account or the number of posts.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/qiita-post-interval/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# Rejected by CrazyGames with no reason given: I recorded the game and found four problems

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/crazygames/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of Sushi Stack / October 2026

  I submitted Sushi Stack (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/), my merge puzzle game, to the browser-game portal CrazyGames, and it was rejected. The only reason given was that “overall quality does not meet expectations.” So I captured the game myself and looked for the problem. I found four. This is written from my commit record.

## When no reason is given

  “Quality” does not tell me what is wrong. The commit notes say that once I actually recorded the game, I recognized the problems. A reviewer plays for a few minutes and judges from what is on the screen. So I decided to look at the same screen the reviewer saw.

## The four I found

### 1. A black line across the screen

  The darkening effect for the background left the edge where the wall meets the floor, so a black straight line ran across the screen and a vertical seam showed at the rim of the tub. It looked broken. I blended the boundary and changed the edge fade from a straight cut to a curve.

### 2. On a wide screen, the play area was only 30%

  On a wide screen the play area took 30% of the screen and the rest was just dark. I put the evolution chain (what merges into what) on the left. In a merge game it is the first thing players look for, and I had hidden it inside the encyclopedia.

### 3. The silhouettes of unlocked tiers were invisible

  Tiers not yet reached are shown as silhouettes. But I drew dark brown silhouettes on a dark background, so they could not be seen. I made it possible to pass a lighter silhouette.

### 4. Tension never happened

  The fourth was heavier than looks. Measured with auto-play, one game was a median of 594 moves, about 7.5 minutes, and my commit says “30 minutes for a human.” The tub never filled up, so the dangerous moments never came. In the few minutes a reviewer spends, tension never occurred even once.

## The fix: measure, then choose

  I decided not to touch the size or area ratio of each tier, since that would damage the feeling of merging into something bigger. I used auto-play to find places I could change without losing that feeling. I also gave my balance-testing tool a way to swap sizes and the spawn distribution from outside, and ran candidates in bulk to compare.

    What changed | Before | After

    Items that fall | 3 kinds | 5 kinds (added salmon and tuna)

    Moves per game (auto-play median) | 594 | 279

    Tub rim / height | 320 / 308 | 250 / 378

    Share of screen used by the play area | 45% | 62%

    Area ratio, conger eel to spiny lobster | 1.76 | 1.40

    Leftover width when two gold tubs sit side by side | 0 px | 36 px

  Now two gold tubs fit side by side, so a gold-tub merge (merging gold tubs together) works in real play. The logic had been there before, but it never happened once in 300 games. A game is half as long, so scores also dropped by about 20% (auto-play median from 59,305 to 46,529). I recalculated the ranking thresholds.

## What I learned

> “Low quality” was four separate problems.
  Two were about appearance, one about where information was placed, and one about the substance of play. When no reason is given, the first thing to do is look at the screen the other person saw. For someone who plays for a few minutes, tension that builds over 30 minutes does not exist.

  This article is written from my commit record (September 10, 2026). The result of a re-review is not included.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/crazygames/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# Japanese text garbled in the CrazyGames preview: the file was correct, the cause was never found, so I escaped to ASCII

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/ascii-text/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of Sushi Stack / October 2026

  When I opened Sushi Stack (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/) in a game portal’s preview, a report said that only the character 連 in “大連鎖！” (Big Chain!) appeared broken. I checked the file and the character was stored correctly. This is how I moved on, without knowing the cause, by making it a form that does not matter if it breaks, from my commit record.

## Only one character breaks

  The report came from the CrazyGames preview. When a chain happens in the game, “大連鎖！” appears on screen. That one character, 連, was rendered broken. The other characters were fine.

  I first checked the game file itself. The byte sequence was correct. So the file on my side was not broken. It had to break somewhere in the hand-off before it reached the portal, or somewhere in how the portal read it. The commit does not say where. I have not identified the cause.

## How to fix something whose cause you cannot find

  If the cause is outside my hands, I decided to make a form that does not matter wherever it breaks.

- Replace displayed text with ASCII-only notation. Do not write Japanese characters directly in the file. In scripts use \uXXXX, in HTML text and attributes use &#xXXXX;. Even if multi-byte characters get corrupted midway, ASCII has nothing to corrupt.

- Leave the replacement to a tool (tools/asciify.mjs). I write in Japanese, then run the tool. It gives the same result no matter how many times I run it. Comments stay in Japanese so they stay readable (they never appear on screen).

- Add a font that has the kanji to the end of the font stack. That also closes the path where a font lacks the character and it does not show.

## Two other problems found in the same check

- Emoji do not show on some devices. The globe and mobile-phone emoji are missing on some devices. I redrew them as SVG shapes.

- Floating text during a chain overlaps and cannot be read. Text that appears at nearby positions now moves upward to avoid overlap.

## The next day: do 14 languages fit in their boxes?

  The game supports 14 languages. Translations are often longer than the Japanese and overflow easily in the side column on PC (192 px wide) and inside cards. I added a tool that switches through the languages in turn and counts anything that sticks out of its parent box or scrolls sideways.

  The result: no overflow in 14 languages × 2 screen sizes. As with broken characters, “nothing overflows” is more reliable counted than eyeballed.

## What I learned

> When you do not know the cause, stop depending on the place where the cause is.

- A correct file does not mean a correct screen. The hand-off and the portal’s reading are things I cannot fix.

- Write down what you do not know. I still do not know why 連 broke. ASCII escaping did not fix the cause. It only made the game unaffected by it.

- Have a machine count visual breakage. Checking 14 languages by eye is not realistic.

  This article is written from my commit record (September 7 and 8, 2026). The cause of the broken character is not in the record, so it is not written here.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/ascii-text/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# Works on my machine, breaks when deployed: four incidents shipping a static site to Cloudflare Pages

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/deploy-gotchas/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of Koshin Studio / October 2026

  This site is assembled from HTML and deployed to Cloudflare Pages. In a single day in September, four incidents of the “works on my machine, breaks when deployed” kind followed one another. This is written in order, from my commit record.

## 1. I fixed it, but the old version kept running

  I fixed how the logo bursts, but returning visitors still saw the old motion. The cause was that the file names of style.css and motion.js did not change. A browser that had loaded them once held them for a day. My own screen was always fresh after a deploy, so I did not notice.

  The fix is to append a mark made from the file’s contents (the first 8 hex digits of its sha1) to the name, like style.css?v=19008d13. When the contents change, it is fetched as a different file. I added the same mark to the font. When I rebuilt the font with more characters and a browser held the old one, characters did not render (tofu boxes).

  Since names now change, I extended the cache lifetime from 1 day to 30 days. I checked that rebuilding does not add marks, and that the same contents give the same mark.

## 2. Contents multiplied every time I rebuilt

  On the Sushi Stack page, the breadcrumb list had grown to 14 items. The build of this site works by rewriting finished HTML. Before inserting, it “removes” the previous insertion. If the removing side does not match, things pile up on every build.

- Breadcrumbs: the removing regular expression only looked for class="crumbs" and did not match the real element, which had an aria-label.

- RSS link: there was no removing side at all, so it was added every time.

  I made a machine find incidents of the same shape. The main check is to build twice and report any page that differs by even one character. It also checks that the header band, footer, body, breadcrumbs and headings are not duplicated. Right after adding it, the RSS case was caught.

## 3. I had committed a symlink that points into my own environment

  tools/node_modules was a symbolic link pointing inside this environment. Once it was in git, other machines had no target for it, and counting files for the deploy (wrangler) stopped. It actually stopped. I removed it from tracking, and added a check that reports any symlink among tracked files.

## 4. It worked only on my machine

  My machine has images that are not in git, and leftovers from earlier builds. Because of those, things work only locally and give a 404 once deployed. The favicon of the play pages was exactly that.

  So I added a check that copies only the committed contents to another place, rebuilds there, and loads every page. Files I decided not to ship (those listed in .assetsignore) are dropped from the copy in the same way. In that run, 8 files were dropped and none was missing on the 12 pages.

## What I learned

> The least trustworthy thing is my own machine.

- A file whose name does not change never delivers its new contents. Put a mark of the contents in the name.

- Rebuild accidents are found by “do it twice, is it the same?” The first result always looks clean.

- What is on your machine and what you ship are different. Check from a fresh clone.

  I did not notice any of the four myself. They were found only after I added checks. Walking through the pages did not reveal them.

  This article is written from my commit record (September 8, 2026).

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/deploy-gotchas/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

URL: https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/hosting-compare/

# Comparing static site hosts by their official terms: Cloudflare Pages, Netlify, Vercel, GitHub Pages and Firebase Hosting

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/hosting-compare/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
A comparison / October 2026

  This site and the systems around my iOS app run on Cloudflare (see my article on deploy pitfalls (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/deploy-gotchas/) and my article on free tiers (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/ranking-free-tier/), both in Japanese). How do the other hosts compare? I read only the official pricing, limits and terms pages and lined them up. I have not used the other hosts to compare in practice.

  This is what I confirmed on October 8, 2026. Pricing changes often (Vercel and Netlify have announced recent changes). Check the sources before deciding.

## Quick table: look up what you want to know

  The answers first. The numbers and sources are in the sections below.

    What you want to know | What the official pages say

    I want to put ads (AdSense and so on) on the site | Vercel’s Hobby plan treats hosting ads as commercial use and does not allow it. GitHub Pages disallows use for online businesses, and I could not confirm anything explicit about ads. For Cloudflare, Netlify and Firebase, I found no restriction in the terms I read (that is not an explicit permission).

    I do not want it to stop when I hit a limit | Netlify (300 credits a month) and Firebase (10 GB storage, 10 GB transfer a month) stop when reached. GitHub Pages bandwidth (100 GB a month) is a soft limit.

    I have many files | Cloudflare: 20,000 files per site, 25 MiB per file. Vercel Hobby: 15,000 source files and 100 MB in total.

    I want to use _redirects / _headers | Cloudflare and Netlify support them. Vercel uses vercel.json, Firebase uses firebase.json. For GitHub Pages I could not confirm.

    I want an official statement about speed from Japan | Cloudflare (locations in Tokyo, Osaka, Fukuoka and Naha) and Vercel (Tokyo and Osaka compute regions) had one. There are no latency numbers anywhere.

  The contents of the table were confirmed on the official pages on October 8, 2026. “I could not find it” does not mean “you can.”

## First, the most important one: are ads allowed?

  Can you put ads or affiliate links on a free plan? If you are thinking of earning from your site, this was the main dividing line.

    Service | What the official pages say

    Vercel | Hobby is for non-commercial, personal use only. Commercial examples explicitly include “hosting ads such as Google AdSense” and “sites whose main purpose is affiliate links.” To show ads, you need Pro or above.

    GitHub Pages | It states that use as “free hosting for running an online business,” e-commerce and commercial SaaS are not allowed. Donation buttons are tolerated. I could not confirm anything explicit about ads.

    Cloudflare | In the terms I read, I found no restriction on commercial use or ads on the free plan (this means nothing is stated, not that it is explicitly allowed).

    Netlify | I found no restriction on commercial use or ads in the terms of use or the agreement. However, it states that free allowances can change or end, and service can be suspended without notice.

    Firebase Hosting | The Firebase terms page I retrieved had no restriction on commercial use or ads (I did not read the full body of the terms).

  “I could not find it” does not mean “you may put ads.” When in doubt, asking the provider is the safe way.

## Free tiers

    Service | What the official pages say

    Cloudflare (Pages / Workers static assets) | Requests for static files are “free and unlimited.” Builds: 500 a month (Pages). Requests that run a Worker: 100,000 a day (Workers Free). I could not confirm a bandwidth limit.

    Netlify (Free) | A hard limit of 300 credits a month. When used up, all projects stop. Bandwidth costs 20 credits per GB, a production deploy 15 credits each. Previews cost 0.

    Vercel (Hobby) | Up to 100 GB transfer, 1 million CDN requests and 1 million function invocations. Beyond that you are usually locked out for about 30 days. Up to 100 deployments a day.

    GitHub Pages | Bandwidth is a soft limit of 100 GB a month. Builds are a soft limit of 10 an hour.

    Firebase Hosting (free) | 10 GB storage, 10 GB transfer a month. When reached, the site is disabled until next month (it comes back right away if you switch to a paid plan).

## Number and size of files

    Service | What the official pages say

    Cloudflare | 20,000 files per site, 25 MiB per file.

    Vercel (Hobby) | For deploys from the command line: 15,000 source files and 100 MB in total. No limit on output files (it slows down beyond 100,000). I could not confirm a maximum for one file.

    GitHub Pages | A published site can be up to 1 GB. I could not confirm a per-file limit.

    Firebase Hosting | Up to 2 GB per file. I could not confirm a file-count limit.

    Netlify | I could not find an official page stating per-deploy file count or size limits.

## Redirect and header configuration

- Cloudflare: _redirects (2,000 static + 100 dynamic) and _headers (100 rules). Redirects are processed before headers. Neither applies to responses produced by a Worker.

- Netlify: _redirects and _headers, or netlify.toml. Headers are not added to proxy or function responses.

- Vercel: vercel.json. Up to 2,048 rules per deployment in total for redirects, rewrites and headers. I did not find _redirects-style files on the pages I read.

- Firebase: firebase.json. The first matching rule is used.

- GitHub Pages: Nothing on the pages I read, so I could not confirm.

## Preview deploys and speed from Japan

- Previews: Cloudflare, Netlify and Vercel create them automatically for each pull request or branch. Firebase has “preview channels,” which expire in 7 days by default and 30 days at most. I could not confirm this for GitHub Pages.

- Speed from Japan: Only Cloudflare (locations in Tokyo, Osaka, Fukuoka and Naha) and Vercel (Tokyo and Osaka as compute regions; the default for functions is US East) had an official statement about Japan. No latency numbers were written anywhere.

## What I learned

> “Free to host” and “free to earn” are different things.

- If you plan to show ads, read the terms first. If the terms stop you after you have put the site there, you have to move.

- They stop differently. When you reach a limit, some sites stop (Netlify, Firebase) and some only have soft limits (GitHub Pages).

- Config files differ by service. Even for the same _redirects, the number you can write and the scope it affects differ. That is where moving costs effort.

## What I could not confirm

- Cloudflare: bandwidth limits and billing for static assets, how custom-domain certificates are issued, an official yes or no on ads for the free plan.

- Netlify: per-deploy file count and size limits, an explicit statement on free custom domains, anything about speed in Japan.

- Vercel: the maximum size of one file in Hobby static output.

- GitHub Pages: an explicit yes or no on ads, header configuration, previews, speed in Japan.

- Firebase: file-count limit, custom-domain cost, the body of the terms (commercial use and ads).

- A speed comparison (I did not do one, because there are no official numbers).

## Sources (all checked on October 8, 2026)

- Cloudflare: Pages limits (https://developers.cloudflare.com/pages/platform/limits/)

- Cloudflare: static assets billing and limitations (https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/static-assets/billing-and-limitations/)

- Cloudflare: Pages redirects (https://developers.cloudflare.com/pages/configuration/redirects/)

- Cloudflare: Pages headers (https://developers.cloudflare.com/pages/configuration/headers/)

- Cloudflare: network (https://www.cloudflare.com/network/)

- Netlify: how credits work (https://docs.netlify.com/manage/accounts-and-billing/billing/billing-for-credit-based-plans/how-credits-work/)

- Netlify: terms of use (https://www.netlify.com/legal/terms-of-use/)

- Vercel: Hobby plan (https://vercel.com/docs/plans/hobby)

- Vercel: fair use guidelines (https://vercel.com/docs/limits/fair-use-guidelines)

- Vercel: limits (https://vercel.com/docs/limits)

- GitHub Pages: limits (https://docs.github.com/en/pages/getting-started-with-github-pages/github-pages-limits)

- Firebase Hosting: usage quotas and pricing (https://firebase.google.com/docs/hosting/usage-quotas-pricing)

  I read some of the official pages through summaries (the numbers have not been checked against the originals character by character). Please check the Netlify credits and Vercel limits against the original text in particular.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/hosting-compare/).

# Comparing comment systems for static sites by their official information: giscus, utterances, Disqus, Remark42 and more

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/comment-services/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
A comparison / October 2026

  The comment box on this site is giscus. It is set up so that nothing connects to an outside site until you press “Open comments.” What are the other options like? I read only the official descriptions and official repositories and lined them up. I have actually used only giscus.

  This is what I confirmed on October 8, 2026. The state of services changes. Check the sources before you use one.

## Quick table: look up what you want to know

  The answers first. Details and sources are in the sections below.

    What you want to know | What the official pages say

    I do not want ads or tracking | giscus, utterances, Cusdis and Remark42 say officially that there is no tracking or advertising. The free version of Disqus is run on ads.

    I do not want to run a server | giscus (GitHub Discussions) and utterances (GitHub Issues) store on GitHub. Both need a GitHub account to write.

    I want people to write without logging in | Cusdis needs no login but has ended. Remark42 can allow anonymous posts by configuration (you need your own server).

    I only want ones that are still maintained | Recent updates were confirmed for giscus (2026-05-26) and Remark42 (2026-09-14). utterances, Staticman and Commento are suspected stopped; Cusdis has ended.

    I want a Japanese UI | giscus and Remark42 have Japanese translation files. I could not confirm for the others.

  The contents of the table were confirmed on official pages and repositories on October 8, 2026. “Suspected stopped” is not an official announcement of closure.

## Where it is stored and who can write

    Service | Storage | What you need to post | Cost

    giscus | GitHub Discussions | A GitHub account | Free (MIT)

    utterances | GitHub Issues | A GitHub account | Free (MIT)

    Disqus | Disqus’s servers (I could not confirm an explicit statement on storage) | Could not confirm | The free version has ads. Paid Plus is $12 to $35 a month depending on monthly pageviews ($12 up to 100,000, $20 up to 350,000, $35 up to 900,000; official help, 2025-04-30 version).

    Remark42 | A server you run yourself (built-in data store) | Various logins (Google, GitHub and so on), email; anonymous by configuration | Free (MIT). Server cost is yours.

    Cusdis | A server you run yourself (PostgreSQL and others) | No login needed | OSS (GPL-3.0)

    Staticman | Saved as files in a GitHub or GitLab repository | Could not confirm | OSS (MIT). You run it yourself.

    Commento | A server you run yourself (PostgreSQL) | Supports login and SSO. I could not confirm anonymous posting. | The self-hosted version is free software. The README says the cloud version is not offered for free.

## What the official pages say about ads and tracking

- giscus and utterances: Both state officially that there is no tracking and no ads. Note that opening giscus comments connects to GitHub, and how GitHub handles that is a separate matter.

- Disqus: The free version is run on ads. The official help describes cookies recording visits to advertisers’ sites, cookie IDs being shared with advertising partners and affiliates, and wording such as “sold or shared.” Adopting it seems to carry the heaviest burden for consent management and ad-related notices (I did not look into how this is treated under its official policy).

- Cusdis: The README says it uses no cookies at all.

- Remark42 and Commento: The official pages say they do not track users and have no ads.

## Is it still maintained?

  You use a comment system for a long time once it is in. Whether it has stopped matters.

    Service | What I confirmed on the official repository or page | Assessment

    giscus | No formal release numbers; it states “rolling-release.” The latest change was 2026-05-26. A warning that features may break because of changes on the GitHub side. | Active

    Remark42 | Latest is v1.17.1 (2026-09-14). | Active

    utterances | The last commit was 2022-02-12. No releases. Not archived. | Suspected stopped (no announcement of closure)

    Staticman | The last commit was 2020-07-06. The only release is v1.0.0 from 2016. | Suspected stopped (I could not confirm an official announcement)

    Commento | The last tag is v1.8.0 (2020-04) and the last commit 2021-02-28. The cloud site and its description pages all return 404. | Suspected stopped (I could not confirm an official notice)

    Cusdis | The repository was archived on 2026-07-17. The README says “deprecated.” | Ended, it is fair to say

    Disqus | The service is running (the pricing help article is dated 2025-04-30). | Running

## Japanese, spam protection and weight

- Japanese UI: giscus and Remark42 have Japanese translation files. I could not confirm for the others.

- Spam protection: giscus only says comments can be moderated on GitHub, with no spam protection described. Disqus has a spam filter even in the basic free version. With Cusdis, the admin approves before display.

- Weight: Only Cusdis gave a number (about 5 kb gzipped). giscus has an option to delay loading comments. utterances says it is “lightweight” but gives no number.

## What I paid attention to with giscus on this site

  The giscus documentation says there is no tracking or ads. Even so, on this site nothing connects to giscus or GitHub until you press “Open comments.” That is so people who only read generate no extra traffic and the page loads lighter. The conditions for connecting are written on the privacy page (https://koshinstudio.com/en/privacy/).

## What I learned

> More than a feature table, ask “is it still going?”

- More services have stopped than I expected. Of the 7 I looked at, 4 (Cusdis, Staticman, Commento and utterances) had ended or were suspected stopped.

- Free services sometimes make you pay with ads or tracking. The free version of Disqus is an example.

- Systems that need a GitHub account to write (giscus, utterances) narrow your readers to people close to development. Depending on who reads your articles, that may not fit.

## What I could not confirm

- Disqus: the official pricing page (its body is drawn by JavaScript and could not be read; the prices are from the help article), requirements for commenters’ accounts, a Japanese UI, an explicit statement on storage, load weight.

- utterances: a Japanese UI, spam protection.

- Cusdis: cloud-version pricing, the list of supported languages.

- Staticman: requirements for commenters, spam protection such as Akismet, statements on ads or tracking, an official announcement of closure.

- Commento: the state and price of the cloud version, a Japanese UI, an official notice of closure.

- How a comment section is treated under AdSense’s official policy (I did not look into it).

## Sources (all checked on October 8, 2026)

- giscus: repository (https://github.com/giscus/giscus)

- giscus: official configuration page (https://giscus.app/ja)

- utterances: repository (https://github.com/utterance/utterances)

- Disqus: pricing and plans (help) (https://help.disqus.com/en/articles/1717110-comments-pricing-and-plans)

- Disqus: privacy FAQ (https://help.disqus.com/en/articles/1717103-disqus-privacy-faq)

- Remark42: repository (https://github.com/umputun/remark42)

- Cusdis: repository (https://github.com/djyde/cusdis)

- Staticman: repository (https://github.com/eduardoboucas/staticman)

- Commento: repository (GitLab) (https://gitlab.com/commento/commento)

  I read some of the official pages through summaries. The Disqus prices were checked against the original text of the official help article (2025-04-30 version) on 2026-10-08. Disqus’s own pricing page is drawn by JavaScript and could not be read, so please check current prices there.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/comment-services/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# Comparing iOS ad SDKs and Firebase by their official information: AdMob, AppLovin MAX, LevelPlay and Supabase

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/ios-sdk-compare/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
A comparison / October 2026

  For my iOS app Torecadash, I pinned Firebase to 11.4.0 and AdMob to 11.5.0 to suit Xcode 15.2 on an old Mac (that article (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/xcode152-sdk/)). The app was also rejected once for ITMS-91064 (that article (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/itms-91064/)). Here I line up the surrounding options I could not look into at the time, using official pages only. I have actually used only AdMob and Firebase. I have not used the others.

  This is what I confirmed on October 8, 2026. SDK versions and requirements change quickly. Check the sources before you use them.

## Quick table: look up what you want to know

  The answers first. The numbers and sources are in the sections below.

    What you want to know | What the official pages say

    Which versions work on an old Xcode | AdMob 11.6.0 and later needs Xcode 15.3 or later. Firebase 11.12.0 and later needs Xcode 16.2, and 12.0.0 and later needs Swift 6.0 (official release notes).

    Minimum payout | AdMob: at least $100 in USD (official table). AppLovin: no amount in the official FAQ; payment is for the previous month on the 15th of the next. LevelPlay and Meta: could not confirm.

    I want to use several ad networks | AdMob, AppLovin MAX and LevelPlay have mediation. The AdMob integration guide lists 24 networks.

    I want to keep using Firebase with CocoaPods | Firebase states that in October 2026 it stops publishing new versions to CocoaPods. SPM is recommended.

    I want server-side processing for free | On Firebase Spark, Cloud Functions is not available (Blaze only). On Supabase’s free plan, a project pauses after one week without activity.

  The contents of the table were confirmed on official pages on October 8, 2026. SDK requirements can disagree between pages, so check with your own build as well.

## Ad SDKs: how they work and payments

    SDK | How it works | Minimum payout

    Google AdMob | Has mediation (serving from several ad networks). The iOS integration guide lists 24 networks including AppLovin, ironSource, Meta Audience Network and Unity Ads. | Payments in USD have a minimum of $100 (official table). The value differs by currency.

    AppLovin MAX | A mediation platform. | No specific amount in the official FAQ (you check it on the dashboard). Payment is for the previous month on the 15th of the next (NET15).

    Unity LevelPlay (ironSource) | LevelPlay ads and mediation. Adapters are separate packages. | Could not confirm.

    Meta Audience Network | A standalone ad network. Listed as a mediation target in AdMob. | Could not confirm.

  For Meta Audience Network, I could not confirm either an official announcement of closure or a statement that it continues. Whether you can newly adopt it now cannot be settled from official primary sources.

## iOS privacy requirements

- Apple’s rule (common to all): if NSPrivacyTracking is true, NSPrivacyTrackingDomains needs a list of domains. If the user has not allowed ATT (tracking permission), connections to those domains fail and the app receives an error, according to Apple’s documentation. This matches what happened in the ITMS-91064 article.

- AdMob: asks for ATT before loading ads (SDK 7.64.0 and later). Privacy manifest support is from 11.2.0 (2024-03-14). I could not find an official list of tracking domains on AdMob’s pages (I cannot say it does not exist).

- AppLovin MAX: 12.4.1 and later supports privacy manifests. Each connected network also has a required version (AdMob 11.2.0 or later, Meta 6.15.0 or later, Unity Ads 4.10.0 or later).

- Meta: the Audience Network SDK has an iOS privacy manifest and recommends updating to 6.15.0. The domains are pre-filled and it does not recommend adding them by hand.

- LevelPlay: I could not confirm any description of ATT or privacy manifests on the integration pages I read.

## Minimum Xcode and iOS, and how to install

    SDK | Minimum requirements | Installation

    AdMob | Latest is 13.11.0 (2026-09-29). The release notes say a minimum of Xcode 26.2 (from 13.4.0). But the quick start says “Xcode 16.0 or later” and “iOS 13.0 or later,” so pages disagree. | SPM (recommended), CocoaPods, manual

    Firebase | Latest is 13.0.0 (2026-10-07). Minimum Xcode 26.2, iOS 15.0. Xcode 16.2 is required from 11.12.0, and Swift 6.0 from 12.0.0. | SPM is recommended. It states that in October 2026 it stops publishing new versions to CocoaPods.

    AppLovin MAX | iOS 12.0 or later, Xcode 15 or later (integration page). | CocoaPods, SPM, manual. With SPM, use SPM for the SDK and all adapters (mixing causes version conflicts).

    LevelPlay | The integration page says iOS 12+ and Xcode 15.4+. Another page (for Unity) says iOS 13+ and Xcode 16+ (from a search summary). Pages disagree. | CocoaPods, SPM (9.3.0 or later), manual

  This table also confirms why Torecadash pinned its versions. The official release notes say AdMob 11.6.0 depends on MarketplaceKit and needs Xcode 15.3 or later, and Firebase 11.12.0 and later needs Xcode 16.2. This matched my article.

## Analytics and backend: Firebase and Supabase free tiers

    Service | What the official pages say

    Firebase (Spark) | Firestore: 1 GiB storage, 50,000 reads a day, 20,000 writes a day, 20,000 deletes a day. Authentication: 50,000 monthly active users (phone auth not available). Cloud Functions: not available on Spark (paid Blaze only). Analytics and Cloud Messaging: no numeric limit (free).

    Supabase (free) | 50,000 monthly active users, 500 MB database, 1 GB file storage, 5 GB egress. Up to 2 active projects. Free projects pause after one week without activity.

## What I learned

> In an environment that cannot keep up with the latest version, the “minimum requirements” table matters most.

- SDK requirements can disagree between pages. Both AdMob and LevelPlay had different numbers in the release notes and the setup guides. You have to look at both and confirm with your own build.

- Privacy settings happen outside the SDK. If you set NSPrivacyTracking to true, you also write the domains. That is Apple’s rule, not a difference between SDKs.

- Look at how a free tier stops first. Supabase pauses with no activity. Firebase Spark cannot use Functions.

## What I could not confirm

- Minimum payouts for LevelPlay and Meta Audience Network.

- Meta Audience Network’s availability (closed or continuing), minimum Xcode and iOS, SPM support, and current version.

- AppLovin’s specific minimum payout amount, and the latest MAX SDK version (the release-notes URL would not open).

- An official list of tracking domains for AdMob, within what I could access.

- The FirebaseDataEncoder bug from Firebase 11.5.0 (as my article says, I confirmed it with my own build and could not find an official record).

- The contents of supabase-swift’s privacy manifest.

- Comparisons of accuracy or revenue (I did not do them, because there are no official numbers).

## Sources (all checked on October 8, 2026)

- AdMob: iOS release notes (https://developers.google.com/admob/ios/rel-notes)

- AdMob: iOS quick start (https://developers.google.com/admob/ios/quick-start)

- AdMob: mediation (https://developers.google.com/admob/ios/mediation)

- AdMob: privacy (https://developers.google.com/admob/ios/privacy)

- AdMob: payment thresholds (https://support.google.com/admob/answer/2772208?hl=en)

- Firebase: iOS release notes (https://firebase.google.com/support/release-notes/ios)

- Firebase: installation methods (https://firebase.google.com/docs/ios/installation-methods)

- Firebase: pricing (https://firebase.google.com/pricing)

- AppLovin: integration (iOS) (https://support.applovin.com/en/max/ios/overview/integration)

- AppLovin: privacy manifests (https://support.applovin.com/en/max/ios/overview/privacy-manifests)

- Unity LevelPlay: iOS SDK integration (https://docs.unity.com/en-us/grow/levelplay/sdk/ios/sdk-integration)

- Apple: privacy manifest files (https://developer.apple.com/documentation/bundleresources/privacy-manifest-files)

- Supabase: pricing (https://supabase.com/pricing)

  I read some of the official pages through summaries (the numbers have not been checked against the originals character by character). Please review the original text before relying on them.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/ios-sdk-compare/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# Claude API vs Gemini API by official numbers: small-model prices, web search, spend limits and deprecation

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/claude-vs-gemini-api/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
A comparison / October 2026

  Torecadash moved from the Claude API to the Gemini API (the story is in the migration article (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/gemini-migration/)). Here I line up the official numbers I did not write down then. I use only what the official pages say. I did not compare accuracy or speed, because there are no official numbers for them.

  All numbers were seen on official pages on October 8, 2026. Prices and limits change. Check each item’s source again before you use it. What the official pages did not say is written as “could not confirm,” not as “does not exist.”

## Quick table: look up what you want to know

  The answers first. Details and sources are in the sections below.

    What you want to know | What the official pages say

    Which is cheapest? | In the current official tables, Claude Haiku 5.5 (input $0.10, output $0.50) and Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite ($0.10, $0.40) are in a similar range. Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite is $0.25 and $1.50.

    I want a setting to cap the number of searches | Claude has max_uses. For Gemini, I did not find a setting for the number of searches on the official pages.

    I want to use search for free | Gemini’s paid tier includes up to 5,000 requests a month free. But on the free tier, search is not available for 3.1 Flash-Lite. Claude is $10 per 1,000 searches.

    I want a spend cap that stops me | Both have a monthly spend limit and stop until the 1st of next month when reached (Claude from Start at $500, Gemini from Tier 1 at $250).

    I want a promise about deprecation notice | Claude states “at least 60 days before retirement.” For Gemini I could not confirm a promise of days; the date in the table is the “earliest shutdown date.”

    I want official numbers for Japanese | Claude’s multilingual page has them (93.5% of English for Haiku 4.5). For Gemini I could not confirm.

  The numbers in the table were confirmed on official pages on October 8, 2026. This is not a conclusion about which to choose; it is an organization of “what is officially written.”

## Prices of small models

  US dollars per million tokens. The model I used before the migration was Claude Haiku 4.5.

    Model | Input | Output

    Claude Haiku 4.5 | $1 | $5

    Claude Haiku 5.5 | $0.10 (prompts up to 100,000 tokens) / $0.50 (beyond that) | $0.50 (up to 100,000) / $2.50 (beyond that)

    Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite (where I moved) | $0.25 (text, image, video) / $0.50 (audio) | $1.50

    Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite | $0.30 | $2.50

    Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite | $0.10 | $0.40

- In the current official price tables, Haiku 5.5 is cheaper than Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite. What I compared against when migrating was Haiku 4.5, and I have not checked whether Haiku 5.5 was available then.

- Claude has batch (50% discount) and a cheap rate for cache reads. I could not confirm Gemini’s batch discount rate.

- The official pages say that from Claude 4.7 onward, a new tokenizer makes the same text about 30% more tokens. I could not confirm whether this applies to Haiku 5.5.

## How web search works and what it costs

     | Claude | Gemini

    Price | $10 / 1,000 searches (plus normal token cost for the results) | Paid tier: up to 5,000 requests a month free, then $14 / 1,000 requests. On the free tier, search is not available for 3.1 Flash-Lite.

    How it is counted | Per search. Not charged on error. | For Gemini 3 models, per search query the model runs (multiple queries mean multiple charges).

    A setting to cap the count | Yes (max_uses). Beyond it, the search result is a max_uses_exceeded error. | I did not find a setting to cap the count on the search page (I cannot say it does not exist).

    Domain restrictions | Allowed and blocked domains can be specified. | Could not confirm.

  The problem I wrote about in the migration article, “web search has no cap on the number of calls,” reads the same within what the official pages say. Nothing equivalent to Claude’s max_uses was written on Gemini’s search page. It is still possible that I just did not find it.

## Limits and how they stop

  This is close to my reason for migrating.

     | Claude | Gemini

    Monthly spend limit | Start $500 / Build $1,000 / Scale $200,000 | From Tier 1 $250 / Tier 2 $2,000 / Tier 3 $20,000

    When the limit is reached | HTTP 429 (enforced_spend_limit_reached). Stopped until 00:00 UTC on the 1st of next month. | All projects in the billing account stop until the 1st of next month.

    A limit you set lower yourself | Can be set (HTTP 400 when reached). | Can be set per project in AI Studio (an experimental feature; billing is reflected with a delay of about 10 minutes, so you can overshoot).

    Free tier | A small free credit for new accounts. I did not find a continuing free allowance. | Yes. 3.1 Flash-Lite tokens are free. But caching and search grounding are not available on the free tier.

    Per-minute limits for small models | Start: Haiku 4.5 / 5.5 both 1,000 requests per minute, 2 million input and 400,000 output tokens per minute. | No specific numbers in the documentation (you check in AI Studio).

  The migration article gives the reason as “I hit Anthropic’s usage limit and got an unplanned charge.” However, Claude’s official pages say it stops when the limit is reached, and I could not explain from the official pages how an unplanned charge arises. The account in that article comes from my own records, not backed by official documents.

## How deprecation is announced

     | Claude | Gemini

    Notice promise | For released models, notice at least 60 days before retirement (by email and documentation). | It says “the exact shutdown date will be announced in advance,” but I could not confirm a promise of days. The date in the table is the “earliest shutdown date.”

    How it is written | “Not sooner than X” (it will not retire earlier than X). | A table of release date, shutdown date and recommended replacement.

    Examples | Haiku 3.5: about 2 months from announcement (2025-12-19) to retirement (2026-02-19). Haiku 4.5: not retired sooner than 2026-10-15. | 3.1 Flash-Lite: released 2026-05-07, shutdown 2027-05-07 (12 months after release). 2.0 Flash: shutdown 2026-06-01.

  The shutdown date of gemini-3.1-flash-lite, which I chose, is also May 7, 2027 in the official table. It matches the migration article. On the other hand, the migration article’s “2.5 Flash-Lite is scheduled to be shut down on October 16” disagrees with the current official table (“no shutdown date announced”). I added a correction to that article.

## Structured output, tool calling and Japanese

- Output in a specified JSON shape: Both support it. Claude says it “guarantees conformance to the schema.” Gemini says it supports “only some JSON schema features” and that “the meaning of values needs validation.”

- Tool calling: Both support it. Using structured output together with tools such as search works only on Gemini 3 models and is described as a “preview feature.”

- Japanese: Claude’s multilingual page has a relative score for Japanese with English as 100% (Haiku 4.5 is 93.5%). On the Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite page I could not find an official statement on supported languages. That does not mean “Gemini’s Japanese is weak”; it means I could not compare using official numbers.

## What I learned

> You cannot choose from a price table alone.

- Prices flip over time. The side that was cheaper at migration can be more expensive now.

- Whether safety devices exist is outside the table. Caps on search calls, spend limits and how things stop (does it stop, or does billing continue) do not appear in a unit price table.

- How deprecation is announced differs in whether there is a promise. Planning a switch is different when one side promises days and the other only shows the earliest date.

## What I could not confirm

- Specific per-minute and per-day limit numbers for Gemini’s free tier and each tier (the documentation has no numbers).

- Gemini’s batch discount rate.

- Whether Gemini’s search has a setting to cap the count (I only did not find it on the page, so I cannot say it does not exist).

- How many days before shutdown Gemini notifies, at minimum.

- An official statement on Gemini’s Japanese and a numeric comparison.

- An explicit statement that Claude Haiku 4.5 / 5.5 support the web search tool (the official pages tell you to check supported models with the API).

- Accuracy and speed comparisons (not obtainable from official primary sources, so I did not do them).

## Sources (all checked on October 8, 2026)

# Migrating from the Claude API to the Gemini API (gemini-3.1-flash-lite): 16 call sites into one function

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/gemini-migration/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of Torecadash / October 2026

  On the server side of my iOS app Torecadash, AI is used for things like deciding “which product an article is about.” On July 25, 2026, I fully migrated this AI from Anthropic’s Claude (Haiku 4.5) to Google’s Gemini (gemini-3.1-flash-lite). What I decided, how I unified the calls, and what I added after the migration are written from my hand-over notes.

  This site has a page for Torecadash (Works (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/)). This is a development log. I do not write amounts of money.

## What triggered it

  According to my notes, the reason was that I reached Anthropic’s API usage limit and got an unplanned charge. Since then only Gemini has run, and I removed the Anthropic SDK and key from the code and from the secret store (Secret Manager). In a check on July 30, I confirmed there are 0 mentions of Anthropic in the code.

## How I chose the model

  I chose gemini-3.1-flash-lite. My notes also keep the reason for what I did not choose.

- Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite, which is cheaper, was scheduled to be shut down on October 16, 2026, so I passed on it (according to my notes. When I reviewed the official deprecation list on October 8, 2026, this model showed “no shutdown date announced.” I have not confirmed whether the entry changed later).

- The shutdown date of the one I chose, gemini-3.1-flash-lite, is May 7, 2027. At the time of migration (July 25) that was still about nine and a half months away.

  If you choose only by price, it will be shut down soon and you migrate again. I added “when will it be shut down” to the selection criteria.

## 16 call sites into one function

  There were 16 places that call AI (deciding the sales format, matching products, discovering listings and so on). I unified them to go through one function (createGeminiInteraction) at the top of functions/index.js. Inside it calls client.interactions.create() from @google/genai.

  Callers pass arguments close to the original Anthropic form (system_instruction, max_output_tokens in generation_config, input) as they are. What comes back is text (output_text). I made it a form where only the inside is swapped, with almost no rewriting of callers.

## Web search had no “call count cap” setting

  In four places (discovering listings, discovering sellers, a Rakuten Books lookup and a list-price lookup), the AI does a web search. With Gemini I use tools: [{type: "google_search"}] (grounding with Google Search).

  Here was a pitfall. Anthropic’s web search had max_uses (a cap on the number of searches), but Gemini has no equivalent setting, and the model searches as many times as it thinks necessary. My notes say: “the absence of this setting can itself be a cause of unexpected cost.”

  So the day after migration (July 26), I added a circuit breaker with a daily counter inside createGeminiInteraction (up to 300 calls a day). When the limit is reached, it returns an error to the caller. In price review, I designed this error to be excluded and kept distinct from “could not find the list price” (I wrote about that in another article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/fail-open/), in Japanese).

## A switch to stop it

  I added one more thing: AI_CALLS_PAUSED, a switch that stops all AI calls from one place. My notes include a reflection from July 25: “I thought I had stopped the calls, but they had not actually stopped, and the automatic job running every 10 minutes kept producing errors.” I decided that when the budget is about to be exceeded, I first set this to true and stop right away.

## A note when adding new processing

  Functions that call AI (Cloud Functions) must always have secrets: ["GEMINI_API_KEY"]. If you forget it, deployment succeeds and then it fails with a permission error.

## What I have not verified

  This article is written from the AI section of my hand-over notes. A before-and-after accuracy comparison of decisions is not part of the material. So I do not judge here whether Gemini is better or worse.

## What I learned

> If you gather calls in one place, the place to stop them is one place too.

- Pass every call through one function. The migration, the safety limit and the stop switch can all live in that one place.

- Count “there is no setting” as a risk. When you move to a service with no cap on call count, build the cap on your own side.

- Check that the stop switch really stops. Thinking you stopped but not having stopped is the most expensive case.

  This article is written from my hand-over notes (AI API information, July 25 and 26, 2026).

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/gemini-migration/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# It let things through when it could not check: how “fail-open” brought in resale items

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/fail-open/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of Torecadash / October 2026

  In my iOS app Torecadash, three in-app bug reports said “lots of resale prices are coming in from Amazon.” One was an obvious resale item at ¥79,800. The cause was a blind spot in a design I had put in on purpose: “if it cannot be confirmed, let it pass.” This is from my hand-over notes and the commit record (July 30, 2026).

  This is a development log of the app.

## The price gate, and the “let it pass” design

  The app picks up listings from online shops (Rakuten, Yahoo! Shopping, Amazon and others) and shows them in a feed. There is a “price gate” that checks whether a listing’s price is reasonable against the product’s list price. It has an AI (with web search) look up the list price, and rejects extremely expensive resale items.

  The gate had a behavior: “if the list price could not be confirmed, let it pass without review.” That was intended. If you exclude products whose list price the AI genuinely does not know just because you cannot confirm it, you also erase genuine listings. This is so-called fail-open (open on failure, meaning let it pass).

## The blind spot: hitting the search cap took the same path

  The AI’s web search has a cap of 300 calls a day (a circuit breaker to prevent unexpected cost). But the gate did not distinguish the reason the list price could not be confirmed.

- The AI answered “I do not know the list price of this product.”

- The daily cap was reached, so the check itself could not be done.

  Both went down the same “price unknown → let it pass” path. The first is as intended. The second is just “the road was closed before looking,” yet the gate became wide open.

## Why the hole did real damage

  The hole surfaced because of a previous change (the one that widened Amazon’s scope). Widening the scope suddenly increased the number of products whose price had to be newly checked. As a result, the daily cap was reached often. While it was reached, the gate was open and resale items mixed in in large numbers.

  There was secondary damage too. A result of “list price unknown” was designed to be cached for 24 hours regardless of reason. So a product that once hit the cap stayed open for up to 24 hours even after the cap was released.

## The fix: distinguish the reason

  I created a dedicated marker (QUOTA_EXCEEDED) so the two could be told apart.

    Situation | What the gate does

    The AI genuinely did not know the list price (null) | Let it pass as before (still fail-open)

    The daily cap meant the check itself could not be done (QUOTA_EXCEEDED) | Exclude (fail-close)

  The latter is not put into the 24-hour cache either. It tries to confirm again the next time it is called. This gate is shared by every feature that uses price review: Rakuten, Yahoo! Shopping, Amazon, AI listing discovery, first-come Rakuten Books and so on, so one fix reaches widely (the commit record says 18 functions were deployed).

  I hid the three reported items by hand. After that, the re-review batch that runs every 5 minutes is expected to pick up the same misses again.

  What I have not verified: my notes say “check in the next session whether resale-price reports stopped after the cap reset.” There is no result for that in the record at the time of writing.

## Is the same hole in other decisions?

  In a later check (July 30, 2026), I looked at the other AI decisions such as deciding sales format and matching products. All of them are designed to fall to the safe side (exclude, or null) on failure, and I found no new fail-open hole.

## What I learned

> “Could not confirm” comes in two kinds: did not know, and could not look.

- Before using a let-it-pass design, make clear the reason it is fine to let through. “Let it through because I do not know” and “let it through because I cannot look” are different things.

- Do not cache the result of a failure regardless of its reason. I froze a temporary failure for 24 hours.

- One change can turn a hole elsewhere into real damage. Widening Amazon’s scope brought the cap’s hole to the surface.

  This article is written from my hand-over notes (session 182) and the commit record (July 30, 2026).

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/fail-open/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)
