# What I read as “fetched” was just a notice page: three days of zero products

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/blocked-page/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of Torecadash / October 2026

  My iOS app Torecadash regularly visits the sales pages of online shops to collect lottery and first-come sale information. One day I found that fetching from Pokémon Center Online had been returning zero products for three days straight. There were no errors, because each fetch was judged “fetched.” What was happening is written from my commit record.

  This is a development log of the app.

## My “fetched” check was too lenient

  Pages are fetched through an external service (Scrape.do). Fetch settings range from cheap to expensive, and the design is that if the cheap setting fails, it escalates to a stronger one (the same mechanism as in my article on scraping cost (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/scrape-cost/), in Japanese).

  The problem was the judgment of “did it fetch.” When the Pokémon Center page was fetched with the cheap setting, what came back was a 2,410-byte page saying “Please enable JavaScript”. It was not a product list, just a notice. But I read this as “fetched” and treated it as a success. If it is a success, there is no escalation to the stronger setting either.

  So from September 4, for three days, fetches kept “succeeding” while products stayed at zero.

## The fix

- Gather the “fetched” check in one place. The check had been scattered over several places. I made one function that looks at whether a page is a blocked page (scrapeDoResultLooksBlocked) and made everything use it.

- Remember the setting that worked. It remembers a setting that succeeded once and tries from there next time. This cut the credits used per fetch from 36 to 25.

## Another bit of dirt found the same day

  The same inspection found another problem. The logic that decides a mismatch between alternative spellings of a product name was written separately at the entrance of matching and in the cleanup side. Only the cleanup side lacked a check for “the product forms differ.” As a result, an alternative spelling of a trial deck stayed attached to a booster pack product, and kept triggering wrong matches every day. I made the check a shared function and removed 46 entries across 27 products.

  I also resolved the “no document to update” error (64 in 7 days). Now products are re-read when their cache is old, and articles that have disappeared are skipped so the remaining dedupe processing continues.

## What I learned

> “Success” and “the contents were fetched” are different things.

- Judge success by the contents. That the communication went through and that what you wanted was fetched are different. If “zero items fetched” continues, that itself must be watched as an anomaly.

- Keep a judgment in one place. If the same judgment exists in two places, one of them goes stale, like the matching entrance and the cleanup.

- No errors is not evidence that things are going well.

  This article is written from my commit record (September 7, 2026). How I noticed the three days of zero is not written in the commit.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/blocked-page/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# I could not listen, so I measured the waveform: building Japanese instruments with WebAudio for Sushi Stack

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/webaudio/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of Sushi Stack / October 2026

  The sound of Sushi Stack (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/) uses not a single audio file. Japanese instruments are synthesized on the spot with the browser’s audio feature (WebAudio). The problem was that I had no way to listen while I was building it. So I measured the waveform and adjusted the volume. This is written with the numbers left in my commits.

## Why no audio files

  Using external libraries or audio files would break the form where the game is delivered as one file (and works offline). So I synthesized the koto (plucked), taiko, hyoshigi (wooden clappers) and kane (gong) from WebAudio parts and composed the music in the yo scale (a Japanese scale).

- BGM: played by a look-ahead scheduler built on eighth notes. Its thickness changes in four steps with how full the tub is; the more dangerous it gets, the more taiko drums are added.

- Sound effects: the number and weight of sounds stack up in this order: merge, chain, otoro, spiny lobster / golden, golden with golden.

- I added a celebratory phrase for ranking up and for beating a personal best. There is a sound on/off button, and the setting stays on the device.

## I cannot listen, so I measure the waveform

  The balance of volume is something you would normally decide by ear. But in this work I could not listen. So I swapped the same synthesis functions onto a render-only audio part (OfflineAudioContext), wrote the sound out as a waveform, and measured the maximum amplitude (peak).

  The initial state was this:

- The jackpot sound peaked at 1.18. Above 1.0 the sound clips and distorts.

- The merge sound was 0.072. It was buried in the BGM and could not be heard.

  After adjusting, the sound effects lined up like stairs below the BGM peak of 0.179.

    Sound | Peak

    BGM (reference) | 0.179

    Merge | 0.16

    3-chain | 0.48

    Otoro | 0.49

    Golden | 0.85

    Jackpot | 0.81

  The distortion is gone, and I can confirm with numbers the order “the more rewarding the sound, the louder.” But whether it sounds pleasant to the ear cannot be told by this method.

## I re-drew the ranks from measurements, too

  The same day I reviewed the rank thresholds. I ran auto-play 12 times and took the score distribution:

    Mode | Score range | Moves placed

    Omakase | 12,532 to 22,413 | 172 to 267

    Menu | 20,992 to 46,395 | 171 to 306

  With the earlier criterion (legend = 30,000 points), an auto-play with no strategy reached the top rank. So I moved the thresholds above that (0 / 4,000 / 10,000 / 18,000 / 30,000 / 50,000 / 85,000). Menu scores come out about 1.8 times higher, so I stretched them by the same ratio. Both auto-plays now stop at “journeyman,” and from head chef up, it depends on skill.

  The next day I ran 120 games and measured the distribution (apprentice 6%, journeyman 32%, head chef 40%, master 14%, legend 8%). Auto-play is better than people, so it does not fall into the bottom two ranks. Those two are a layout meant to matter when humans play.

## I also changed how chains are shown

- I added the chain bonus to Omakase as well. Under the same conditions, the score nearly doubles.

- A 3-chain happened more than 20 times in a game and had no value. I now show the center-screen notice from 4-chain (2- and 3-chains only get floating text and sound).

## What I learned

> Even if you cannot listen, you can measure.

- Decide with numbers what you cannot decide by feel. Both the audio balance and the ranks were built on measurements.

- Being measurable is different from being verified. A waveform tells me whether there is distortion and the order of loudness. It does not tell me whether it is pleasant.

- Test a “criterion” against something that should break it. A criterion that let a strategy-less auto-play reach the top rank was not working as a criterion.

  The numbers in this article come from my commit record (September 7 and 8, 2026). The sizes of the pieces changed after those days (the conger eel article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/anago/), in Japanese), so the current score ranges and thresholds differ from what is written here.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/webaudio/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# Making a ranking server use only half of the free tier: from 5 calls to 2

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/ranking-free-tier/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of Sushi Stack / October 2026

  Sushi Stack (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/) has an online ranking. It runs on Cloudflare Workers and D1 (a database), within the free tier. I halved how much of the free tier this ranking server uses. What I counted and what I changed are written with the measured values in my commits.

## The free tier is shared

  Cloudflare’s free tier is per account. All Workers and D1 databases in the account share it. If other projects live there too, it is best to keep the ranking thin. My commit also says that from September 1, 2026, D1 really refuses queries at this limit. The limit is on “rows read,” 5 million a day.

## What happens when one person plays

  For the most ordinary flow, “one person plays once, submits a score, and views the ranking once,” I counted calls to the server and rows read. I counted by actually running the Worker with node:sqlite in place of D1.

     | Before | After

    Calls | 5 | 2

    Rows read | 421 | 221

    Rows written | 1 | 1

  The ceiling is rows read. Dividing 5 million rows by the rows per person gives how many people can play within the free tier. Before: 5,000,000 ÷ 421 ≈ 11,876 people (the commit says “about 11,000,” a little off from the division). After: 5,000,000 ÷ 221 ≈ 22,624 people (about 22,000 in the commit). By either count, the daily ceiling roughly doubled.

## Two changes

### 1. Count the rank on the server

  Before, the game fetched the top-100 list twice and looked for itself in it. I changed it so the server counts the rank and returns it. The counting is a COUNT that cuts off after a fixed number of top rows (SCAN). The higher you are, the fewer rows are read.

### 2. Remove the preflight call

  I made /submit, which sends the score, accept text/plain. The content is still JSON. But when sent with this type, the browser does not send the preflight check call (OPTIONS). One call is gone.

  The shared database on the artifact side has no mechanism to count rank. That side still counts in the game as before. Only when submit returns null does it fetch the list.

## What I verified

- Submitting two people to an empty ranking gives 1st and 2nd.

- In a ranking of 500 people, the server-counted rank (including “outside the top 100”) comes out correctly.

- Tampered score submissions are still rejected as before, in both Japanese and English.

## What I learned

> What you count is not money but calls and rows.

- A free-tier limit is the one that runs out first. Here it was rows read, not the number of calls.

- Measure one “ordinary play.” I could say “half” because I fixed one flow of a person playing and counted it.

- The same free-tier story is in the 10-second stopwatch ranking article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/stopwatch-rank/) (in Japanese). There it was the number of writes (1,000 a day on KV).

  The numbers in this article come from my commit record (September 7, 2026). The free-tier limits (such as 5 million rows a day) are as stated in the commit.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/ranking-free-tier/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# Four things that stopped my iOS app before App Review: iPad screenshots, ITMS-91064, account deletion, reporting posts

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/torecadash-review/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of Torecadash / October 2026

  When I tried to submit my iOS app Torecadash to App Review, I was stopped before submitting several times: things caught by Apple’s automated checks, things caught on the submission screen, and things I found by checking against the guidelines. From my commit record, here are four.

  The result of review is not included in this article.

## 1. I was asked for iPad screenshots

  When I tried to submit for review in App Store Connect, it stopped me with “You must upload a screenshot for 13-inch iPad displays.” The project settings had been iPhone and iPad (1,2) from the beginning.

  But there was no sign that I had built it with iPad in mind. Device checks and layout adjustments were all on iPhone. Submitting it unverified as “iPad supported” was a risk, so I changed it to iPhone only (1).

## 2. “Invalid Binary” in the automated check (ITMS-91064)

  Build 877 was rejected by Apple’s automated review as an “invalid binary.” The cause was in the privacy manifest (PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy): I had written that it tracks (NSPrivacyTracking=true), but the list of tracking domains (NSPrivacyTrackingDomains) was empty. Apple’s check rejects this combination as a contradiction.

  The app shows AdMob ads (banner, native, app-open) personalized after ATT consent. It does track, so “true” was correct. What needed fixing was the empty domain list. But Google does not publish an official list of domains for AdMob. So I added widely used ad-serving domains (googlesyndication.com, googleadservices.com, doubleclick.net, google.com). I confirmed that a Release build passes.

## 3. Account deletion (Guideline 5.1.1(v))

  An app that lets you create an account must let you delete it from within the app. The deletion also removes the user’s map posts (sighting reports) and their related data (owner, reports, flags, thanks). For people signed in with Apple, the app re-authenticates with Apple, then deletes on the server and revokes the token. I also matched the explanation in the settings screen and the privacy policy to the real behavior.

  In addition, deleting the account does not cancel a subscription. I added this to the settings text and to the deletion confirmation screen (as a review requirement).

## 4. User-generated posts (Guideline 1.2)

  Map posts can be written freely by users. Until then there were only format checks such as length and coordinate range, and nothing that rejected by content. So I added a simple banned-word check to three free-text fields (shop name, product name, note). If it matches, the post is created but starts in a pending-review state.

  One more thing. Reports of posts would go unnoticed unless I myself remembered the admin screen’s URL and opened it. I added the count of items pending review to my daily operations notice so they are not overlooked.

## What I learned

> Review is not something you fail after submitting; half of it is found by checking before you submit.

- Of the four, two (iPad, ITMS-91064) were stopped by a machine. The other two (deletion, posts) I found by reading the guidelines and checking myself.

- “Do not submit what is unverified” was faster and safer than “support everything” (the iPad case).

  This article is written from my commit record (September 16 to October 6, 2026).

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/torecadash-review/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# I re-measured a “nothing can be done” assumption and scraping cost dropped to one eighth

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/scrape-cost/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of Torecadash / October 2026

  My iOS app Torecadash regularly visits sales pages on online shops and collects lottery and first-come sale information. Pages are fetched through an external service (Scrape.do), and each fetch setting uses a different number of credits. For one site, I re-measured something I had accepted as “it cannot be helped,” and it became 3 times faster using about one eighth of the credits. This is from my commit record.

  This is a development log of the app. I do not write amounts of money, only numbers of credits.

## The reason for “it cannot be helped” was cost

  I thought the fetch interval for two sites, AEON Style Online and Amiami, could not be shortened. The reason was that fetching was expensive. In other words, a conclusion based on an old unit price. I decided to measure it again.

## Fetching the same page with three settings

  There are three levels of fetch settings: a plain fetch (1 credit), render in a browser and then fetch (render, 5 credits), and render through a stronger route (super + render, 25 credits). I fetched AEON’s list page with all three and compared contents, two pages three times each.

    Setting | Credits | Size (bytes) | Products | Prices

    Plain | 1 | 649,734 | 20 | 25

    render | 5 | 663,026 | 20 | 25

    super + render | 25 | 669,510 | 20 | 25

  All three returned exactly the same products and prices. So rendering was a complete waste. I had been paying 25 credits for something that 1 credit was enough for.

## The fix

- Try the cheap setting first. For AEON, fetch plainly first. Only when the “access is busy” page that appears at the start of a first-come sale comes back does it escalate automatically to a stronger setting.

- Interval from 15 minutes to 5 minutes. Every 5 minutes is 288 times a day. For 2 pages, that is 576 credits. Before, it was about 4,600 credits a day (as stated in the commit). It is 3 times faster and uses about one eighth.

- I applied the same measured result to Amiami. Removing rendering took one fetch from 5 credits to 1, saving about 1,200 credits a day.

  But for Amiami I kept the interval at 15 minutes. That day it had hit timeouts twice, and one run took 284 seconds. Fetching overall was getting crowded, so I decided not to touch it. What I measured was “is rendering needed,” not “is it safe to shorten the interval.”

## What I learned

> When was the number behind “it cannot be helped” measured?

- Re-measure old conclusions. Unit prices, settings and how sites are built all change. “AEON cannot be helped” turned out not to be true when measured.

- Strong settings tend to get added “just in case.” Whether they are needed can be seen by comparing results. If the results are the same, the cheaper one is enough.

- When you fix one thing, check the other conditions. The same measurement fixed Amiami’s setting, but I left its interval because of a separate issue (timeouts).

  The numbers in this article come from my commit record (September 7, 2026). “4,600” is as written in the commit and is a little off from the calculation of 25 credits × 2 pages × 96 runs (every 15 minutes) = 4,800.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/scrape-cost/).

# A bulk update hit “all articles”: count before you write, and break your tests to prove they work

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/bulk-accident/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of Torecadash / October 2026

  In my iOS app Torecadash, a new job that fixes article status in bulk hit every article, including ones I never meant to target, the first time I ran it. 18 items from other sites were wrongly restored to visible. This is how I fixed the accident, and how I checked that the test I built afterward to close the same hole actually works, from my hand-over notes.

  This is a development log of the app.

## What the job was for

  The app has a “price gate” that checks whether a listing’s price is reasonable (I wrote about it in another article (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/fail-open/)). Among articles hidden by this gate only because of price, I added a job that restores those that were actually correct and had been hidden because of a product mix-up. The condition for restoring is “the correct product’s list price matches the listing price.”

## The accident: it hit all articles

  At first this job hit all articles without distinguishing the source. As a result, 18 articles from other sites (Amazon, Card Labo, Ministop and others) were restored to visible. They should have stayed hidden.

  There were two fixes.

- Narrow the scope. I limited the job to articles from that source only (those whose site identifier starts with that source).

- Put back what I had restored. I identified the 18 wrongly restored articles from the status history (statusHistory) and put them back to their original state (hidden, rejected by price).

  But there was something I could not get back for these 18. The job had overwritten the original list-price field with the listing price. The value stays as the listing price.

  The cause was that I had not counted the target range before writing. My notes say so: “count the target range before a bulk write.”

## Building tests to close the same hole

  To make sure the problems found in that day’s inspection (wrong splitting of 9-pack sets, single cards slipping in, non-card products slipping in) never happen again, I built tests: 66 cases in catalog-guards.test.js, and all six test files together can be run in one procedure (run-all.sh).

  I also added warnings to my daily operations notice: when the miss rate of matching falls below the criteria (Chusen Zukan 80%, Pokechu 75%, X roundup 75%), when nothing has run for 30 hours, and when single cards or non-card names appear in the product list. The judgments are pure functions with no side effects, so once things are fixed, the warning disappears by itself on the next run.

## Breaking it to check that the tests work

  You cannot tell whether a test works just by writing it. A test that always passes may protect nothing. So I took a copy of the production code and removed its rules one at a time to confirm the tests fail.

- Remove one rule (break it).

- Run the tests.

- If they fail, the test is protecting that rule.

  With this procedure, I tried 6 kinds of modification, and the tests failed for all 6 (all were detected).

  I also wrote down an operating rule: if I touch functions/index.js, I always run all the tests before deploying.

## What I learned

> Count before a bulk write. Break the test to prove it.

- Before writing, count “how many it will hit.” If you run it without a preview, you notice the range was wrong only after it has finished writing.

- Write in a form you can undo. I could restore the 18 because I could identify them from the history. The overwritten field, though, cannot be restored.

- Prefer a test that fails when broken to a test that passes. Only after removing a rule and seeing it fail can I trust the test.

  This article is written from my hand-over notes (§272) (October 7, 2026). The counts are as written in the notes.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/bulk-accident/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# Python splitlines() breaks JSONL: the culprit was U+2028, an invisible line separator

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/u2028/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of the Anime Type Quiz / October 2026

  While building the data for the Anime Type Quiz (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/shindananime/), I fixed a bug where the JSON broke. The cause was splitlines(), a perfectly ordinary function.

## What broke

  The quiz data comes from Filmarks and is stored in data/filmarks_works.jsonl. JSONL puts one JSON object per line, and you read it by splitting into lines and passing each one to json.loads. In Python I had first written:

  for line in path.read_text(encoding='utf-8').splitlines():
    r = json.loads(line)
  But when a synopsis contained U+2028 (LINE SEPARATOR), that line was split in the middle, and json.loads was handed JSON that ended inside a string, and failed.

## What U+2028 is

  U+2028 is a Unicode character meaning “line separator.” It looks almost like a newline. In JSON, it is valid to put it raw inside a string, and the writing side (json.dumps(..., ensure_ascii=False)) outputs it as is.

  The problem was on the reading side. Python’s str.splitlines() splits not only on \n but also on Unicode line boundaries such as U+2028. split('\n') splits only on \n.

  s = json.dumps({"a": "x\u2028y"}, ensure_ascii=False)
len(s.splitlines())   # 2  (one line splits in two)
len(s.split('\n'))    # 1
  Passing each half to json.loads raises Unterminated string. The short example above reproduces exactly that.

## The numbers in the real data

  I recounted both ways on the current data file.

    How it is split | Number of lines

    split('\n') (real newlines only) | 7,247

    splitlines() | 7,255

  The difference is 8. Counting U+2028 in the file gave exactly 8, in the lines of 2 works. Two works out of 7,247, under 0.03%, were enough to make the whole file unreadable.

## The fix

  One line:

  - for line in path.read_text(encoding='utf-8').splitlines():
+ for line in path.read_text(encoding='utf-8').split('\n'):
  I left the reason in a comment so that my future self would not be puzzled: when making JSONL, the only line separator is \n, so reading should split on \n only.

## Why it is hard to notice

- You cannot see it. Depending on the editor, U+2028 looks like a newline or a space. Staring at the synopsis will not find it.

- It is rare. 2 of 7,247 works. While you test with a small sample, it may never show up. It is the kind of bug that appears only once you have fetched everything.

- The writer is correct. Nothing written is wrong as JSON. What broke it was the reader’s assumption about what a “line” is.

## One more fix from the same day

  The same commit fixed another bug caused by characters that look alike but are different. When matching titles, Annict’s ＜物語＞ (full-width angle brackets) and Filmarks’s 〈物語〉 (Japanese angle brackets) did not match even though they were the same work. NFKC normalization turns the full-width ＜＞ into half-width, but 〈〉 stays as it is, so I removed both from the comparison string.

  Both are the same lesson: characters are not always what they look like.

## What I learned

> A function I used “for newlines” had a wider idea of newlines than I assumed.
  When reading JSONL, do not use splitlines(). Split on the character the writer used as the separator (\n), or use for line in f:, which splits only on \n. I am writing it here for the next time the data grows.

  The numbers in this article come from recounting the data file on October 7, 2026.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/u2028/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

# “It should shrink” was wrong twice: cutting AI calls and what I measured afterward

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/torecadash-ai/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of Torecadash / October 2026

  My iOS app Torecadash collects information on reservations, lotteries and first-come sales of trading cards (Pokémon, Yu-Gi-Oh!, One Piece) and notifies users. It uses an AI (Gemini) to decide “which product an article is about.” While trying to reduce calls to that AI, things I had written down as “it should shrink” were wrong twice. In order, with the numbers left in my commits:

  This is a development log of the app.

## What I ask the AI

  The article title (for example “30th CELEBRATION Premium Deck Set Espeon”) is matched against a list of recent product candidates (the latest 60), and the AI answers which product it is. One call is about 3,083 tokens, of which about 1,800 were the same fixed instruction text every time.

## First: if the title is exactly a product name, no need to ask

  If a title matches a known product name exactly, there is no need to ask the AI. When I added this “short circuit,” 43% of X monitoring matched in real data. There were 0 disagreements (the short circuit’s answer differing from the AI’s). So I recorded that it should cut about 45%.

  But 90 minutes after deployment, the short circuit had not fired even once. Recounting, it looked like this:

    Source | Could short-circuit | Already free before | Newly saved

    X monitoring | 813 | 768 | 45 (2%)

    Others | 419 | 188 | 231 (32%)

  Before this step, there was an already free path that checks against the official catalog. Most articles that could be short-circuited were already settled there. Adding up what is newly saved, it is about 39 calls a day, about 4.5% of the total. Not 45%, but 4.5%.

> The share a rule applies to and the calls it actually removes are different things.
  If there is a free path before it, you have to count the difference. That is what the lessons field in my commit says. The logic itself was correct and safe, so I kept it. But as an AI reduction, it was small.

## Second: ask in batches

  The next main idea was to combine several articles into one call, because the fixed instruction text is then paid only once. Articles of the same genre share “the latest 60,” so the merged candidate list barely grows.

  In the design I took care of two things.

- Do not add waiting time. In measurement, a short window of a few hundred milliseconds could not batch anything (only 12 times in 24 hours did articles arrive in the same second). But waiting a few minutes would slow X monitoring’s rounds by 5 times. So I chose to “send the moment every still-running article has come to wait.” The safety cap is 20 seconds.

- Do not lose accuracy. When batched, the candidate list becomes the union for everyone, so an article can see other articles’ candidates. So the answer is returned as a real product ID, and I always verify that it is among that article’s own candidates. If not, I do not accept it. For an article with a missing reply, I ask again for that one alone.

  I measured the effect by reconstructing candidate lists from the real articles of the last two days (characters sent).

    Batch size | One by one | Batched | Reduction

    2 | 21,762 | 13,427 | −38%

    3 | 32,673 | 14,964 | −54%

    4 | 43,571 | 16,192 | −63%

    6 | 65,000 | 17,729 | −73%

## Third: deployed, and it never batched once

  Six hours after deployment, there were 47 product-matching calls and 0 batches. Although 2 to 7 calls came in the same minute, each was asked one at a time.

  The cause was the “send condition.” I had checked “number waiting ≥ number of unfinished jobs (pending),” but jobs that had come to wait were also counted in pending. X monitoring runs 32 accounts at once. If 31 had already finished, pending was 1. The moment the last one came to wait, the condition held and it was sent immediately as a single item.

  The fix was to check “are there zero jobs that have not even come to wait yet.” When the number completely finished plus the number now waiting reaches the total, send. I also shortened the safety cap from 20 seconds to 6 seconds. If only one item comes, waiting 20 seconds every time would be longer than one X monitoring run (17.8 seconds measured) and delay the rounds.

  During this check, the first short circuit was also reviewed. In 6 hours, 28 of 47 calls (60%) were handled without calling the AI. The short circuit was working correctly.

## What I learned

- Do not write the “share it applies to” as the amount saved. If there is a free path before it, only the difference is saved.

- Deploying does not mean it ran. “0 batches” was found because I recounted. If I had decided in advance that a log should say “batched,” I would have noticed sooner.

- The three numbers (4.5%, −38 to 73%, 60%) are all not what I first estimated. They are numbers re-measured on real data after deployment.

  The numbers in this article come from my commit record (September 4 and 5, 2026). I do not write amounts of money.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/torecadash-ai/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)

URL: https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/shindan12/

# What changes when an anime quiz goes from 50 questions to 12?

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/shindan12/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of the Anime Type Diagnosis / October 2026

  The Hardcore Anime Type Diagnosis (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/shindananime/) has 50 questions in total. People said it was long, so I made it possible to get a result from just the first 12 questions. The remaining 38 are for those who want to answer them.

  But the result must change a bit by being shorter. I wanted to know how much with numbers, not feelings.

## How the 12 were chosen

  The quiz measures taste on 6 axes (worldview, aftertaste, structure, subtaste, visuals, viewing style). The 12-question version takes 2 questions from each axis, 12 in total. The calculation that produces the result is the same as with 50; unanswered questions are simply not counted.

  The 50 questions are 18 on the 6 axes, 2 on image quality and era, and 30 on taste elements (romance, horror, robots and so on). The 12-question version does not ask the last two (era and taste elements), so they do not affect the ordering of titles.

## How I measured: 1,000 synthetic respondents

  I cannot quickly have real people answer both 12 and 50 questions. So I used synthetic respondents. I say this up front: the numbers below are not the results of real people.

- For each respondent, I draw a “true taste” as a random number from −1 to +1 for the 6 axes, era, and 30 taste elements.

- Each answer is that “true taste” plus noise, rounded to 5 levels (leans A, slightly A, neither, slightly B, leans B).

- These answers are run through the same calculation as the real app (logic.js), once using only 12 questions and once using all 50.

  I do not know the size of the noise. People’s answers wobble even in the same mood, so I measured with three values: small (0.3), medium (0.5) and large (0.8). The titles used are the 6,074 with enough clues on the axes.

## The type mostly matches even with 12

  First, whether the type code (6 letters) is the same with 12 and 50 questions.

    Answer noise | All 6 letters match | Match per letter

    Small (0.3) | 75.6% | 94.7 to 96.1%

    Medium (0.5) | 60.8% | 90.9 to 93.7%

    Large (0.8) | 43.2% | 85.5 to 87.6%

  Looking letter by letter, even with medium noise more than 90% fall on the same side. Matching all 6 letters gets harder because you have to be right six times in a row. Even with 90% per letter, six in a row is a little over half.

## The single “title of fate” changes a lot

  Next, the “title of fate” the quiz shows at the end. It is one pick out of 6,074 titles, so the situation is different.

    Answer noise | Same single title | Any of the top 3 in common

    Small (0.3) | 21.7% | 63.4%

    Medium (0.5) | 15.7% | 52.7%

    Large (0.8) | 12.4% | 39.9%

  The title shown with 12 questions comes first with 50 questions for about 1 person in 5 to 8. With medium noise, about half have something in common in the top 3.

## At which stage does it change?

  I checked whether the reason is only “the 30 taste-element questions.” Between 12 and 50, I inserted 18 questions on the 6 axes only (no taste elements or era) and compared the single title (medium noise, 600 respondents).

    Compared | Same single title

    12 and 18 (axes only) | 33.8%

    18 and 50 | 27.5%

    12 and 50 | 15.0%

  Even just adding 6 axis questions before adding taste elements changes the single title for 2 in 3 people. When choosing one out of 6,000, a small difference in input reshuffles the order. It was not that “taste elements are doing harm.”

## Is 50 questions really closer to the right answer?

  In this setup I know the “true taste,” so the one title chosen from it can be treated as the correct answer. Do 12 and 50 get closer to it (medium noise)?

     | Same as the correct title | In the correct top 3

    12 questions | 8.2% | 14.9%

    50 questions | 14.3% | 28.5%

  50 questions is about 1.7 to 1.9 times closer to the correct answer. With small noise, the difference is 17.9% to 29.0% (single title) and 29.0% to 52.6% (top 3). The remaining 38 questions were not wasted. But even with 50, hitting the exact single title is a little over one in ten.

## Weak points of this measurement

- The respondents are synthetic. Real people’s tastes are not scattered like random numbers, and they are noisy in different ways.

- The noise size is a placeholder. That is why I measured with three values; I do not know the true one.

- The “correct answer” is correct on the quiz’s own yardstick. Whether it is something a person would really love is not measured.

- What I measured is “is it the same,” not “is it fun.”

## What I learned

> The type is set even when short. The single title of fate wobbles each time you add questions.
  The current design of giving a result at 12 questions and making the rest optional does not contradict these numbers. If you only want to know your type, 12 questions are enough, and only those who want a more accurate single title need continue. I think the result screen should say it that way.

  What I really want to check is real people’s answers: showing the same person the 12-question and the 50-question result and asking which feels right. If I get that far, I will write it in the next record.

  The measuring script is in the quiz’s repository (random numbers are fixed, so the same numbers can be reproduced).

  Take the quiz (https://koshinstudio.com/app/shindananime/en/)About the quiz (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/shindananime/)

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/shindan12/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)


---

URL: https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/sushi-measure/

# “The pile settles at 89%” was wrong: my measurement was what was wrong

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/sushi-measure/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of Sushi Stack / October 2026

  Sushi Stack (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/) is a falling-block puzzle where you bump the same toppings together to merge them and grow them until the tub is full. While adjusting balance, I realized my own measurement result had been wrong. What was wrong, how I found it, and how I fixed it are written with the numbers in my commits.

  The numbers in this article are as of September 7, 2026. After this, the sizes of the pieces were scaled by 0.8 across the board, and changed again on September 10 (the kinds of falling pieces and the shape of the tub) (written in the conger eel article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/anago/), in Japanese). They differ from today’s numbers.

## “It settles at 89%” was wrong

  My first measurement said “the pile settles at 89% of the tub’s height.” That would mean you can stack without overflowing and never lose.

  When I measured again, this was an illusion from counting the falling piece. The real pile kept rising. But it rose so slowly that even after dropping 240 pieces, only a third of the tub was filled. “A game you cannot lose” did not mean safe. It meant the pile does not grow enough to lose.

## Three causes

  The commit splits the causes into three. Each was confirmed by measurement before I removed it.

### 1. The size ladder went backward in three places

  When I lined up the sizes by the radius of a circle of the same area (equivalent radius), in three places the merged piece was smaller than the one before.

- Tamago was smaller than shari

- Otoro was smaller than uni

- Anago was smaller than otoro

  Merging produced a smaller piece than before. On the busiest path, “shari → tamago,” more than half of what I dropped vanished on the spot. So I rebuilt it as a monotonically increasing ladder with a size ratio of 1.19.

### 2. The pieces were too small for the tub

  I had used the 9:16 portrait tub directly as the drop area, so it was a vertical pit rather than a real sushi tub. I made the tub shallow enough to fit in the lower half of the screen, and drew a noren curtain (with the game name) and a plank wall in the empty space above. The deadline (past it, you lose) became the rim of the tub itself.

### 3. Big pieces fell through the floor

  The physical thickness of the walls and floor was only 12, the same as how it looked, so heavier pieces tunneled through the single plank and fell out of the tub. I made the thickness 80, and also rounded the position for pieces born from a merge that sink into a wall. I also added a cleanup for spilled pieces (sweepStrays).

## The numbers after the fix

    What I measured | Before | After

    How full the tub is after dropping 240 | about a third | —

    Drops until game over | not reached | 385 (rank: journeyman)

    Score (same conditions) | 7,298 | 10,658

  The pile moves up and down in front of the rim and opens up at once with a big merge. The tension this kind of game should have appeared. The score rose because the pieces that had been falling through and vanishing came back. I verified that 9:16 holds from iPhone SE to 15 Pro Max, in landscape and on desktop, that there is no overflow or errors, and that 60 fps holds with a full tub.

## What I learned

> What you measure is not necessarily what you want to know.
  The first “89%” counted the falling piece, so it was not measuring “the height of the pile.” I want to record that when a measurement looks too good, it is better to doubt what is being counted than the number itself. After the fix, I measured the numbers again with the same method as the conger eel article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/anago/) (hundreds of auto-played games).

  The numbers in this article come from my commit record (September 7, 2026).

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/sushi-measure/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)


---

URL: https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/adgap/

# Measuring the gap between ads in time, not in plays

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/adgap/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of Sushi Stack / October 2026

  Sushi Stack has a mechanism that can insert one ad at the break between one game and the next. At first I set it to “one ad per 5 plays,” and the next day I changed it to count time, not plays. This is the reason and a record of how it behaves.

  This site does not show ads yet (the ad loader is left empty). This is about a mechanism I built ahead of time for when ads are turned on.

## The first rule: one ad per 5 plays

  In the first version on September 7, an ad was inserted before “one more game” every 5 plays, and never on the first play. The idea was to skip the first game to protect the first impression. The game detects which of CrazyGames, Poki or Google it runs on, uses that SDK if there is one, and passes through if there is none.

## Why it did not fit

  The next day, September 8, I dropped this counting. The commit gives two reasons.

- If one game is long, ads never appear. A game can last 30 minutes, so the 5th play comes 2.5 hours later. Almost nobody plays that long.

- If games end quickly, ads appear one after another. After several quick losses, several ads show up within minutes.

  Both come from counting plays. What bothers a player is not the number of ads but the time between ads. So I changed what I count to time.

## The rule after the change

- No ad on the first game (as before).

- For someone who has not seen an ad yet, one ad at the break after the second game.

- After that, only when at least 7 minutes have passed since the last ad, one ad at the next break.

  The time of the last ad is remembered in the browser (localStorage). Nothing is sent to a server. The behavior I checked:

    Situation | Ad

    First play | None

    Second play (no ad shown yet) | Shown

    1 minute / 6 minutes since the last ad | None

    8 minutes since the last ad | Shown

    After a long game (40 minutes) | Shown

  For the earlier version (one ad per 5 plays), I ran 7 games with a fake CrazyGames SDK and confirmed that “an ad appears once after the 5th game” and that “with no SDK, none appears and there are zero errors.” For the time-based version too, I checked that the screen always returns after an ad ends.

## What I noticed while writing

  How I chose “7 minutes” is not in the commit. I will be honest: the reason is not recorded.

  What bothers me most is the length of a game. The commit’s “a game can take 30 minutes” was later, in the September 10 commit, written as “median 7.5 minutes in auto-play, 30 minutes for a human.” So 30 minutes is a guess, not a measured number. The 7.5 minutes of auto-play (7.7 minutes in the conger eel article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/anago/), in Japanese) is the measured one.

  And on September 10 a game became half as long, so the earlier table is out of date. Recalculating (I put an auto-play game at half of 7.7 minutes, about 3.8 minutes):

    Length of one game | One per 5 plays (old) | One per 7 minutes (new)

    About 3.8 min (auto-play, after halving) | One per about 19 min | About one per 2 games

    About 15 min (half of “30 for a human”) | One per about 75 min | Every game

  I still have not measured how long a game takes a person. Whether 7 minutes is long or short cannot be decided without that. Measuring the length of a game comes before turning ads on.

## What I learned

> Counting plays makes ad frequency swing with how people play. Counting time does not.
  But changing to time did not make the frequency right. My current conclusion is that whether 7 minutes is long or short cannot be decided until I know how long a game takes a person. When I am ready to turn ads on, I will measure that first.

  This is the English version of the original Japanese article (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/adgap/).

  More in English

- All English pages (https://koshinstudio.com/en/)


---

URL: https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/anago/

# The conger eel was too big: finding why a merge puzzle’s last piece was out of reach

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/notes/anago/)

Written by Koshin (https://koshinstudio.com/en/about/#operator) (web engineer and app engineer) · published 2026-10-09
Development log of Sushi Stack / September 2026

  Added on October 8, 2026. The numbers in this article are from the September 8 version. On September 10 I changed the sizes and the falling pieces once more (see “Afterward” at the bottom).

  After finishing Sushi Stack (https://koshinstudio.com/works/sushitsumu/), one thing bothered me: I could never reach the last piece, the golden sushi tub.

  However many times I played, I rarely even saw the spiny lobster before it. My feeling was “the conger eel is too big.” But if you tweak sizes by feel, something else usually breaks. I decided to measure first.

## Building a way to measure

  The game is a single HTML file, and time is driven by requestAnimationFrame. As it is, a game takes minutes, so I swapped in my own clock. I intercept requestAnimationFrame and setTimeout and advance them at any speed I like. If I also empty the drawing code, a game finishes in about 2 seconds.

  After that I wrote a bot of modest skill — merge first, and wait until the pile settles before placing — and let it run.

## What a hundred games showed

  First, a hundred games as it was.

  score   min 12,337 / median 21,664 / max 44,622
best piece reached   otoro 43 games  anago 52  spiny lobster 4  golden tub 0
  Zero for the golden tub. So where does it get stuck? Lining up the yield for moving up one tier (the share of times two of the lower piece became one of the next) made it clear.

    Merge | Yield

    Salmon → tuna | 94.0%

    Tuna → ikura gunkan | 91.9%

    Ikura gunkan → uni gunkan | 86.9%

    Uni gunkan → otoro | 71.4%

    Otoro → anago | 55.2%

    Anago → spiny lobster | 13.1%

    Spiny lobster → golden tub | 0.0%

  It falls gently and then there is a cliff at the anago. Of the 61 anago made, 53 (87%) were still sitting on the final board. Only 8 made it to a merge.

## The conger eel really was off

  Lining up the dimensions made it obvious at a glance. The inner width of the tub is 336.

    Piece | Width | Height | Width / inner | Growth from previous

    Otoro | 149 | 83 | 44% | ×1.34

    Anago | 247 | 71 | 74% | ×1.66

    Spiny lobster | 230 | 107 | 68% | ×0.93

    Golden tub | 210 | 210 | 62% | ×0.91

  The anago was the widest piece in the game. Wider than the spiny lobster after it, and wider than the final golden tub. Its width growth is 1.66 where other tiers are 1.0 to 1.34.

  As a result, when one anago lies down, the gap left beside it is 336 − 247 = 89. Only up to salmon (width 85) fits there; neither uni nor otoro. The anago spanned the tub and blocked the road ahead.

  By the way, the ladder of areas was clean. Every tier was a constant “0.70 to 0.71 times the two pieces below.” Only the order of widths was broken.

## Fix it, but measure first

  I made only the width 4/5 (247 → 198) and ran another hundred games.

     | Median | Max | Anago | Spiny lobster | Anago → lobster yield

    247 × 71 (original) | 21,664 | 44,622 | 61 | 4 | 13.1%

    198 × 71 | 24,858 | 47,392 | 79 | 12 | 30.4%

    205 × 85 (keep the area) | 25,149 | 36,350 | 33 | 1 | 6.1%

  The third row was interesting. The version that got thinner while keeping its area made the late game not move at all. What mattered was not “thin” itself but that the anago no longer spanned the tub and big pieces could sit beside it.

## Still, the golden tub is out of reach

  Spiny lobsters appeared three times as often. But the golden tub was still zero. Here another wall showed up.

  The falling pieces were only three kinds: shari, tamago and shrimp. After subtracting gari, each drop is only 2.217 shari-equivalents. Meanwhile:

    To make | In shari | Drops needed with zero waste

    1 anago | 256 | 115

    1 spiny lobster | 512 | 231

    1 golden tub | 1,024 | 462

  The measured number of drops was a median of 280 and 426 at most. Even with zero waste, there were not enough moves. 231 drops for a spiny lobster is right at the border, which matches the measured 12 in a hundred.

## The real cause: the sushi was too big

  In Suika Game some people make “twin watermelons.” That works because the last fruit is small enough compared with the box. What about mine?

  With one golden tub in place, I must make a second spiny lobster
  golden tub 210 + lobster 107 + lobster 107 = 424px  >  usable height 302px
  side by side: lobster 230 × 2 = 460px               >  inner width 336px
  It fits neither vertically nor horizontally. This is not a matter of luck or skill: there is no gap for it to fit in.

  So I tried scaling all the pieces by 0.8 across the board. The diameter of the golden tub goes from 210 to 168, exactly half of the tub’s inner width of 336.

     | Median | Max | Reach golden tub | Reach lobster | One game

    Original size | 24,858 | 47,392 | 0 / 100 games | 12% | 3.7 min

    0.8x | 58,741 | 103,630 | 7% | 65% | 7.7 min

  At last the road was open. The spiny lobster is reached nearly every game, and the golden tub appears once in a dozen or so. The twin never appeared in sixty games, which is not a failure; it is probably the right state. It became a legend within reach.

## I redrew the ranks too

  Scores came out 2.4 times higher, so I had to redo all the rank thresholds. For the top rank, matching the fact that games reaching the golden tub all scored 86,000 or more, I set 85,000. The number is the same as before but its meaning changed. Before, it was a decoration nobody could reach; now it is “make the golden tub and you are a legend.”

## I measured again after release

  With the fixed version, using the same contents as what is published, I ran three hundred games again. The shape I saw at 100 games continues.

    Measured | 300 games

    Median score | 59,305

    Highest score | 163,426

    Reached grilled anago | 99%

    Reached spiny lobster | 73%

    Reached golden sushi tub | 10% (31 games)

    Two golden tubs in one game | 0

    Length of one game (median) | 7.7 min

    Pieces placed (median) | 589

    Longest chain | 10

  The bot is tools/sim/bot.js. It merges first and waits for the pile to settle before placing. A human can play better or worse, but it was enough to compare before and after with the same yardstick.

## What I learned

> My feeling was right. But the cause was not where I thought.
  The feeling that “the anago is too big” was correct. But thinning only the anago did not move the late game, and the real cause was that all of the sushi was too big for the tub. If I had suspected and fixed one place, I probably would never have gotten there.

  Collecting statistics from three hundred games took about ten minutes in total. It was much faster and more reliable than tweaking by feel three times and checking.

## Afterward (September 10): I changed it again

  After this article, I submitted the game to CrazyGames and was rejected (details in another article (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/crazygames/)). What I reconsidered was that tension in the tub did not happen even once in the few minutes of review. The commit says: measured with auto-play, one game is a median of 594 moves, 7.5 minutes. 30 minutes for a human. The tub never fills, and dangerous moments never come.

  I left each tier’s dimensions and area ratios alone and changed only places where I could fix without losing the feeling of “growing as you merge.” I chose them by measuring with auto-play.

- Falling pieces from 3 kinds to 5. I added salmon and tuna to shari, tamago and shrimp (weights 1:1:2:3:2). More piles up per move and the median went from 594 to 279 moves. The rate of reaching higher tiers also went up.

- The shape of the tub. Rim from 320 to 250, height from 308 to 378. The play area went from 45% to 62% of the screen.

- Spiny lobster and golden tub scaled another 0.89x. The area ratio from anago to spiny lobster alone had jumped to 1.76 and is now 1.40, in line. The leftover when two golden tubs sit side by side went from 0 px to 36 px, and a double golden tub (golden tubs merging) became possible in real play. The logic had been there before but never happened once in 300 games.

  With a game half as long, scores also fell by about 20% (auto-play median from 59,305 to 46,529). I re-took the rank thresholds from quantiles of 60 games and restored the same distribution as before (apprentice 7%, journeyman 28%, head chef 40%, master 17%, legend 8%). I also raised the double-golden-tub reward from 8,000 to 25,000, because merges up to making one golden tub already give about 34,000 points.

  The moves needed for a double golden tub are 275 even with zero waste. Auto-play makes one golden tub in about 2.0 times the ideal, so auto-play cannot reach it (0 in 40 games). It is set up so that only a person who tidies the pile and plays well can reach it.

  The numbers in the “0.8x” table above (median 58,741, 7.7 minutes a game and so on) are from the September 8 version. They differ from the current numbers.

# About

  日本語版 (https://koshinstudio.com/about/)

  Koshin Studio is a place for taking on anything, alone.
Make, try, write. Games, a quiz app and more, with records of how they were made and verified.

## What you can do here

- English hub (https://koshinstudio.com/en/) — games, tools and development logs in English

- Sushi Stack (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/sushitsumu/), Negaeri Shogi (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/negaeri-shogi/), Stop at exactly 10 seconds! (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/stopwatch10/) — free browser games

- Hardcore Anime Type Diagnosis (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/shindananime/) — an anime quiz with 64 types and 6 axes

- Gacha calculators (https://koshinstudio.com/en/calc/gacha/) — rate and pity calculators

## How I work

  Mostly alone, running things on my own machine as I go. Because I do everything from design to art to sound, I can fix what needs fixing on the spot.

  For balance, I always prepare a way to measure. For a game, I let it play itself hundreds of times and look at where it gets stuck in numbers. It is much faster and more reliable than tweaking by feel three times and checking. The process is in a development log (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/anago/).

> My feeling was right.
But the cause was not where I thought.
  No install and no sign-up. It starts right away when you open it in a browser. That is the one thing I try not to break.

## About the operator

  Koshin Studio is run by Koshin (a nickname), alone. I work as a web engineer and an app engineer, and I make all sorts of things. I make and publish browser games, a quiz, and iPhone apps (such as Toreca Dash (https://koshinstudio.com/en/works/torecadash/), available on the App Store). This site carries introductions to what I made, numbers I measured while making it, and records of bugs and how I fixed them.

  The numbers in articles are ones I checked against my own app’s logs, data and source code, or official pages. What I could not confirm, I say I could not confirm. For feedback, corrections, interviews or work enquiries, please use the contact section below.

## How the articles are written, and corrections

  The articles in the development logs are written from real commits (work records) and measured numbers. I follow three rules.

- I write where the numbers come from. At the end of an article I say which record it was written from and when it was measured.

- I write “not verified” when I have not verified. Causes I never found and things I did not confirm on a real device are written as they are.

- I fix mistakes, and say I fixed them. When I learn something later, I add it to the article and change the update date (for example, the conger eel article (https://koshinstudio.com/en/notes/anago/) got an addendum with the numbers after sizes changed).

  If you notice a mistake in an article, please tell me using the contact below.

## Tools I use

- Languages: JavaScript (the main one: games and the site), Python (fonts, image conversion, statistics tools), Swift (iOS apps), plain HTML and CSS written by hand.

- Games: Matter.js for physics, Canvas 2D for drawing every frame instead of using images, Web Audio for synthesized sound.

- The site: GSAP and ScrollTrigger, Lenis, and SVG (I even drew the logo letters myself).

- Hosting: Cloudflare Pages, Workers and D1 for this site and the ranking server, and Firebase for app backends.

- Tooling: Git and GitHub, Playwright (to let games play themselves and to walk the whole site), fontTools, Pillow and Xcode.

  I add a framework only when I need it. This site added GSAP only when it came to thickening the motion. It does not connect to outside CDNs; everything it uses is on my own server, which is fast and unaffected when others go down. Fonts are trimmed to the characters needed instead of pasting a stock font.
